author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Deer Hunting
body:
The deer hunt has proved one of our most successful games.

The deer is a dummy, best made with a wire frame, on which soft hay is wrapped till it is of proper size and shape, then all is covered with open burlap. A few touches of white and black make it very realistic.

If time does not admit of a well-finished deer, one can be made of a sack stuffed with hay, decorated at one end with a smaller sack for head and neck, and set on four thin sticks.

The side of the deer is marked with a large oval, and over the heart is a smaller one.

Bows and arrows only are used to shoot this deer.

A pocketful of corn, peas, or other large grain is now needed for scent. The boy who is the deer for the first hunt takes the dummy under his arm and runs off, getting ten minutes' start, or until he comes back and shouts "ready!" He leaves a trail of corn, dropping two or three grains for every yard and making the trail as crooked as he likes, playing such tricks as a deer would do to baffle his pursuers. Then he hides the deer in any place he fancies, but not among rocks or on the top of a ridge, because in one case many arrows would be broken, and in the other, lost.

The hunters now hunt for this deer just as for a real deer, either following the trail or watching the woods ahead; the best hunters combine the two. If at any time the trail is quite lost the one in charge shouts: "Lost Trail!" After that the one who finds the trail scores two. Anyone giving a false alarm by shouting "Deer" is fined five.

Thus they go till some one finds the deer. He shouts: "_Deer!_" and scores ten for finding it. The others shout: "_Second_," "_Third_," etc., in order of seeing it, but they do not score.

The finder must shoot at the deer with his bow and arrow from the very spot whence he saw it. If he misses, the second hunter may step up five paces, and have his shot. If he misses, the third one goes five, and so on till some one hits the deer, or until the ten-yard limit is reached. If the finder is within ten yards on sighting the deer, and misses his shot, the other hunters go back to the ten-yard limit. Once the deer is hit, all the shooting must be from the exact spot whence the successful shot was fired.

A shot in the big oval is a body wound; that scores five. A shot outside that is a scratch; that scores two. A shot in the small oval or heart is a heart wound; it scores ten, and ends the hunt. Arrows which do not stick do not count, unless it can be proved that they passed right through, in which case they take the highest score that they pierced.

If all the arrows are used, and none in the heart, the deer escapes, and the boy who was deer scores twenty-five.

The one who found the dummy is deer for the next hunt. A clever deer can add greatly to the excitement of the game.

Originally we used paper for scent, but found it bad. It littered the woods; yesterday's trail was confused with that of to-day, etc. Corn proved better, because the birds and the squirrels kept it cleaned up from day to day, and thus the ground was always ready for a fresh start. But the best of all is the hoof mark for the shoe. These iron hoof marks are fast to a pair of shoes, and leave a trail much like a real deer. This has several advantages. It gives the hunter a chance to tell where the trail doubled, and which way the deer was going, It is more realistic, and the boy who can follow this skillfully can follow a living deer. In actual practice it is found well to use a little corn with this on the hard places, a plan quite consistent with realism, as every hunter will recall.

It is strictly forbidden to any hunter to stand in front of the firing line; all must be back of the line on which the shooter stands.

There is no limit to the situations and curious combinations in this hunt. The deer may be left standing or lying. There is no law why it should not be hidden behind a solid tree trunk. The game develops as one follows it. After it has been played for some time with the iron hoof mark as above, the boys grow so skilful on the trail that we can dispense with even the corn. The iron mark like a deer hoof leaves a very realistic "slot" or track, which the more skilful boys readily follow through the woods. A hunt is usually for three, five, or more deer, according to agreement and the result is reckoned by points on the whole chase.
summary: The deer hunt has proved one of our most successful games. The deer is a dummy, best made with a wire frame, on which soft hay is wrapped till it is of proper size and shape, then all is covered with open burlap. A few touches of white and black make it very…

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: The Bear Hunt
body:
This is played by half a dozen or more boys. Each has a club about the size and shape of a baseball club, but made of straw tied around two or three switches and tightly sewn up in burlap.--One big fellow is selected for the bear. He has a school bag tightly strapped on his back, and in that a toy balloon fully blown up. This is his heart. On his neck is a bear-claw necklace of wooden beads and claws. (See cut.)

He has three dens about one hundred yards apart in a triangle. While in his den the bear is safe. If the den is a tree or rock, he is safe while touching it. He is obliged to come out when the chief hunter counts one hundred, and must go the rounds of the three till the hunt is settled.

The object of the hunters is to break the balloon or heart; that is, to kill the bear. He must drop dead when the heart bursts. The hunter who kills him claims the necklace.

But the bear also has a club for defence. Each hunter must wear a hat, and once the bear knocks a hunter's hat off, that one is dead and out of this hunt. He must drop where his hat falls.

Tackling of any kind is forbidden.

The bear wins by killing or putting to flight all the hunters. In this case he keeps the necklace.

The savageness of these big bears is indescribable. Many lives are lost in each hunt, and it has several times happened that the whole party of hunters has been exterminated by some monster of unusual ferocity.

This game has also been developed into a play.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Spearing the Great Sturgeon
body:
This water game is exceedingly popular and is especially good for public exhibition, being spectacular and full of amusement and excitement.

The outfit needed is:

(1) A sturgeon roughly formed of soft wood; it should be about three feet long and nearly a foot thick at the head. It may be made realistic, or a small log pointed at both ends will serve.

(2) Two spears with six-inch steel heads and wooden handles (about three feet long). The points should be sharp, but not the barbs. Sometimes the barbs are omitted altogether. Each head should have an eye to which is attached twenty feet of one-quarter inch rope. On each rope, six feet from the spearhead, is a fathom mark made by tying on a rag or cord.

(3) Two boats with crews. Each crew consists of a spearman, who is captain, and one or two oarsmen or paddlers, of whom the after one is the pilot. All should be expert swimmers or else wear life-belts during the game.

The Game.--Each boat has a base or harbor; this is usually part of the shore opposite that of the enemy; or it obviates all danger of collision if the boats start from the same side. The sturgeon is left by the referee's canoe at a point midway between the bases. At the word "Go!" each boat leaves its base and, making for the sturgeon, tries to spear it, then drag it by the line to his base. When both get their spears into it the contest becomes a tug of war until one of the spears pulls out.

The sturgeon is landed when the prow of the boat that has it in tow touches its proper base, even though the spear of the enemy is then in the fish: or it is landed when the fish itself touches base. The boats change bases after each heat.

Matches are usually for one, three, or five sturgeon. Points are counted only for the landing of the fish, but the referee may give the decision on a foul or a succession of fouls, or the delinquent may be set back one or more boat lengths.

Sometimes the game is played in canoes or boats, with one man as spearman and crew.

_Rules_.--It is _not allowable_ to push the sturgeon into a new position with the spear or paddle before striking.

It is _allowable_ to pull the sturgeon under the boat or pass it around by using the line after spearing.

It is _allowable_ to lay hands on the other boat to prevent a collision, but otherwise it is forbidden to touch the other boat or crew or paddle or spear or line, or to lay hands on the fish, or to touch it with the paddle or oar, or touch your own spear while it is in the fish, or to tie the line around the fish except so far as this may be accidentally done in spearing.

It is _allowable_ to dislodge the enemy's spear by throwing your own over it. The purpose of the barbs is to assist in this.

It is _allowable_ to run on to the sturgeon with the boat.

_It is absolutely forbidden to throw the spear over the other boat or over the heads of your crew_.

In towing the sturgeon the fathom mark must be over the gunwale--at least six feet of line should be out when the fish is in tow. It is not a foul to have less, but the spearman must at once let it out if the umpire or the other crew cries "fathom!"

The spearman is allowed to drop the spear and use the paddle or oar at will, but not to resign his spear to another of the crew. The spearman must be in his boat when the spear is thrown.

If the boat is upset the referee's canoe helps them to right. Each crew must accept the backset of its accidents.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Tilting In The Water
body:
For this we usually have two boats or war canoes manned by four men each. These are a spearman, who is also a captain, a pilot, and two oarsmen.

The spearman is armed with a light pole or bamboo eight or ten feet long, with a soft pad on the end. Sometimes this is further provided with a hook. This is a forked branch with limbs a foot long; one is lashed to the bamboo, the other projecting out a foot, and slightly backward. The end of the spear and the fork are now thoroughly padded with burlap to the shape of a duck's head and bill. And it must be cased in waterproof, to keep it from getting wet and heavy. The object of the hook is to change suddenly from pushing, and to pull the enemy by hooking round his neck. Each boat should have a quarter-deck or raised platform at one end, on which the spearman stands.

The battle is fought in rounds and by points.

To put your opponent back into the canoe with one foot counts you five; two feet, ten. If he loses his spear you count five (excepting when he is put overboard). If you put him down on one knee on the fighting deck, you count five; two knees, ten. If you put him overboard it counts twenty-five. One hundred points is a round.

A battle is for one or more rounds, as agreed on. It is forbidden to hook or strike below the belt. The umpire may dock for fouls.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Canoe Tag
body:
Any number of canoes or boats may engage in this. A rubber cushion, a hot-water bag full of air, any rubber football, or a cotton bag with a lot of corks in it is needed. The game is to tag the other canoe by throwing this into it.

The rules are as in ordinary cross-tag.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Scouting
body:
Scouts are sent out in pairs or singly. A number of points are marked on the map at equal distances from camp, and the scouts draw straws to see where each goes. If one place is obviously hard, the scout is allowed a fair number of points as handicap. All set out at same time, go direct, and return as soon as possible.

Points are thus allowed:

Last back, zero for travelling.

The others count one for each minute they are ahead of the last.

Points up to one hundred are allowed for their story on return.

Sometimes we allow ten points for each turtle they have seen; ten for each owl seen and properly named; five for each hawk, and one each for other wild birds; also two for a cat one for a dog.

No information is given the scout; he is told to go to such a point and do so and so, but is fined points if he hesitates or asks how or why, etc.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: The Game of Quicksight
body:
Make two boards about a foot square, divide each into twenty-five squares; get ten nuts and ten pebbles. Give to one player one board, five nuts, and five pebbles. He places these on the squares in any pattern he fancies, and when ready the other player is allowed to see it for five seconds. Then it is covered up, and from the memory of what he saw the second player must reproduce the pattern on his own board. He counts one for each that was right, and takes off one for each that was wrong. They take turn and turn about.

This game is a wonderful developer of the power to see and memorize quickly.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Farsight, or Spot the Rabbit
body: Take two six-inch squares of stiff white pasteboard or whitened wood. On each of these draw an outline rabbit, one an exact duplicate of the other. Make twenty round black wafers or spots, each half an inch across. Let one player stick a few of these on one rabbit-board and set it up in full light. The other, beginning at one hundred yards, draws near till he can see the spots well enough to reproduce the pattern on the other which he carries. If he can do it at seventy-five yards he has wonderful eyes. Down even to seventy (done three times out of five), he counts high honor; from seventy to sixty counts honor. Below that does not count at all.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Pole-star
body:
Each competitor is given a long straight stick in daytime, and told to lay it due north and south. In doing this he may guide himself by sun, moss, or anything he can find in nature--anything, indeed, except a compass.

The direction is checked by a good compass corrected for the locality. The one who comes nearest wins.

It is optional with the judges whether the use of a timepiece is to be allowed.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Rabbit Hunt
body:
The game of rabbit hunting is suited for two hunters in limited grounds.

Three little sacks of brown burlap, each about eight inches by twelve, are stuffed with hay.

At any given place in the woods the two hunters stand in a ten-foot circle with their bows and arrows. One boy is blindfolded; the other, without leaving the circle, throws the rabbits into good hiding places on the ground. Then the second hunter has to find the rabbits and shoot them without leaving the circle. The lowest number of points wins, as in golf. If the hunter has to leave the circle he gets one point for every step he takes outside. After he sees the rabbit he must keep to that spot and shoot till it is hit once. One shot kills it, no matter where struck. For every shot he misses he gets five points.

After his first shot at each rabbit the hider takes alternate shots with him.

If it is the hider who kills the rabbit, the hunter adds ten points to his score. If the hunter hits it, he takes ten off his score.

If the hunter fails to find all the rabbits, he scores twenty-five for each one he gives up.

The hider cannot score at all. He can only help his friend into trouble. Next time the two change places.

A match is usually for two brace of rabbits.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Hostile Spy
body: Hanging from the totem pole is a red or yellow horse-tail. This is the grand medicine scalp of the band. The hostile spy has to steal it. The leader goes around on the morning of the day and whispers to the various braves, "Look out--there's a spy in camp." At length he gets secretly near the one he has selected for spy and whispers, "Look out, there's a spy in camp, and you are it." He gives him at the same time some bright-coloured badge, that he must wear as soon as he has secured the medicine scalp. He must not hide the scalp on his person, but keep it in view. He has all day till sunset to get away with it. If he gets across the river or other limit, with warriors in close pursuit, they give him ten arrow heads (two and one half cents each), or other ransom agreed on. If he gets away safely and hides it, he can come back and claim fifteen arrow heads from the council as ransom for the scalp. If he is caught, he pays his captor ten arrow heads ransom for his life.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: The Man-Hunt
body:
This is played with a scout and ten or more hostiles, or hounds, according to the country, more when it is rough or wooded.

The scout is given a letter addressed to the "Military Commandant" (usually the lady of the house that he gets to) of any given place a mile or two away. He is told to take the letter to anyone of three given houses, and get it endorsed, with the hour when he arrived, then return to the starting-point within a certain time.

The hostiles are sent to a point half-way, and let go by a starter at the same time as the scout leaves the camp. They are to intercept him.

If they catch him before he delivers the letter he must ransom his life by paying each two arrow heads (or other forfeit) and his captor keeps the letter as a trophy. If he gets through, but is caught on the road back, he pays half as much for his life. If he gets through, but is over time, it is a draw. If he gets through successfully on time he claims three arrow heads from each hostile and keeps the letter as a trophy.

They may not follow him into the house (that is, the fort), but may surround it at one hundred yards distance. They do not know which three houses he is free to enter, but they do know that these are within certain limits.

The scout should wear a conspicuous badge (hat, shirt, coat, or feather), and may ride a wheel or go in a wagon, etc., as long as his badge is clearly visible.

To "tag" the scout is not to capture. "The blockade to be binding must be effectual."

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Hunt the Coon
body:
This is an in-door game, founded on the familiar "Hunt the Thimble."

We use a little dummy coon; either make it or turn a ready-made toy rabbit into one by adding tail and black mask, and cropping the ears.

All the players but one go out of the room. That one places the coon anywhere in sight, high or low, but in plain view; all come in and seek. The first to find it, sits down silently, and scores one. Each sits down, on seeing it, giving no clue to the others.

The first to score three coons is winner, usually. Sometimes we play till everyone but one has a coon; that one is the booby. The others are first, second, etc.

Sometimes each is given his number in order of finding it.

Then, after seven or eight coons, these numbers are added up, and the lowest is winner. If no coon is available use a thimble.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Spear Fights
body:
This is an in-door game with out-door weapons. The soft-headed, eight foot spears of the tilting-match are used. The contestants stand on barrels eight feet apart. Each tries to put the other off his barrel. It is well to have a catcher behind each player to save him if he falls.

Games are for seven, eleven, or thirteen points.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Navajo Feather Dance
body: An eagle feather hung on a horse-hair, so as to stand upright, is worked by a hidden operator, so as to dance and caper. The dancer has to imitate all its motions. A marionette may be used. It is a great fun-maker.
summary: An eagle feather hung on a horse-hair, so as to stand upright, is worked by a hidden operator, so as to dance and caper. The dancer has to imitate all its motions. A marionette may be used. It is a great fun-maker.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Feather Football or Feather Blow
body:
This is an in-door, wet-weather game.

The players hold a blanket on the knees or on the table. A soft feather is put in the middle. As many may play as can get near. They may be in sides, two or four or each for himself. At the signal, "Go!" each tries to blow the feather off the blanket at the enemy's side, and so count one for himself.

A game is usually best out of seven, eleven, or thirteen.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Cock-Fighting
body:
Get two stout sticks, each two feet long (broomsticks will do). Pad each of these on the end with a ball of rag. These are the spurs. Make an eight-foot ring. The two rivals are on their hunkers, each with a stick through behind his knees, his hands clasped in front of the knees, and the arms under the ends of the spurs.

Now they close; each aiming to upset the other, to make him lose his spurs, or to put him out of the ring, any of which ends that round and scores one for the victor. If both fall, or lose a spur, or go out together, it is a draw. Battle is for seven, eleven, or thirteen rounds.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Hand-Wrestling
body:
This is a jiujitsu game, introduced by Dr. L. H. Gulick. The two contestants stand right toe to right toe, each right hand clasped, left feet braced, left hand free. At the word, "Go!" each tries to unbalance the other: that is, make him lift or move one of his feet. A lift or a shift ends the round.

Battles are for best out of five, seven, eleven, or thirteen rounds.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Badger-Pulling
body:
The two contestants, on hands and knees, face each other.

A strong belt or strap is buckled into one great loop that passes round the head of each: that is, crosses his nape. Half-way between them is a dead line. The one who pulls the other over this line is winner.

The contestant can at any time end the bout by lowering his head so the strap slips off; but this counts one against him.

Game is best out of five, seven, eleven, or thirteen points.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Poison
body:
This is an ancient game. A circle about three feet across is drawn on the ground. The players, holding hands, make a ring around this, and try to make one of the number step into the poison circle. He can evade it by side-stepping, by jumping over, or by dragging another fellow into it.

First to make the misstep is "it" for the time or for next game.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Hat-Ball
body:
When I was among the Chepewyan Indians of Great Slave Lake, in 1907, I made myself popular with the young men, as well as boys, by teaching them the old game of hat-ball.

The players (about a dozen) put their hats in a row near a house, fence, or log (hollows up). A dead line is drawn ten feet from the hats; all must stand outside of that. The one who is "it" begins by throwing a soft ball into one of the hats. If he misses the hat, a chip is put into his own, and he tries over. As soon as he drops the ball into a hat, the owner runs to get the ball; all the rest run away. The owner must not follow beyond the dead line, but must throw the ball at some one. If he hits him, a chip goes into that person's hat; if not, a chip goes into his own.

As soon as some one has five chips, he wins the booby prize: that is, he must hold his hand out steady against the wall, and each player has five shots at it with the ball, as he stands on the dead line.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Duck-on-a-Rock
body:
This is a good old grandfather game.

Each player has a large, smooth, roundish stone, about five or six inches through. This is his duck. He keeps it permanently.

Toe rock is any low bowlder, block, stump, bump, or hillock on level ground. A dead line is drawn through the rock, and another parallel, fifteen feet away, for a firing line.

The fellow who is "it," or "keeper," perches his duck on the rock. The others stand at the firing line and throw their ducks at his. They must not pick them up or touch them with their hands when they are beyond the dead line. If one does, then the keeper can tag him (unless he reaches the firing line), and send him to do duty as keeper at the rock.

But they can coax their ducks with their feet, up to the dead line, not beyond, then watch for a chance to dodge back to the firing line, where they are safe at all times.

If the duck is knocked off by anyone in fair firing, the keeper is powerless till he has replaced it. Meantime, most of the players have secured their ducks and got back safely to the firing line.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Road-side Cribbage
body:
This is a game we often play in the train, to pass the time pleasantly.

Sometimes one party takes the right side of the road, with the windows there, and the other the left. Sometimes all players sit on the same side.

The game is, whoever is first to see certain things agreed on scores so many points.

Thus: A crow or a cow counts 1 A cat 2 A hawk 3 An owl 4 A sheep 5 A goat 6 A horse 7

The winner is the one who first gets twenty-five or fifty points, as agreed.

When afoot, one naturally takes other things for points, as certain trees, flowers, etc.
summary: This is a game we often play in the train, to pass the time pleasantly. Sometimes one party takes the right side of the road, with the windows there, and the other the left. Sometimes all players sit on the same side. The game is, whoever is first to see…

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Chalk the Arrow
body:
This is usually played in the city streets, one player running and trying to keep out of sight of the others who follow. The runner is given time to disappear around the first corner before the others start after him, and at every corner he turns he marks (with chalk) an arrow pointing in the direction he takes. Those pursuing follow by the arrow, the first one seeing him being the runner for the next time.

This may also be played by having any number run and only one follow, the first becoming "it" for the next time.
summary: This is usually played in the city streets, one player running and trying to keep out of sight of the others who follow. The runner is given time to disappear around the first corner before the others start after him, and at every corner he turns he marks…

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Dodge Ball
body:
Of any number of players, half of that number form a circle, while the other half stand inside of the ring (centre) facing outward. Now, the game for those in the centre is to dodge the ball which is thrown by any of those forming the circle with the intention of striking the centre ones out. Every time a member is struck he is dead, and takes his place among those of the circle. Now he has a chance to throw at those remaining in the centre. This arrangement keeps all taking part busy. Only one is out at a time. This being kept up until finally only one is left. He is hailed the king. For next round, players exchange places, i. e., those who were in the centre now form the circle.

Note: If the touch is preceded by a bound of the ball it does not count.
summary: Of any number of players, half of that number form a circle, while the other half stand inside of the ring (centre) facing outward. Now, the game for those in the centre is to dodge the ball which is thrown by any of those forming the circle with the…

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Prisoner's Base
body: Goals are marked off at both ends of the playground, the players divided into two equal divisions, occupying the two goals. About ten paces to the right of each goal is a prison. A player advances toward the opposite goal, when one from that goal starts out to catch him. He retreats, and one from his side runs to his rescue by trying to catch the pursuer--who in turn is succored by one from his side, and so on. Every player may catch anyone from the opposite side who has been out of goal longer than he has. Any player caught is conducted to the prison by his captor and must remain there until rescued by some one from his side, who touches him with the hand. The one who does this is subject to being caught like any other player.
summary: Goals are marked off at both ends of the playground, the players divided into two equal divisions, occupying the two goals. About ten paces to the right of each goal is a prison. A player advances toward the opposite goal, when one from that goal starts out…

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Throwing the Spear
body:
The game is an old Greek and Persian pastime. "Throw the spear and speak the truth," was a national maxim of the Persians that we may copy with advantage.

The apparatus required is some light spears and an archery target. The spears should vary from five to six feet in length; the point should be shod with a steel tip, having a socket into which the wooden handle is fitted, and made fast by small screws passing through holes in the sides of the metal, and then into the wood itself. The wood, for about a foot above the barb, should be about three quarters of an inch in diameter, and from thence gradually taper to about a quarter of an inch in thickness until the end of the spear is reached.

Some spears are fitted with feathers, like an arrow, but these are not necessary to obtain a good throw, and soon get dismantled in continually falling upon the ground. Any ordinary target will serve. It may be an archery target, a sack full of straw, or a sod bank.

The object of the contest is to hit the target from a given mark, the firing line. Whoever throws nearest to the centre of the target the greatest number of times out of six shots is hailed the winner.

The best form for throwing is with the left foot forward, the leg perfectly straight, body well back, its weight resting on the right leg. Now extend the left arm forward, in a line with the shoulder, and over the left leg; poise the spear horizontally in the right hand, holding at the centre of gravity by the forefinger and thumb. Bring the right arm backward until the hand is behind the right shoulder.

Now, inclining the point of the spear slightly upward, make your cast, bringing the right arm forward, followed by the right side of the body, the right leg forward and the left arm backward. Count yourself fortunate if you even hit the target in the first few attempts, but practice will make a wonderful difference. The distance should be mutually agreed upon, but fifty feet for a boy of fifteen and one hundred feet for an adult will be found about right.

To "throw the javelin" is another phase of this pastime. The javelin is four to five feet in length, three quarters of an inch in thickness, and fitted with a barbed end, slightly heavier than the spear end. The "object of the game" is to throw the javelin as far as possible but not at a target; instead, the javelin must stick into the ground.

In throwing the javelin, hold it in the right hand, the left leg and hand being advanced; the barb and arm at this point should be at the rear. Then, describing a semicircle with the arm over the right shoulder, and leaning well to the rear, hurl the weapon as far as possible forward.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Follow My Leader
body: With a large number of boys this can be made a very effective display, and is easy to do at a jog trot, and occasional "knee-up" with musical accompaniment. It also can be done at night, each boy carrying a Chinese lantern on top of his staff. If in a building all lights, of course, would be turned down. A usual fault is that the exercise is kept on too long, till it wearies both audience and performers.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Unprepared Plays
body:
Give the plot of a short, simple, play and assign to each player his part, with an outline of what he has to do and say, and then let them act it, making up the required conversation as they go along.

This develops the power of imagination and expression on points kept in the mind, and is a valuable means of education.

It is well before starting to act a play in this way to be a little less ambitious, and to make two or three players merely carry out a conversation on given topics leading up to a given point, using their own words and imaginations in doing so.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: The Treasure Hunt
body:
The treasure hunt needs observation and skill in tracking, and practically any number can take part in it.

Several ways of playing the game are given below.

1. The treasure is hidden and the scouts know what the treasure is; they are given the first clew, and from this all the others can be traced. Such clews might be (a) written on a gate post: "Go west and examine third gate on north side of stream"; (b) on that gate, scout's sign pointing to notice board on which is written, "Strike south by south-east telegraph post, No. 28," and so on. The clews should be so worded as to need some skill to understand, and the various points should be difficult of access from one another. This method might be used as a patrol competition, starting off patrols at ten-minute intervals, and at one particular clew there might be different orders for each patrol, to prevent the patrols behind from following the first.

2. The clews may be bits of colored wood tied to gates, hedges, etc., at about three-yard intervals, leading in a certain direction, and when these clews come to the end it should be known that the treasure is hidden within so many feet. To prevent this degenerating into a mere game of follow my leader, several tracks might be laid working up to the same point, and false tracks could be laid, which only lead back again to the original.

3. Each competitor or patrol might be given a description of the way--each perhaps of a slightly different way; the description should make it necessary to go to each spot in turn; and prevent any "cutting" in the following way: "Go to the tallest tree in a certain field, from there go one hundred yards north, and then walk straight toward a church tower which will be on your left," etc. All the descriptions should lead by an equal journey to a certain spot where the treasure is hidden. The first to arrive at that spot should not let the others know it is the spot, but should search for the treasure in as casual a manner as possible.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Will-o'-the-Wisp
body:
This game should take place across country at night. Two scouts set off in a given direction with a lighted bull's-eye lantern. After two minutes have passed the patrol or troop starts in pursuit.

The lantern bearer must show his light at least every minute concealing it for the rest of the time. The two scouts take turns in carrying the light, and so may relieve each other in difficulties, but either may be captured. The scout without the light can often mingle with the pursuers without being recognized and relieve his friend when he is being hard pressed. They should arrange certain calls or signals between themselves.
summary: This game should take place across country at night. Two scouts set off in a given direction with a lighted bull's-eye lantern. After two minutes have passed the patrol or troop starts in pursuit. The lantern bearer must show his light at least every minute…

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Treasure Island
body: A treasure is known to be hidden upon a certain island or bit of shore marked off, and the man who hid it leaves a map with clews for finding it (compass, directions, tide marks, etc.). This map is hidden somewhere near the landing-place; the patrols come in turn to look for it--they have to row from a certain distance, land, find the map, and finally discover the treasure. They should be careful to leave no foot tracks, etc., near the treasure, because then the patrols that follow them will easily find it. The map and treasure are to be hidden afresh for the next patrol when they have been found. The patrol wins which returns to the starting place with the treasure in the shortest time. (This can be played on the river, the patrols having to row across the river to find the treasure.)
summary: A treasure is known to be hidden upon a certain island or bit of shore marked off, and the man who hid it leaves a map with clews for finding it (compass, directions, tide marks, etc.). This map is hidden somewhere near the landing-place; the patrols come in…

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Horse and Rider Tourney
body: In playing this game it is necessary to have a soft, velvety piece of grass, or if in doors, in the gymnasium, cover the floor with regular gymnasium mats. It requires four boys to play the game, two being horses and the other two riders. The riders mount their horses and dash at each other with great caution, striving to get a good hold of each other in such a way as to compel the opponent to dismount. This can be done either by dragging him from his mount or by making the horse and rider lose their balance so as to throw them off their feet. A great deal of sport can be gotten out of this game, and boys become very skilful after a little practice.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Reading a Map in the Field
body:
a) On a hill with a wide view, a scout patrol gathers. They orient the map—first using a compass, then by matching map symbols—and determine the patrol’s position on it (see below). Next, while examining the surroundings, they identify various terrain features, starting with closer ones and then moving to more distant ones, and locate their corresponding symbols on the map; then they reverse the process: they find a feature drawn on the map and locate it in the terrain.

In this way, they not only learn a series of new symbols but, having the ability to calculate any distance using the map’s scale, they estimate the distance of terrain features by eye and verify their estimate using the map. Thus, the study of map reading is combined with practice in estimating distances. Knowing the distance, one can also calculate the marching time to a given point.

After completing the exercise, the observation point should be changed—that is, move to another hill and from there look toward the former position, i.e., at the same previously observed area, but from the opposite side. How differently the same area will appear to our eyes!

### Using a Map in the Field

To use a map in the field, it must first be «oriented», i.e., positioned so that its edges correctly align with the cardinal directions, which can be done by marking the geographic meridian (N-S). In an oriented map, the top edge faces north, the bottom south, the left west, and the right east. All lines drawn on the map will then be parallel to their corresponding lines in the terrain, and a line connecting one’s position on the map to the symbol of a terrain feature, when extended, will fall precisely on that feature in the terrain (Fig. 5).

Next, one must mark one’s own position on the map, i.e., the point in the terrain where one is currently located.

1. **Orienting the Map:**
   a) *With a Compass.* Place the compass on the map so that the N-S (N-S) line aligns with or is parallel to the map’s side edge, with the letter N (N) facing the top of the map. Then rotate the map along with the compass (without changing the compass’s position) until the north end of the needle (black) aligns with the N (N) on the compass. Finally, account for the «declination» (p. 43), i.e., rotate the map further to the right (east) by the angle corresponding to the magnetic declination of the area. (Since the declination in Polish lands is small, omitting it will not be a major error). The map is then oriented (Fig. 5).

   b) *With a Watch, etc.* In the absence of a compass, determine the N-S direction as described on p. 42 and align the map accordingly. At night, the North Star can be used.

   c) *By Map Symbols.* If there are several prominent terrain features in the area that are marked on the map, orient the map by rotating it so that the directions of the lines connecting your position to the corresponding symbols on the map align with the actual directions in the terrain (as in Fig. 5).

   ![img-4.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-053-img-4.jpeg)
   
   Fig. 5.

   Often, this can be done by aligning the map with the direction of a road, railway, etc.—simply position the map so that a line on it aligns with (or is parallel to) a line in the terrain (Fig. 6).

   ![img-5.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-054-img-5.jpeg)
   
   Fig. 6.

   Sometimes, in the absence of prominent terrain features or clear lines, the map can be oriented by comparing the depiction of the terrain’s relief on it (contour lines, hatching) with the shapes of the surrounding elevations, though this requires greater skill.

2. Marking one’s position on the map usually only involves accurately identifying it (if necessary), as one does not move blindly with a map in hand, and a scout should always know approximately where they are.

   a) *By Pacing.* If you are on a road marked on the map, find a prominent feature on that road in the terrain (also marked on the map) and measure its distance from your position in paces (sometimes an estimate by eye is sufficient). Convert the measured distance to the map’s scale, then measure that distance from the feature’s symbol on the map toward your position; the point you find on the map is your location. (To avoid mistakes, it is better to orient the map first).

   Example: A prominent feature on the road you are traveling is a road sign. It is 320 paces (240 m) away from you and is marked on the map. Since the map has a scale of 1:100,000, 240 m corresponds to 24/100 cm, or about 2½ mm. Orient the map and determine that your position on the road is 2½ mm from the road sign symbol.

   b) *By Resection (Intersection).* If there is no prominent reference feature on the road (as in a), but there is a church, windmill, etc., nearby (also marked on the map), orient the map and align a ruler through the symbol on the map toward the corresponding feature in the terrain. Your position is at the intersection of this line with the road line (Fig. 7).

   ![img-6.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-055-img-6.jpeg)
   
   Fig. 7.

   c) *By Back Resection.* If you are in an area where there is no road marked on the map (as in a and b), you must aim at least two directions by sighting prominent terrain features and drawing lines from their symbols on the map back toward your position; their intersection on the map will correspond to your position in the terrain. Search for several reference features in the surrounding terrain, sight them one by one through their corresponding symbols on the map, and draw lines backward from those symbols with a pencil; their intersection on the map will be the point corresponding to your position in the terrain. You can first orient the map, which will make the task easier, but the described method simultaneously orients the map.

   ![img-7.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-056-img-7.jpeg)

   Fig. 8.

   If you perform back resection from three terrain features (a more precise method) that form a triangle in the terrain, with your position inside it, the sighting lines to these points may not intersect at a single point (as in Fig. 9), and a small triangle, called the *error triangle*, will form on the map. Your position will be easier to locate within this triangle.

   ![img-8.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-057-img-8.jpeg)

   Fig. 9.

   As can be seen from the above descriptions, locating one’s position on the map is done in a similar manner to orienting the map.

b) On another day, the patrol goes to a place where it is not as easy to mark their position on the map. The exercise is similar to the previous one but begins with marking the patrol’s position. Sometimes they do this with a compass to orient the map, other times without one—sometimes knowing the road they are on, other times not even knowing the line along which the patrol is moving, etc.—in short, creating various conditions for the patrol, some easier, some more difficult, to locate their position. Then they describe the visible terrain, identifying its most important features—rivers with crossings, vegetation, communication lines, etc.—and compare what they see with the map.

c) From another observation point, the patrol locates in the terrain a feature or point indicated on the map, or vice versa, locates on the map a point indicated in the terrain. (In both cases, the map must first be oriented and one’s position found on it. Then, in the first case, determine the direction of the sought feature by connecting your position on the map with the feature’s symbol—the extension of this line will lead to the feature in the terrain. In the second case, align through your position on the map toward the feature in the terrain—the symbol of that feature on the map will lie on this line).

The patrol also calculates, based on the map, the difference in elevation between a point indicated in the terrain and their own position. (After orienting the map and determining both positions, read the absolute elevations of your position and the indicated point, then calculate the difference).

They also determine, based on the map, what should be visible from the observation point and verify this by observing the terrain, etc.—in short, in the field, they repeat and expand upon the map-reading exercises previously conducted indoors.

d) This kind of terrain insight, i.e., comparing the map with the surroundings, is practiced by the patrol during a march—first in familiar terrain, then in unknown, obscured, or mountainous areas. The route is then traveled in segments from one observation point (a point with a wide view in all directions) to another. At the end of each segment, the map is oriented, the position is marked by comparing it with the surroundings, and a glance is cast at the next segment of the route.

Along the way, attention is paid to prominent features encountered (tower, chimney, interesting terrain formations, etc.), the visible features are constantly compared with the map, and an effort is made to memorize their locations. Often, the already traveled route is reviewed to recognize it on the return march.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Cross-Country with a Map
body:
The patrol leader draws a line on the map, leading it through passable terrain. He hands the map to one scout and orders him to lead the patrol exactly along the line. The rest, with maps in hand, are to monitor the march and, if called upon, correct his mistaken direction. The leader must constantly observe the terrain passed and compare the features encountered with the map’s drawing, so as not to deviate from the marked course and to reach the designated destination. All observations are to be made aloud. This is an excellent exercise in map reading.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Determining the Cardinal Directions
body:
On a sunny day, the patrol stands in an open space, each scout several paces apart from the next.

Each, using a watch (see p. 42), determines the cardinal directions and places his staff on the ground in the North–South direction. The patrol leader checks the position of the staffs with a compass.

Similarly, the patrol is ordered to determine the North–South direction with a staff in the evening by the North Star.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Cross-Country with a Compass
body:
After explaining the construction and use of the compass (busola) in the field, the patrol sets off with a compass in hand, heading north, south, east, or west. (For repeated exercises, intermediate directions are chosen). The requirement is only to maintain the general prescribed direction, and it is the patrol leader’s duty to choose the most suitable route for the patrol. He also checks the march using the compass.

a) Suppose I need to go in the direction N—E. I place the compass on my palm and turn, holding it at chest height, until the black end of the needle (the north pole) aligns with N. Then, I place a matchstick on the glass so that, passing through the axis of the needle (i.e., the center of the compass), it covers the line marking the N—E direction. Now, I aim at the terrain, looking for a distant object (a tree, a hut, etc.) lying exactly in the extension of the matchstick, and head toward it (Fig. 10). Upon reaching it, I repeat the process, finding a second point on my line of march in the same way, and so on.

If, during the march, the target disappears from sight due to the terrain’s configuration, this will not affect the direction of the march as long as I keep the compass set, i.e., constantly ensuring I do not deviate from the direction, and continue moving in the direction of the matchstick, i.e., the N—E line.

If I encounter an obstacle (e.g., a swamp), I memorize a visible point on the terrain that lies on the line of march beyond the obstacle, and after bypassing it, I return to that point and continue cross-country.

(The angle contained between the magnetic needle and the direction to any point on the terrain, read to the right of the magnetic meridian (in this case, the angle between N and N—E = 45°), is called the directional angle or azimuth.

We orient ourselves according to the azimuth during a march through a large forest and generally when it is difficult to navigate using a map).

To verify whether the scouts are indeed moving in the assigned direction and to spark greater interest, a scout can be placed in hiding at a terrain feature lying exactly on the line of the assigned direction. It will later be seen who deviated the least and who the most from the correct direction. In this case, the scouts set off separately, at intervals.

b) Instead of placing a matchstick on the compass, I can aim at the point I need to reach using the N—S line drawn on the bottom of the compass. Since there is a degree scale (from 1°—360°) on it, it is sufficient to subtract the angle indicated by the north pole of the needle from 360°. The resulting azimuth of the given point

![img-9.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-060-img-9.jpeg)

Fig. 10.

![img-0.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-061-img-0.jpeg)

Fig. 11.

![img-1.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-061-img-1.jpeg)

Fig. 12.

(in Fig. 11, the needle indicates 315°, so the azimuth is 360°—315° = 45°, as above under a).

If the degree scale is placed in the opposite direction, i.e., to the left rather than the right of N (Fig. 12), I can read the directional angle directly from the compass after aiming the N—S line at the point in the terrain (in this case, 45°). It is sufficient to aim as under a), but instead of the matchstick, use the N—S line, ensuring the needle aligns with 45° (in the first case, 315°), since I was to go in the N—E direction¹).

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: In the Forest with a Compass
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

a) In impassable terrain, such as the middle of a forest, a flag is planted. From this point, scouts set out individually or in pairs, compass in hand, in different cardinal directions, each at a different bearing (see above). They must walk for 5–15 minutes cross-country, strictly maintaining their initial direction. After this time, they turn back and return exactly in the opposite direction, i.e., to the starting point. Meanwhile, the patrol leader removes the flag and makes a mark known only to himself at the spot where it stood, then moves to another location. After the march, it is checked which scout shows the smallest deviation from the prescribed direction. It is not an error if the returning scout does not reach the mark (or misses it), as the terrain may be sloping, so the return uphill will take longer; however, a greater deviation from the marching direction is an error.

A variation and, to some extent, an extension of the exercise is to place numbered cards at easily memorable points along the route during the march, which are then collected on the return. It is also possible to go out with a compass in hand in one direction and return only by orienting oneself by the appearance of the path and collecting the cards. In the latter case, it would be advisable to send the scouts from a forest glade to which they must return, rather than from a single point as before.

b) The exercise is conducted as the previous one, but after 3–5 minutes of marching, the scout changes direction by 45° or 90° (e.g., from east to northeast or north) and continues in this new direction for another 3–5 minutes. They must return to the starting point by the same route, after which errors are assessed.

Suppose the scouts set out at bearings of 45°—110°—225°, aiming at points along the N–S line (as in Exercise No. 4b), and after 5 minutes they are to continue, changing direction by 90° to the right. In this case, at the point of direction change—note that if the compass has a degree scale on the left—each adds 90°: the first sets the needle to 135° (45+90), the second to 200° (110+90), the third to 315° (225+90). These are the azimuths for their new directions.

If the compass scale is on the right, they subtract 90°: the first, having initially set the needle to 315° (azimuth: 360–315 = 45°, see Fig. 12), sets it to 225° (315–90 = 225); the second, from 250° (azimuth: 360–250 = 110°), sets it to 160° (250–90 = 160); the third, from 135° (azimuth: 360–135 = 225°), sets it to 45°. At these new azimuths, all three continue in the direction of the N–S line as in Exercise No. 4b.

Here, not only the compass will be helpful. Scouts will use aids to facilitate orientation, i.e., they will memorize characteristic details of the path they pass, especially at the point where the path bends, such as a broken tree, a large boulder, a pit, a hut, etc. These things should be observed after passing them, as they appear differently from the opposite side. In short, both observation and orientation along the entire route.

A certain variation of the exercise is its previously mentioned form. At the point where the path bends, an orientation mark should be made to facilitate the return.

c) The difference between this exercise and the previous one is that after marching in two directions, the scout does not return by the same route but by the nearest route to the starting point. The path thus bends twice. Initially, basic and therefore easy directions are given, as in Fig. 16—then directional angles, as in Fig. 10. As in exercise b), assistants should be stationed at the points of direction change to help establish the new marching route.

The last exercise is more difficult and should only be attempted once the previous two are mastered. These exercises are harder to perform at dusk, but this should still be attempted.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: In Search of the Runner
body:
Based on a map, scouts are positioned at various points in the terrain, each several hundred paces apart. The location of each is unknown to the others. One stands, for example, at a road junction, another at a bridge, a third in a ravine, at the edge of a forest, under a solitary tree, etc. Each has a number that they must memorize.

One scout remains with the patrol leader, who is then sent to Scout No. 1. He is given instructions on where to find him, as well as written orders for all the positioned runners. The messenger delivers these orders to Scout No. 1. This scout reads the order intended for him and, based on it, searches for No. 2 and hands him the remaining orders. No. 2 searches for No. 3, and so on, with the last scout searching for the patrol leader. The question is: at what time will the last scout arrive? From the map, one can calculate the distance and judge whether the entire exercise was completed in good or poor time. (The orders are brief, e.g., direction NNE, distance 300 paces, halfway up the eastern slope of the forest, distance 300 paces). Scouts should be positioned so that they form a closed polygon, as returning when arranged in a line takes a lot of time. The patrol leader stands either in the middle or forms one of the polygon's corners.

If two patrols are to compete, outposts are formed with two scouts each (white and red), and two messengers are sent in opposite directions with orders to the nearest outposts. These orders are indeed different. The patrol that completes the task in the shortest time wins.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: To a Vanishing Target in Concealment
body:
Point out to the patrol a distant but not overly prominent object—yet not so difficult to recognize and locate. Allow them to observe it for a moment to determine its position relative to other notable landmarks, then order them to reach it by any route, and if possible, in concealment. Choose such an object in unfamiliar or at least little-known terrain, one that will disappear from sight during the march. Make the exercise more difficult by first having them march for 5–10 minutes in a certain direction, and only then turn back to search for the indicated object.

After observing the object’s position relative to surrounding landmarks, the patrol must constantly look around and orient themselves, especially if they approach from a different side than they started, as the entire terrain configuration will appear differently to them—they will circle around until they finally reach the target. While accompanying the patrol, you must control their path, i.e., require them to advance in concealment. It is precisely this adaptation of the march to the terrain’s shape that makes finding the sought-after object more difficult.

Such situations often occur when sending a patrol on reconnaissance, when the patrol lacks a map, when they must leave the road to avoid enemy units, or when they must bypass inhabited places, etc.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: The Same Path Back
body:
This exercise takes place in unfamiliar terrain, or at least known roads must not be used. The patrol knows that after covering a certain distance—e.g., several kilometers—and changing direction several times, they must return to the starting point by the exact same route they took. Therefore, each scout tries to memorize distinctive features of the path during the march, such as a characteristic boulder, a forest barrier, a broken tree, a factory chimney visible from a certain point, etc., and frequently looks back to observe these features from the opposite side, as they appear differently when viewed from behind. Even in a forest, the route can be memorized by paying attention to the terrain’s shape, the course of valleys, and the layout of elevations.

During the march, the patrol leader places numbered slips of paper with the scouts’ names at various points—sometimes under a rock, sometimes in a tree hollow, etc. Upon reaching the destination, the scouts are sent back individually at intervals of several minutes, and each must bring all their slips back to the starting point as proof that they returned by the same route they had taken earlier.

The second time, the exercise is made more difficult by keeping the return a secret from the patrol; it is only announced upon arrival at the destination.

For less experienced scouts, it is permitted to mark the route in an inconspicuous manner and only in certain places, e.g., at crossroads. Alternatively, the entire patrol may return together (with one leading), in which case the slips are not distributed.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: The Shortest Way Back
body:
a) The leader marks his position with a flag and sends out several patrols in different directions, instructing them to dispatch scouts at set intervals with fictional reports—i.e., merely a note indicating the report’s serial number, the dispatch location (as per the map), and the time the messenger was sent. Each messenger is given a direction in which to seek the leader. He must take the shortest route. Upon arrival, the leader records the time of arrival on the note for later verification of who returned on time.

A patrol should not proceed in the same direction continuously but should change it several times. The exercise should first be conducted on a sunny day to facilitate orientation, and in any case in unfamiliar or little-known terrain. One must not forget to designate a rallying point for any who may get lost.

The exercise can be made more difficult if the leader does not remain in place but, after some time, moves to another point. He must inform the departing patrols (or patrol) of his route and the destination he is heading toward.

b) On a cloudy day, when orientation by the sun is impossible, and also without a compass or map, I lead a patrol through unfamiliar terrain—across fields, forests, ravines, and hills, in many zigzags, along various roads and paths, constantly changing the direction of the march. I move, as it were, in a circle. After some time, the order is given: return by the shortest route (i.e., the straightest line) to the starting point. Untrained scouts will then scatter in all directions! One must not forget to designate a rallying point (a prominent, easily noticeable feature of the terrain).

This exercise can also be arranged differently. Here is how: on the return, one designated scout leads, while the leader, map in hand, monitors his route without correcting him at all. When the first scout truly gets lost and proceeds, as it were, by feel, the next in line takes over as guide, and so on, until finally one leads the group to the destination. It is also permissible to allow the use of a compass during the march.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Stage by Stage to the Goal
body:
Patrol follows patrol every 10 minutes. The route, cleverly laid out, leads through rocks, ditches, fences, bushes, forests, etc.—in short, through varied terrain, but over a small area of no more than a few kilometers. Each patrol has its route precisely marked on a map, or better yet, on a rough sketch, which also indicates the individual stages of the route, where each patrol must stop for 2 (3) minutes. Which patrol will reach the finish line, marked by a small flag, in the shortest time? At each stage, an impartial observer is present to record the patrol’s arrival and verify the rest period. Others, stationed at vantage points with a view of the surroundings, monitor the march. Running is strictly forbidden under threat of disqualification.

If the route is shorter, it may be unnecessary to make stops at the stages; instead, each patrol must leave the colored paper scraps previously given to it at each stage in a highly visible location as proof of having been there. The last patrol is followed by the leader, who collects the control slips.

Since this is not an ordinary race but rather an exercise in rapid orientation while locating stages, the drill can be slightly modified: instead of providing the patrol with a sketch, give them verbal instructions on where to find the first stage (e.g., a wayside shrine in the north-northeast direction) and that, under a stone (e.g., marked with a cross), they will find instructions for the second stage, and so on. These instructions must be left for the next patrol, which should be explicitly ordered. Who knows if this form of the exercise is not better.

The exercise should take place in unfamiliar terrain.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Along the Direction Line
body:
A direction marked on a map can be transferred to the field using a compass:

Find a prominent terrain feature on the map, such as a cross, bridge, etc., and calculate the angle by which its direction line (i.e., the line connecting your position on the map to that feature) deviates from the direction of the magnetic needle (directional angle, azimuth—see p. 54).

 a) First, orient the map and draw a straight line from your position on the map to the symbol of the windmill you need to reach. Then place the compass on it so that the N–S line aligns with the drawn line (N in the direction of march!) and read the angle between this line and the north pole of the magnetic needle. If you now place the compass horizontally on your palm in the field (with the N mark facing outward) and turn until the north pole of the needle aligns with the previously read angle (α), the N–S line will indicate the direction that, if followed in a straight line, will lead you to the desired windmill (Fig. 17). During the march, proceed as described in Exercise No. 4 a or b.

![img-6.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-071-img-6.jpeg)

*Fig. 17.*

b) Another method can be used, which does not require orienting the map. Place the compass on the map so that the N–S line on the compass dial is parallel to the side edge of the map. Now read the degree mark on the dial that, when connected to the center of the compass, is parallel to the direction marked on the map (i.e., the direction connecting your position to the symbol of the feature you are heading toward). Transfer this direction to the field: turn with the compass until the N–S line aligns with the direction of the magnetic needle (accounting for declination). Then, the straight line extending from the center of the compass through the previously read degree mark will indicate the direction to the sought feature in the field.

![img-7.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-072-img-7.jpeg)

*Fig. 18.*

The march should last, for example, half an hour—that is, the time you estimate is needed to reach the windmill.

You yourself should follow the patrol, and after a half-hour march—or when the patrol reaches the vicinity of the windmill—stop the patrol and indicate how much it has deviated from the prescribed direction.

If the patrol must temporarily deviate from the chosen direction due to a terrain obstacle, it should, of course, after bypassing it, return to the point it had previously marked as an intermediate point in the direction of march and continue from there under the original angle.

Scouts will take great satisfaction in reaching the designated point in unknown terrain. With precise angle calculation and strict adherence to the direction, the error can be very small.

If the scouts are proficient in using the compass, you may not need to specify the point they must reach; if it is known and visible from afar, some may unconsciously veer toward it once they spot it on the horizon.

If more compasses are available, each scout can proceed independently, and it will then be clear who followed the best direction. This exercise is very beneficial.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Finding the Way
body:
Lay out a map and draw on it with a pencil, very precisely, the route the patrol is to take. Lead it partly along a road, then through a forest, a meadow, a bridge, etc., and mark the point the patrol is to reach. The patrol observes this route on the map for several minutes, then sets out—but without the map. Each segment of the route is led by a different scout, and each marks the traversed path with chalk, twigs, stones, etc. Upon arrival at the destination and after a rest, they return along the same route, but now with the map in hand, and check where they deviated from the prescribed path. (When reading the map, each scout should memorize the image of the entire route, dividing it into sections, e.g., *along the road to the north to the wayside shrine — along the path through the field to the east to the bridge — towards the factory chimney until the forest — along the forest path to the northwest*, etc.).

A better variation of this exercise may be that each scout in the patrol traverses the entire designated route, marking it with their own signs, not just their segment. In this case, the scouts are sent out at such time intervals that each travels independently, not following the one before. It is not advisable to send all scouts at the same time in this variation, as the less confident ones will thoughtlessly follow the better-trained.

This exercise is somewhat the reverse of the exercise from item 47 b. Here, the appearance of the route on the map and important features of the surrounding terrain are memorized, and then the route is located on the ground; there, the route on the ground is memorized, and then it is sketched from memory.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: On Reconnaissance by Any Route
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

The patrol leader points out on the map to each scout a location they must find in the field and the reconnaissance they must bring back from its vicinity. For example: measuring the speed of a river’s current and its width, describing a nearby grove, or noting the visibility of prominent terrain features from the marked point, etc. Each scout receives a different task. All study the map for several minutes, trace the route they are to take, and try to memorize it; then each searches for their point without the map’s help (a compass may be permitted).

The distance should be roughly the same for everyone, and the task itself should take approximately the same amount of time. Who will bring back a written report within the set time? (One must return regardless of whether the task is completed.) The accuracy of the report must be verified. The entire exercise should take place in less familiar terrain.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Following the Route Sketch — to the Hideout
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

The exercise takes place in unfamiliar terrain. From a marked point on the terrain, one patrol sets out and, after a half-hour march, hides in the area. During the march, a route sketch 1) is made, which is then given to the second patrol. The second patrol must use this sketch to locate the first within a specified time.

The sketch is drawn without a map, and it must not include the names of any localities. During the search, it is also forbidden to use a map, ask passersby for directions, or send individual scouts to search the area. Naturally, the hideout cannot be in a deep forest. The scout holding the sketch should be careful not to reveal the direction of the hideout through the path they take.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Can You Find It?
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

A scout patrol, and each scout individually, must locate a specific terrain feature within a pre-designated area of several square kilometers. This could be a hut, a cellar, a copse, a stack of beams, etc. To force the scout to orient themselves by cardinal directions, add that the object lies in the NW direction from a roadside cross, another in the S-SW direction from a solitary tree, etc. These instructions should be precise, based either on direct observation or a map.

Each scout must find their object, examine it thoroughly, memorize its distinctive features, and sketch its position relative to the cardinal directions and the nearest surrounding features. At the assembly point, the sketches are compared, and errors are pointed out. A time limit for the search may be set in advance.

Now, imagine that the order includes a small addition: *"the area is occupied by enemy patrols"*—and send the red patrol earlier with the order that, if they spot a white scout reconnoitering the area, they must prevent it by driving him from his position and, if possible, taking him prisoner. The entire exercise will not only take a different shape but, by presenting great difficulties to the whites, will force them to change their approach.

Each white scout will now have to search for their object unnoticed, approach it cautiously, and constantly scan the surroundings with a watchful eye to avoid falling into a trap, and return just as cautiously after completing the task.

A rule can be added that the reds must act together and are not allowed to scatter to act individually. The method of taking prisoners should also be defined in advance—whether by calling out from a distance of 10–15 steps, by touching with a hand, or by tearing off a ribbon from the arm.

Here is an example of how a seemingly small addition can fundamentally change the nature of the exercise. This can be applied to a whole range of other exercises, thereby vastly expanding their scope.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: With a Rough Sketch in Hand
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

Scouts receive a sketch of a certain area, on which only a few of the most important landmarks are drawn and the north direction is marked. Each has a point in their sketch marked with a cross, which they must locate using a compass and stop at. The patrol leader checks, using a map, whether each scout is in the correct place.

At the start of the march, everyone is only told that the sought-after section of terrain is, for example, in the Z direction, and if one wishes to make the task easier, the distance (e.g., 3–5 km) or the time it will take to reach it is also provided.

The exercise can be varied by adding the task of supplementing the sketch by drawing in a few more prominent terrain features, whose positions must be determined using the compass so that the sketch now represents a complete and valuable depiction. Scouts must first locate the terrain shown in the sketch and then continuously orient themselves to the cardinal directions in order to place new details in the correct spots on the sketch.

As with the previous exercise, an enemy patrol can also be added here.

![img-8.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-077-img-8.jpeg)

Fig. 19.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Following the Compass Rose
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

In partially wooded terrain, I place 5–10 small flags made of colored tissue paper. They stand upright from the ground, about a dozen centimeters tall. For each flag, I assign 1–2 scouts, and to each of them I provide the color of the flag they must find and its exact location on the map. Each scout "reads the map," i.e., studies the route they must take to reach their flag without losing their way, and then sets off on the search.

![img-9.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-078-img-9.jpeg)

Fig. 20.

The distance may range from 500–1500 paces. Whoever finds their flag will also discover a small box next to it, containing a note with the bearing (azimuth) they must follow to the next objective and the distance to that objective (100–300 paces). The objective is a second flag of the same height and color as the first. Who (or which pair) will return with one flag, and who—this being the proper task—will bring back both? (Fig. 20).

For the game to succeed, the leader must first place the initial flags in locations that can be precisely marked on the map. Then, after setting each flag, they must proceed strictly along the given bearing line (i.e., at the specified azimuth) and place the second flag exactly at the given distance. These second flags should be equally visible to all.

If someone fails to find the second flag on their first attempt, they should return to the first flag and try again along the given bearing, rather than aimlessly searching around. Therefore, the first flag should not be taken until the second one is found.
