author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Finding a Marching Troop
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

a) In this exercise, the goal is to locate one's own troop, which is marching in a designated direction known to the scouting patrol.

The marching troop is represented by one scout squad, and the scouting patrol by another. The troop marches, for example, along road A—B, while the patrol is sent to C with the task of checking if the enemy is present there, and then to L to search the grove. From both locations, messengers are to bring reports to the advancing troop on the road.

Each messenger, after completing their task, heads in the direction where they are most likely to encounter the marching troop and orients themselves to avoid losing the road. If they find the troop, all is well; if not, they must rely on intelligence gathered from passersby, or on tracks along the road the troop was supposed to take (which may have been prearranged and deliberately left along the way), or by observing the surroundings from a high vantage point, etc., to conclude whether the troop has already passed or is yet to arrive. They must then either catch up to the troop or wait for it.

This provides ample opportunity for keen observation and orientation, relying solely on one's own wit and strength.

The time at which the report arrives (with the place and time of dispatch recorded) allows one to determine whether the task was completed properly or not. It also provides an opportunity, during a later inspection of the terrain (or based on a map), for an instructive discussion of the messenger's actions and to give appropriate guidance for the future.

Both squads then meet at a designated assembly point.

b) Let us add a small variation to the previous exercise: the main troop, without the knowledge of the patrol sent off to the side, changes its marching direction (e.g., based on information that the original road is occupied by the enemy). This creates a new situation, giving the messenger room to demonstrate their skills.

The messenger will not find their troop where they expected it to be. They lack any indication of whether the troop has not yet arrived or has already passed that point. They must rely solely on their own wit and sense of direction to fulfill the order and deliver the report.

If, in fact, an enemy detachment has been placed along the main troop's marching route, forcing the marching troop to deviate from its original direction, the difficulties for both the messenger and the scouting patrol—now cut off—will increase tenfold. It will no longer be just about delivering reports and finding their own troop, or independent orientation in the terrain, but also about breaking through the enemy, who aims to intercept the reports. Both the messenger and the entire scouting patrol must accomplish this.

![img-10.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-079-img-10.jpeg)

*Fig. 21.*

For example, the red team is ordered to occupy points M and L, capture any messenger heading toward B, and prevent or hinder the scouting patrol from breaking through in that direction.

The white troop advances along road A—B and has orders to avoid any enemy patrols encountered on the road. After leaving A, it sends scouts toward grove L and to point M. Upon receiving information that the red team is at M, it deviates from its original direction around point C to bypass the threatened area.

Meanwhile, from grove L (where the scouting patrol was sent), the patrol dispatches a messenger with a report in the direction of approximately C₁, assuming (based on the information they had) that the main troop is still advancing along road A—B. The messenger must break through the enemy line, and if successful, will not find the troop and must rack their brains to locate it and deliver the report. Behind them, the patrol breaks through either as a group or in a skirmish line, to later regroup at the designated assembly point.

Before the exercise, the conditions for any potential encounter with the enemy must be established.

![img-0.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-081-img-0.jpeg)

*Fig. 22.*

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Visibility of Objects
body:
The following exercises, in addition to developing visual acuity and observance, aim to teach how lighting, color, background, the size of an object, and whether it is stationary or moving affect its visibility—that is, how easily or difficult it is to distinguish.

Two patrols stand facing each other with signaling flags at a distance of several hundred paces and present as observation targets several Scouts of the same height, always all at the same distance from the opponent. Each time, the whites set up the targets, and the reds observe. After the observation is complete, a prearranged signal is given with the flag, and the patrols switch roles.

a) Two Scouts stand: one in the sun, the other in the shade; the latter is less visible. Conclusion: during reconnaissance, avoid standing in the sun.

b) One Scout, dressed in white, stands against a very bright background (e.g., a house wall) in such a way that he casts no shadow; a second, dressed in black, stands against the same background; a third, dressed in black, stands against greenery; a fourth and fifth stand there as well, one in a gray-green Scout uniform and the other dressed in white. Each will notice the differences in the clarity of the target and conclude that one should stand against a background similar to one’s clothing, and in any case, never against the sky (e.g., on the top of a hill).

c) One stands, another kneels, a third lies down, all close to each other, dressed the same, and against the same background. The third is the least visible; therefore, in a pinch, try to make yourself as small a target as possible.

d) Against the same background and in the same clothing, one Scout stands or lies still, while the other walks, kneels, etc. Then both disappear and reappear, but the first appears and disappears slowly, while the second does so quickly. Conclusion: if they are looking in your direction, do not move; and if you must, move slowly.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: March in a Straight Direction
body:
From a staff planted in the ground by the patrol leader, the scouts march one after another in a straight line toward a designated target (a tree trunk, the edge of a house, etc.). During the march, they help themselves maintain an accurate direction by selecting intermediate points (pebbles, clumps of earth, light or dark patches of ground, etc.) lying on the line of march. After walking 100 (or 200–400) paces, each scout plants their staff where they have stopped. The patrol leader, looking through his staff at the target, measures the extent of the deviation from the line of march; the winner is the one who deviated the least.

The deviation is always measured from the same position, holding a ruler horizontally, with the arm extended. If the scouts march one after another to the same target, each must remove their staff after measuring the deviation, as it could mislead the next scout during their march.

At first, they march shorter distances, then longer ones (also running), first on level ground and then on uneven terrain, but always with the target constantly in sight.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Marking a Straight Line with a Compass
body:
The task is to mark a straight line in a specific direction, e.g., W–E. The first scout stands with a compass in hand, facing west. The second scout walks 30–50 paces in that direction according to the compass, and the third scout walks another few dozen paces, then aligns with the two previous scouts. The first scout then moves forward, positioning himself in line with the others, and so on. The line can be extended as needed, marking each abandoned position with a stick or stone.

The same method can be used to mark a line in the required direction at night using flashlights.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Kim’s Game in the Field
body:
Everyone stands with their back to the terrain that is to be observed. Its boundaries to the left and right are marked by prominent, easily noticeable objects. ("You will observe the terrain from the railway line on the left to the river on the right.") Now, "About turn!" and each person observes intently for 1 minute. Then, "About turn!" again, and each person writes down answers to a series of questions: "How many chimneys are on the factory building by the river? — What color is the cottage under the forest? — What is interesting on its roof? — What is the background of the chapel by the road? — What stands by the poplar in the meadow?" and so on. Guessing is not allowed; each person provides an answer only if they have noticed the thing in question. By counting the points for correct answers, the patrol leader will see who was the best observer.

It is also possible to focus the observation on a single object, such as a factory building, and then ask appropriate questions: "How many chimneys does it have? — What kind? — How many windows? — What is its background?" and so on. With practice, the observation time can be shortened.

Instead of answering questions, one may require a description of the terrain, and at first, without turning away from it. This is more difficult than it appears. Begin with the terrain’s layout, then move on to describing the objects. In any case, after the exercise, the terrain should be viewed once more so that everyone can check for omissions in their answers.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: What Do You See?
body:
—During a march to exercises, the patrol leader poses a series of questions, such as: «How many cows are grazing in the pasture? — How many trees are in the group on the meadow? — How many windows are in the building by the road? — How many broken panes? — How many cars are in the passing train? How many people are working in the field? How many of them are without head coverings? — How many ducks are swimming in the pond?» etc. After a brief observation (count to 5 or 10), each scout records their answer. The answers are then checked, and points are awarded for the best responses. Who will have the most points upon reaching the destination? This kind of competition can also take place between two patrols. In such cases, each correct answer counts toward the patrol’s score, not the individual scout’s.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: The Grid
body:
A piece of cardboard, divided into 16 squares measuring 6 × 6 cm, is placed on a tree trunk at eye level.

Single- or double-digit numbers are placed in these squares, leaving some empty (see Fig. 24).

Scouts, each equipped with a similarly gridded sheet, line up at a distance of several dozen paces from the cardboard and attempt to read the numbers, recording the ones they decipher in the corresponding squares on their own sheets. Naturally, one will manage this from a greater distance, another from a shorter one. They therefore advance slowly, and each scout who has filled their entire sheet stops and marks the spot they have reached.

The patrol leader checks the sheet, confirming its correctness or identifying errors (in which case the scout moves closer to correct the mistake). Finally, the distance in paces from which the numbers were correctly read is recorded. When the game is repeated at a later time, the results are compared to determine any improvement—i.e., whether a given scout has read the numbers from a greater distance than before.

The cardboard is intended for long-term use, so the numbers are not drawn directly on it but on separate slips of paper, which are placed in the squares. Both the numbers and their arrangement are changed each time.

|  14 |  | 26 |   |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|   | 18 | 5 |   |
|  77 | 3 |  | 32  |
|  19 |  | 85 |   |

*Fig. 24.*

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Observation of the Road
body:
Observation can be directed not only at specially indicated objects but also at everything encountered during the march—both the terrain configuration to the right and left of the road and objects near and far. Moreover, observations should be memorized. This forms a distinct exercise:

It is announced that close observation of the road over a distance of, for example, 3 km is required. After covering this distance—a halt is called, and the leader asks a series of questions: *"What were the horses like at the first cart passed? — Who was sitting on it? — What was interesting on the roof of the small church? — What inscription was on the roadside chapel? — How many telegraph wires ran along the road? — What was heard at the entrance to the bridge? — What was on the left bank of the river right by the bridge?"* and so on.

As before, each person writes down their answers without revealing them to the others, and then the answers are scored in favor of the scout or their patrol. The patrol leader must, of course, note all observations during the march that they will later ask about.

The exercise is significantly easier if it is announced that questions will only concern nature, or only artificial objects passed during the march, or actions seen along the way, or unusual things, etc. It will also be easier if questions are asked immediately after passing a given object rather than only after completing the entire route.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: A Strange Path
body:
A route—chosen by the patrol leader—leads through varied terrain (sections of forest, buildings, thickets, hollows, etc.) and is several hundred or even one or two thousand paces long. The entire patrol walks this route to become thoroughly familiar with it and then stops at the end of the path.

Meanwhile, the patrol leader returns and places a series of unusual objects along the route, sometimes on the ground, sometimes above it: he might place a mushroom on a tree branch, make a small pyramid of sticks on the ground, drive an axe into a tree, stretch a thread overhead across the path, bury a bottle in the ground with its base up, place a hawthorn berry on a blackthorn bush, or draw a bird in chalk on a fence, and so on. The more of these unusual things, the better.

At a given signal, the scouts return to the patrol leader at set time intervals (the patrol leader may use regular signals), and each writes down on a piece of paper what interesting things they noticed. From the papers, it will be clear who observed the most.

It is also possible to set in advance the maximum allowed time in which the route must be covered for the observations to count. The scouts do not know how many strange objects have been placed along the route.

This game is also suitable for competitions between patrols. In that case, scouts from one patrol and then another are sent along the route, and each noted object counts as 1 point for their patrol.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Who will spot it?
body:
We stand on a hill from which there is a fairly extensive view. The question is asked: «Where is the wayside shrine surrounded by trees?» Everyone eagerly scans the area. A shout — someone has spotted it and points in that direction. Now they describe its exact location, and for the discovery, they receive a point. We turn to the opposite side, then the question: «Who sees the black cow?» Eyes scan the distance, everyone observes intently, someone has found the cow. «Where is the statue by the road? Where is the footbridge over the stream?» and so on. Ten such questions, always one point for each discovery. Who will collect the most?

For the skilled, small, hard-to-spot objects are chosen; for beginners, easy ones.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: The Magical Corner
body:
The patrol observes for several minutes a section of terrain with boundaries precisely defined by the patrol leader (a few hundred meters in width and depth). After the observation, they move to a concealed spot from which this section is not visible.

Meanwhile, several scouts alter the appearance of the terrain: either removing certain objects, rearranging them, or adding things that were not there before. For example, they might take one log from a woodpile and place it aside on the ground; turn a cart by its shaft in the opposite direction; move a large stone and chalk another; remove previously stuck branches that imitated a bush and place them elsewhere; and finally, they themselves hide behind the terrain’s cover. (All changes made must be recorded).

At a signal given by them, the patrol emerges from hiding and tries to catch the changes that, as if by a magician’s wand, have occurred in the terrain. Each scout observes separately and notes the changes they notice. After the observation is complete, at a given signal, the perpetrators of this change in the scene emerge from hiding.

Beforehand, the patrol leader instructs that observation must not be haphazard: first, the closer terrain is observed, then the farther, moving in sections across and in depth.

This game can be turned into a competition between two patrols.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: From Outpost to Outpost
body:
At the assembly point, the red patrol remains. The white patrol sets out and, every few hundred paces, leaves a small group of scouts. In one spot, three remain; in another, one; then two, and so on. The patrol’s route passes through varied terrain and in different directions, such that the last group is approximately the same distance from the assembly point as the first.

![img-2.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-094-img-2.jpeg)

Fig. 25.

Once the setup is complete, the red scouts are sent out one by one, each at three-minute intervals. Each must visit all the outposts, starting from the last and ending at the first, then return to the assembly point. When a messenger approaches, the outpost assumes a specific position or performs a certain action, maintaining the same posture or movements for every messenger. (For example, one sits cross-legged and writes, another wipes his brow with a handkerchief, a third kindles a fire, etc.). Upon arrival, the messenger receives instructions on where to find the next group (e.g., *"Go along the stream until you reach a solitary alder, then turn right along the boundary to the road; beyond the road, behind the birch grove, is the next outpost"*) and immediately sets off, committing to memory the posture and actions of all members of the outpost. Upon reaching the second outpost, he receives further directions, and so on, until he returns to the assembly point. The patrol leader records the departure and return times of each scout.

When all have returned, a series of questions follows, such as: *How many were in group 2? How were the scouts dressed in group 3? What was the posture of the people in group 1? What were they doing in group 4?* Each scout writes his answers on a piece of paper and submits them to the patrol leader. After the outposts return at a given signal, the accuracy of the answers is verified. The winner is the one who provides the best answers, but he must also have a good time for visiting the outposts; otherwise, he is moved down one place in the ranking or even disqualified from the results. (The leader knows the distances between outposts and sets a minimum time required to complete the circuit).

The same process is then repeated with the red scouts as outposts and the white scouts as messengers. If this is a competition between two patrols, half of the white and half of the red scouts are stationed as outposts, while the rest take turns visiting them. Suppose a white scout gives the best answer. Then the scouts switch roles, and if a white scout again proves the best, the whites win; otherwise, the match is undecided.

Scouts should be reminded that the instructions given to messengers must be exactly the same for each one. Messengers travel in the opposite direction from the one in which the outposts were placed, as otherwise they could not receive directions for the next leg of their journey. When setting up the groups a second time, the same distances must be maintained between them.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Scout Hunts
body:
In a coniferous forest, there is a polygon enclosed by a rope with a diameter of several dozen paces.

Inside the polygon, there is game: a dozen or so cardboard figures imitating a squirrel, hare, badger, woodpecker, jay, etc., placed either on the ground or on trees and bushes.

The patrol, armed with pine cones (previously collected), sets out to find this hunting ground. Each scout searches separately. Whoever finds it shoots with pine cones to either knock over the animal or dislodge it from a branch. When they run out of pine cones, they go to fetch a new supply without revealing their discovery. Shooting is only allowed from outside the rope. Hidden judges (e.g., in trees) oversee the hunt and remain concealed so as not to reveal the location of the hunting ground with their presence. Who will be the king of the hunt?

If the animals are placed in good hiding spots so that they can only be seen from certain points, spotting them will not be too easy. A whistle ends the hunt$^{1}$.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Searching for Plants
body:
The patrol leader distributes among the scouts samples of 10 previously collected plants and orders them to find and bring them back to camp. These are, of course, plants that are either in the wider vicinity of the camp or are not encountered at every step.

This search can be turned into a kind of competition among the scouts, who are sent out individually or in pairs. The winner is the one who returns to camp the fastest with the requested plants.

After the exercise, one must never omit identifying the plants brought back, as this expands the scouts' botanical knowledge and helps them memorize the names of the plants.

One can also order them to bring leaves from 10 arbitrary trees or shrubs, or 10 species of mushrooms, and distinguish between edible and poisonous ones. (However, one must never attempt to cook food from supposedly edible mushrooms due to the ease of making a mistake).

One can also ask them to bring 10 plants known to a given scout so that others may learn them, or something unusual, rarely encountered, something that will intrigue everyone.

For such games, the patrol leader should have a key for identifying plants if their botanical knowledge is not sufficiently extensive.

A similar collection can be made with insects or minerals.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Who Made the Mistake?
body:
Signalling can be practiced in the form of a game or play. Here is one for beginners:

Two patrols stand at a distance of several hundred paces and send out signalmen. The white [patrol] gives a word of 3–4 letters, the red [patrol] reads it (no one is allowed to help), and to prove they have read it, they repeat the word. After repeating, they themselves give a word of 3–4 letters, which the white [patrol] must then repeat, and so on. Eventually, one of them cannot do this, and then they drop out, passing the flag to the next [signalman] (fig. 23).

The patrol that drops out first loses. Therefore, it is necessary to know the Morse alphabet well. Here is the best way to memorize it:

For each letter, memorize one word that begins with that very letter. The number of syllables in the word corresponds to the number of symbols in Morse code. In whichever syllable you find the letter *o*, there is a dash, while the other syllables represent dots in the Morse alphabet.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Through a Chain of Stations
body:
Several patrols (at least two) position themselves in the field at equal distances from a location indicated to them on a map, e.g., from hill ×. At the designated time, all patrols set out toward this hill, leaving 3 scouts at their starting point with a planted flag. Along the way, they set up signaling stations (at least one) so that, in the end, a group of 2–3 scouts reaches the hilltop. This creates a chain of stations, arranged in such a way that each station is visible only to its neighboring stations.

Whoever reaches the hill receives a written order from the scout stationed there, which must be passed along the chain back to the initial station. The initial station immediately executes the order, and the judge present there records the time when the order was carried out. Which patrol will execute the order the fastest?

The order should be short and the same for all patrols, e.g., *"Light a fire with strong smoke."*

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Secret Dispatch
body:
A vital, secret dispatch from the Whites is being transmitted through a chain of signaling stations. The objective is to intercept it.

This chain, consisting of 3–4 stations, is well concealed (choose suitable terrain!); it is not easy to track down.

The Reds know only that a station is located, for example, in the western direction from their position. They divide into groups of 2–3 scouts and set out to locate it. The intercepted dispatch must be delivered to the flag at the assembly point.

The Whites transmit the dispatch only at a designated hour, which should be timed so that the patrols have sufficient time to search for the chain and position themselves in a favorable, concealed spot.

Each group operates separately and tries to intercept the dispatch in its entirety or at least fragments of it. Which group will do this best?

It should be added that the Whites are not allowed to begin signaling before the designated hour. Furthermore, the dispatch must consist of 3–4 sentences, each of a few words, with a 3-minute interval between each sentence.

The content of the secret dispatch is handed only to the initial station by the leader.

If any patrol is spotted by one of the stations, it is disqualified from the competition, even if it successfully intercepts the dispatch.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: By Signs
body:
At greater distances, Scouts communicate using flag signaling (or a lantern at night), while at shorter distances, they use hand, cap, or stick signals. There is a series of such signals expressing the most important actions during stalking, e.g., *"forward — run — backward — assembly — take cover"* and so on. However, these are not sufficient, as there are often orders that are difficult to convey with these few conventional signals, and which cannot be given by signaling or voice. A Scout should learn, as it were, to read the thoughts of his patrol leader as conveyed through signs that illustrate those thoughts as clearly as possible. This is a field for creativity on the part of the one giving the signals, and for intuition on the part of the one receiving them. This skill—both in deftly giving signals and in accurately interpreting them—must be acquired through appropriate practice.

The patrol leader lies on the ground, with the Scouts positioned at a distance where they cannot hear him. The patrol leader gives an order in signs, e.g., *"Climb the tree on the left side."* The first Scout tries to understand the given signals. If he does not understand, he signals this with a pendulum-like motion of his hand. The patrol leader repeats the order, possibly altering the signals slightly, until the message is understood. Then, in turn, an order is given to the second Scout, e.g., *"Crawl to the ditch on the right,"* or *"Circle the house,"* or *"Go to the hill on the right, see if there is an enemy there, and signal back"* and so on. After a short time, the Scouts will learn to read their patrol leader’s thoughts. If these can often be read from the eyes or facial expression, they can be even more easily grasped from appropriate gestures.

As a last resort, one can also use the Morse alphabet, signaled by hand from a prone position. The "call" of the sender and the "response" of the receiver is raising the hand vertically upward. A *"dot"* is indicated by raising the hand upward, a *"dash"* by extending it horizontally. After each signal, the hand is lowered to the chest. (If lying facing toward or away from the receiver, the arm is raised horizontally to the side; if lying sideways, horizontally forward—otherwise the movement will not be noticed).

A pause is naturally made after each letter. The end of each word is indicated by a circle traced in the air with the fist; the receiver gives the same sign to indicate *"understood."* Three circles in succession signify the end of the order. An *"error"* is signaled by a pendulum-like motion of the open palm.

Now, let us apply the reading of the patrol leader’s thoughts in the following exercise:

Several Scouts stand on a hill, making no attempt to conceal themselves. They are visible from afar. The surrounding terrain is obscure, hilly, full of thickets, gardens, fences, ditches, etc., facilitating stalking. The rest of the Scouts, from a distance of 1,000 paces, approach the enemy, guided solely by the patrol leader’s signals. The goal is to approach from the front, side, or rear to within 200 paces. The patrol leader himself creeps forward, seeking the best route with plenty of cover; the rest follow him, obeying the given signals (no verbal orders are allowed!), sometimes advancing individually, sometimes in groups of 2–3, some to the right, some to the left, etc., and always executing the given signals—not acting on their own initiative. Naturally, as long as the patrol advances as a whole, the assistant patrol leader receives the orders; once the patrol scatters, individual groups receive orders directly or via the assistant. A permanent liaison can also be introduced between the patrol leader and the patrol, who takes the orders and relays them backward.

The enemy observes from where the foe is approaching and, upon spotting them, tries not to lose sight of them. They note all clumsiness in the stalking, all mistakes, and later report them to the patrol leader. In this way, there is good control over the proficiency of individual Scouts, and lessons are drawn for the future.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Following the Signs in the Sketch
body:
The patrol leader hands the scouts a sheet of paper on which only conventional symbols of various terrain features are drawn, in the order in which the marching patrol may encounter them. The route of the march is unknown to the scouts, as only the initial direction is given, e.g., North-West. The sheet may contain, for example, a drawing of a roadside cross, then a field road, a factory chimney, a bridge, etc. The last symbol is the destination of the march.

Based on this sheet, the patrol must reach the destination within the specified time. Sometimes this is easy, but at other times they get stuck when they encounter several similar objects and do not know which one is marked on the sheet. Then the scouts must scatter in different directions until one of them finds the next sign.

Alternatively, such a sheet can be given to each member of the patrol, in which case they are sent off one after another at 10-minute intervals, and the time of arrival of each is recorded at the destination. Who will arrive within the prescribed time?

The exercise becomes more difficult if, in addition to reaching the designated point, the scouts are also tasked with drawing a sketch of the route taken$^{1}$.

The exercise is made even more difficult if this sketch is drawn from memory during a halt.

On the return journey, the sketches are compared with the terrain, and inaccuracies or errors are marked on them. This is done not by the scout who drew the sketch in question.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Following the First Scout's Signs
body:
One scout walks along a route marked on a map and makes various agreed-upon signs (with chalk, arranged sticks, laid stones, tied grass or branches, etc.). He records the order and type of signs on a piece of paper. The rest follow him, one scout after another, every few minutes. Each scout follows the signs and notes the ones he observes on his own paper. The last scout additionally erases all the signs. Who recorded the most signs? — In this exercise, the scouts do not track the signs but merely search for them, knowing the route of the march.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: As the Signs Command
body:
The previous exercise can be arranged differently. Here, the scout leading the way does not make the agreed-upon but meaningless signs, but only those that have a specific meaning. The patrol following him observes the signs and acts accordingly. There are many such signs; in addition to the generally known ones, each patrol may have its own secret signs. For example, an arrow—whether made of sticks or chalk—indicates the direction of the march; then the patrol encounters a sign forbidding them to proceed further and a sign that a hidden letter is nearby, which explains the matter, followed by a sign to stop, a sign of danger (quick dispersal), and so on.

These signs can be of all kinds. For example:

| → | Go in the direction of the arrow. | ⊕ | Wait 10 minutes. |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| → | Go quickly. | ⊕ | " 15 " |
| → | Run! | ⊕ | " 20 " |
| ← | Turn back. | ⊕⊕ | " 40 " etc. |
| ← | Turn back quickly. | ⊙ | I went home. |
| ← | " run | ⊙ | We will wait in the nearest village. |
| ⊕ | Proceed cautiously. | □ | Upon arrival here, shout. |
| × | Do not go this way. | □ | Upon arrival here, shout several times. |
| × | Stop, look for another path. | — | Upon arrival here, whistle. |
| * | Help! | □→ | A letter a few steps away. |
| ⊕ | We will meet here in one hour. | ⊖ | Good water. |
| ⊕ | We will meet here in 2 hours. | × | Enemy! |
| ⊕ | We will meet here in 3 hours, etc. | × | We have bypassed the enemy. |
| ⊙ | Stand in place (time unlimited). | ⊕ | Danger. |
| ⊙ | Wait 5 minutes. | ⊕ | We have split up. |

Signs can also be made from arranged stones, tied grass, twigs, etc. For example, arranged as:

![img-0.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-105-img-0.jpeg)

Go to the left.

Danger.

Each patrol may also have its own secret signs, known only to themselves.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Estimating Distances
body:
a) Measure a space of 100 m (on a road, you have it between two roadside stones) and have the entire patrol walk it in double steps, i.e., counting each time the left foot steps. After taking 66.5 such double steps, the patrol should reach the finish line. However, some will not reach it, others may pass it—the former took steps that were too small, the latter too large. Now the patrol walks back, and if necessary, repeats this a third and fourth time until every Scout, taking 133 steps, covers exactly 100 m. In this way, each will feel the muscle tension required to take a step of 75 cm, and later, when measuring any distance by steps, will strive to always feel the same degree of tension, i.e., will take normal steps of 75 cm.

![img-2.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-106-img-2.jpeg)

Fig. 27.

Now, have four Scouts stand in a straight line at distances of 100, 200, 300, and 400 m, one behind the other. With the rest of the patrol, stand in the extension of this line but slightly to the side. The patrol observes those standing and first tries to firmly impress upon their eyes the distance of 100 m as the basic measure for estimating greater distances.

Then draw the Scouts' attention to the fact that an object appears smaller as it moves away, that details of the image gradually blur, and that the distances between the standing figures seem to decrease as they move farther away. These circumstances are always taken into account when estimating greater distances.

Next, position Scouts at the same distances of 100, 200, 300, and 400 m, but in different directions and against the same background. During positioning, the patrol should face away from those being placed. Based on the previously seen image, each Scout then estimates the distance of all those positioned.

Afterward, the actual distances are given, and the entire patrol observes them to better imprint these distances in their minds.

This concludes the first exercise. Each exercise should always be repeated with the previously positioned Scouts.

b) Two patrols stand opposite each other at a distance of 500 m. This space is marked by two sticks. Each patrol has a signaling flag. The white patrol turns away, and the red patrol sends one Scout to a distance of 300 m, so he stands at a distance of 500–300 m, i.e., 200 m from the whites. Flag up: The whites turn around, and each estimates the distance of the red Scout, writing it on a piece of paper (corrections are not allowed). After 50 seconds, the red Scout returns, his comrades turn away, and the whites send one of their own to a certain distance, e.g., 100 m (500–100 = 400 m from the reds). On the flag signal, the reds now estimate his distance, and so on. After an agreed number of estimates, the patrol leader collects the notes, compares them with the actual distances (held by the opposing patrol), and then both patrol leaders determine which patrol made fewer errors in estimation. That patrol wins.

c) Position Scouts at the same distances in different directions. One stands against a light background, another against a dark one; one on a uniform plain, another in undulating terrain, partially obscured; one lies down, another kneels or stands (always both at the same distance). Instruct the rest to estimate the distance of each pair, and when errors are made, point out the apparent difference in distances and thus the underestimation or overestimation of the same distance, depending on the conditions in which the observed object is found. Also note that distances are estimated differently on a bright or cloudy day, a dry or humid day, when the sun is behind or in the face, etc. (see the relevant handbook). Then have the estimators lie on the ground and note that the same object appears more distant from this position.

d) In the fourth exercise, independent estimation is already practiced within 100–400 steps, taking into account various estimation conditions. Each Scout individually and independently records in a corresponding card (below) the estimated distance of all objects in sequence from left to right. The patrol leader then provides the actual distances and enters them into each Scout’s card, also calculating the percentage of error (see below). In this way, each Scout becomes aware of the type of error made in estimation.

Next, those who were previously positioned take their turn at estimating.

As for competitions between whites and reds, both patrols gather together, and each estimates individually and independently. After calculating the percentage of errors in the cards, it is easy to see which patrol estimated better.

e) Next, proceed to estimating distances not as before in depth, but across the terrain, i.e., not the distance of an object from oneself, but the space between two objects in the terrain. For this purpose, position Scouts in a straight line as in exercise a), but stand with the rest not in its extension but to the side. Note that, as before, the distances between those standing appear smaller the farther one stands from them.

Then position Scouts at various distances from each other (within 100–400 m) and estimate them from different points.

f) Only when Scouts can accurately estimate distances up to 400 m under various conditions with a relatively small error should you proceed to estimating up to 800 m, and gradually even greater distances. The procedure is as in a) and d).

Such larger spaces are divided by eye into halves or even quarters, and then the half or quarter is estimated. This greatly facilitates estimation and guards against excessive error.

One should always strive to gain practice in estimating from a prone position. The standing position is only an introductory posture in learning.

Relatively quickly, one gains skill in estimation, but it is also quickly lost with prolonged neglect. These exercises should therefore be practiced frequently, and every march on an excursion provides an opportunity: a few or a dozen Scouts sent ahead mark the starting point for estimation and, positioning themselves at various distances, wait for the approaching patrol. After estimation, the marching patrol joins them to send others ahead for a similar exercise at another location. This approach saves a lot of time and adds variety to the march.

In such an exercise, each Scout sent ahead must be given the distance at which to stand, the position to take (standing, kneeling, lying), and the signal (whistle or flag) on which to change position, and on which to change distance and to what. If these things are not established, much time will be lost, and the exercise will fail. After the exercise, the actual distances should be provided to the Scouts.

Similarly, after estimating people, various terrain objects are also estimated, e.g., the distance to a church, house, cart, etc.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Judging in the Dark
body:
A dark evening. One scout sets off into the field, counting his steps. After some time, he stops, and at the patrol leader’s whistle, he flashes an electric torch for 5 seconds. Then he makes a mark where he stood and moves aside or hides. The rest estimate how far away the light was and in which direction it flashed. Then everyone sets off, and each stops at the spot where, in their estimation, the light had flashed. Who stands closest—and who went in the best direction? The one who judged best takes the torch and goes into the field, while the rest will do the judging.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Will-o'-the-wisp
body:
Two scouts go into the field with an electric torch. Two minutes later, the rest set off in pursuit of them. The pursued flash the light every minute, constantly changing position in order to escape the chase. If things go badly, they separate to divide the pursuers; the one without the torch tries to draw as many pursuers as possible to himself in order to help his comrade. Both fugitives should previously agree on signals between themselves. The torch passes from hand to hand, always to the one in less danger.

Within the designated time, the one carrying the torch must be surrounded and taken prisoner. The area designated for the exercise should be quite spacious but bounded.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Keep Your Eyes Open
body:
A white scout is given the order: «You will walk 10 minutes along the road, then 300 paces in the direction of NW, where you will find a wayside shrine surrounded by trees—hide there. A red scout will arrive; follow him, for you must later describe what he did.»

The red scout is ordered to take a different route to the same shrine so that he arrives

![img-3.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-112-img-3.jpeg)

Fig. 28.

a few minutes after the white scout. Upon arrival, he may, for example, be tasked with drawing the outline of the shrine or sketching on paper the most prominently visible terrain features from that spot, etc.

After the red scout leaves, the white scout also departs unnoticed. The patrol leader, upon receiving the drawing from the red scout, asks him if he saw anything else interesting. If the answer is no, he has the white scout describe all of the red scout’s actions. Next time, the red scout will keep his eyes open.

In this way, a series of scouts can be stationed at various points, while others are given tasks to perform at those same locations. An entire patrol can also be sent out, which will find it harder to hide, especially if not one but several enemies arrive.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Scouting
body:
On a terrain extending up to 1,000 meters in depth and several hundred meters in width, with its lateral boundaries established, a patrol of *reds* is positioned. One lies, kneels, or stands closer, another farther away; in one spot stands a single scout, in another two together, and so on. Distances of 100—200—300 meters, etc., up to 1,000 meters have previously been measured and noted by both patrol leaders, along with the terrain features located at these distances.

At the observation point stands the patrol leader of the *whites*, who, upon the signal to begin the exercise, raises a flag upward. The *reds* remain motionless so as not to reveal their positions (hiding is not permitted), while the *whites* approach their patrol leader from concealment, and each individually searches the terrain for the *reds* (the number of whom should be known to them). If the *whites* cannot locate one of the *reds*, the patrol leader narrows the observation area to assist them; if even then no one finds him, the flag is moved left and right, and at this signal, the *reds* begin to move, making them easier to spot.

After all have been located, their distances are estimated. Each records their estimates in their own card, in the order prescribed by the patrol leader. Then, the actual distances are provided to verify any errors.

The *whites* return to their concealment, the flag is lowered, and the *reds* change their positions. When they are ready, they signal with a whistle. The flag is then raised again. The *whites* emerge once more and search the terrain again, then estimate the distances. This is repeated three times, after which both patrols switch roles.

If the exercise is competitive, upon completion, the percentage of errors for both patrols is calculated to determine the winner.

This exercise can be varied by setting a time limit for observation (e.g., up to 5 minutes), during which each individual records their observations, noting precisely where and in what position the sought scout is located. Then, the notes are collected to determine who discovered the most scouts.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Disappearing Heads
body:
In a hidden spot, in a ravine or on a hillside, a scout patrol (in this case, 8 scouts) takes position, while the patrol leader stands at the edge of the ravine with a whistle and a flag in hand. The wings of the hiding place, which is several dozen paces long, are marked with clearly visible distant signs (flags). At a distance of 300–500 paces, another patrol stands similarly hidden, with its patrol leader visible and holding a flag. The first patrol will appear at intervals in various formations, while the second will observe. The patrol leader has a sheet with 8–10 consecutive formation changes noted. For example:

![img-4.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-115-img-4.jpeg)

Fig. 29.

1. Eight heads in a 3—2—1—2 formation
2. Six heads in a 1—1—2—2 formation
3. Five heads, with three more joining after 1 minute
4. Six heads, then two disappear, and two new ones appear on the flank, etc.

On the patrol leader’s command, the scouts line up along the ravine in the first formation and poke their heads out so that they can clearly see the opposing patrol leader in full height. Then, a whistle and a flag signal toward the opponent to draw their attention. At this moment, the second patrol emerges from its ravine and observes the first for 2 minutes, with each scout noting the heads they see, as shown in the example. After two minutes, another whistle sounds, and everything disappears. Next, the patrol leader arranges the scouts for the second change (according to the diagram on the sheet), followed by another whistle and flag signal, observation for 2 minutes, then the third change (during which the heads are observed for 1 minute as they appear, and for the second minute, those that have joined are also observed—similarly for the 4th change), and so on, until all changes are completed. Now, the roles are reversed: the second patrol appears according to its own sheet, and the first observes. After the exercise, both patrols gather and check the accuracy of their observations based on the submitted sheets. The patrol with fewer errors wins.

The exercise can be made easier by reducing the distance, having the scouts poke their heads out a bit higher, or keeping the formation unchanged for the full 2 minutes of observation (without removing some and adding others, etc.). Conversely, it can also be made more difficult in various ways. In any case, the edge of the ravine should be smooth, not overgrown with tall grass, which would make it difficult to spot a head.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: In Cossack Fashion
body:
a) The red patrol lies in hiding, while the whites, twice as numerous, are positioned 200–300 paces away. Everyone has a three-digit number pinned to the front of their cap. Each digit is 5–6 cm tall and 3 cm wide, drawn in ink with a stroke 1 cm thick.

The terrain between the two parties should be carefully selected. Let there be solitary trees, scattered bushes, stones, hollows, molehills, etc.—in short, as many small coverings as possible to conceal the head. The area where the reds lie hidden, roughly in a line, should look similar; thus, it cannot be dense thickets through which one can see but which the opponent cannot penetrate with their gaze.

At a given signal, the whites advance, creeping stealthily, moving quickly from cover to cover—now by leaping, now by crawling. On one hand, they try to spot the reds’ numbers; on the other, they hide their own heads so that the reds cannot read their numbers.

Any scout, white or red, who reads an opponent’s number calls it out aloud. Neutral observers (one with the whites, one with the reds) record the called numbers, excluding the caller—i.e., the "killed"—from further participation in the exercise.

In this way, the whites draw ever closer to the reds, but in ever-dwindling numbers. The reds also decrease, but far less so. When, finally, one (or possibly 2–3) of the whites manages to reach within 30–40 paces of the reds, a whistle blows, and the remaining living members of both sides fall in for roll call. If the reds have maintained their original ratio to the whites (1:2), they win; if this ratio has shifted in favor of the whites, the whites win.

During the exercise, under penalty of being "killed," no one may remove their cap, turn it so the number faces sideways, or cover it with their hand. The neutral observer ensures this. If a number comes loose, is obscured, etc., it must be corrected.

b) This game can also take a different course. Here, both parties lie opposite each other at a distance of 300–400 paces. In the middle of this battlefield lies a neutral strip, 40–50 paces wide, marked by two rows of small flags. Both parties creep toward each other, trying to reach this strip.

"Killing" proceeds as before, and as soon as one scout from either side reaches the strip, a whistle signals the end of the battle.

The evaluation is as follows: Calculating the distance in paces from the strip for all "living" members of both parties and summing them would grant victory to the side with the smaller total—a victory that seems fair but is, in reality, unjust. For example, there might be only 4 whites alive and 12 reds, yet the whites’ total, as the victors, would be significantly smaller than the reds’. Conversely, those 4 might have reached very close, while the 12 might be far away because they were afraid to approach, lest they be "killed."

Therefore, the evaluation considers the distance of all "living" members of the party that remains in the minority, and from the other party, those living who are no farther from the strip than the farthest member of the first party. With this calculation, victory goes to those who show the greater total distance.

These games train the eye and teach how to approach the opponent while exploiting all available cover along the way.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Sketching a Route
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

In many exercises, there is a need to make a sketch of a certain section of terrain, a cartographic or perspective sketch. This is usually a cursory sketch, i.e., a very simplified drawing containing only the most important lines and objects of the terrain for the given purpose. However, even to create such a sketch, a certain skill is required, and this can be easily and quickly acquired through practice, but one must first learn the principles and methods of sketching from appropriate manuals.

One should start by making a cartographic sketch from a single point using the polar method, and only then proceed to sketch a route, which is essentially a polygonal sketch created by traversing. Specifically, after orienting the sketch and marking one's position with a point, aim a ruler toward the nearest bend in the road and draw a line in that direction. Then, move toward that bend, counting steps (or estimating the distance by eye, which is simpler but less accurate), and mark each passed branch of the road to the right or left in the sketch at the appropriate place according to the scale. Upon reaching the bend in the road, mark this point in the sketch, reorient the sketch, aim toward the direction of the new section of the road, and so on as before. Additionally, if necessary, one can mark prominent terrain features located beside the traveled road.

Equally important is learning to make a perspective sketch, which should be as simple as possible, executed in general outlines, as this makes the drawing stand out clearly, which is the primary goal.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Sketch from Memory
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

a) A section of terrain to be used for the exercise is marked by prominent boundaries, e.g., a forest on the left and a river on the right. The patrol observes this terrain intently for 15 minutes (or even 10 or 5), trying to fix the seen image in their memory. During this time, they may mark only 4 objects or lines in their sketchbook.

After the prescribed time has elapsed, everyone turns away and draws a perspective sketch from memory, inserting the terrain between the four marked signs. Who will reproduce the seen image most faithfully and include the most details in it?

b) The patrol observes the road they are walking along—its turns, forks, observation points, etc.—as if imprinting the appearance of the road in their memory, following its course, estimating distances from one prominent point to another, etc., so that after fixing this winding line, which the road represents, in their memory, they sketch it only upon reaching the designated place.

Later, the sketch of the road is compared with a map to see what errors were made.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: The Abandoned Bivouac
body:
A patrol camps on a glade: they pitch tents, set up campfires, cook, etc., performing various camp duties. After some time, they leave the camp and not only do they fail to erase the traces of the campsite, but on the contrary, they leave behind various small objects and signs of their stay. (All of this can be noted down).

The opposing patrol (which, in the meantime, was conducting an exercise elsewhere) tries to discover the location of the abandoned bivouac (note: the search area must be predetermined), and once found, to gather as much information as possible about the campers based solely on the traces left behind. Each scout notes what they observed, what they found, and what conclusions they draw from it.

Later, both patrols gather, and individual scouts report based on their notes. The leader awards priority to the one who observed and reasoned best, scoring the value of observations and conclusions (naturally, a good deduction earns more points than merely stating a fact). The second patrol, after hearing the reports, confirms what was overlooked in the observations.

What should be paid attention to? How many fires were there, — how long the fire burned, — how long ago it was extinguished, — from which direction the patrol arrived and from which they left, — how many tents were pitched and where, and how many were in the camp, — what was cooked, — what objects were left behind and what conclusions can be drawn from them, etc. He who has his eyes open and knows not only how to look but also how to see will notice much, even if it seems at first glance that there is little to see.

When repeating the exercise, the type of traces is changed.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Torn Letter
body:
The task is to reconstruct the content of a letter from torn scraps of paper.

The patrol leader writes an order on a quarter sheet of paper, tears it into small pieces, and scatters them in the wind. Then, he returns to the patrol and instructs them, for example, to go 100 paces north, where on the slope of a hill, the paper scraps can be seen. These must be collected and the message read from them. It is difficult to find all the torn pieces, so the goal is to deduce the content from the fragments. If the patrol carries out the given order, it provides proof that it has completed the task. The exercise can be made more difficult by specifying a time limit within which the order must be executed.

Several patrols can compete in this exercise. In that case, as many quarter sheets of paper as there are patrols are taken. The same order is written on each, ensuring that the number of lines is the same, each line ends with the same syllable, and the content occupies the same area of paper. Then, each is torn into the same number of pieces. Each quarter sheet is scattered in a different location, at an equal distance from the camps, and each patrol is directed to the place where they must search.

At a given signal, the patrols scatter. Some carefully collect the scraps, others assemble them and try to read the content. Then, the written order is carried out. The patrol that executes it first wins. The order might read, for example: *"The patrol must line up in a row along the right bank of the stream, place their equipment behind them while holding their sticks, and the patrol leader must come to me and announce that the patrol is ready."*

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Recognizing Tracks
body:
On damp sand or freshly turned earth, the patrol leaves footprints. Each marks their own track, after which everyone observes all the tracks for several minutes. Finally, one scout steps aside, and one of the remaining scouts walks a dozen or so steps, leaving tracks. The first scout must then identify who passed by and justify their judgment based on the track. Next, a second scout steps aside, and so on. This is the simplest way to learn to distinguish tracks.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Reading Trails
body:
The art of drawing conclusions from reading tracks is just as important as the skill of tracking itself. Tracks are merely the material from which one builds, i.e., derives the appropriate conclusions.

One scout walks across terrain where visible tracks remain. At intervals, he changes his gait

![img-0.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-123-img-0.jpeg)

Fig. 30.

or performs certain actions strictly according to the patrol leader’s instructions. For example, in one place he makes a large leap, in another he limps heavily on his right leg, then he sits on the ground, removes one shoe, and continues walking barefoot on one foot; elsewhere, he crawls on his knees, etc. After a quarter of an hour, the patrol sets off along the tracks and must deduce, from the various changes in the trail, what the tracked scout did at each location.

Such tracks work particularly well in snow.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: On the Trail
body:
Under the conditions in which we live, tracking over long distances by natural signs is usually impossible. We must create artificial trails. The simplest are colored scraps of paper, scattered along the marching route. At first, use more eye-catching scraps—red or yellow—then green, blue, etc.

**a)** The patrol leader lays out the trails, each about 10–20 paces apart. One scrap is placed visibly on the ground, another hung on a bush, a third on the opposite side of a tree trunk, and so on. Sometimes the trail follows a road or path, then veers off into thickets, gaps, etc., only to return to the original route after some time. Trails are laid out over a distance of 1–3 km. The patrol leader then brings the patrol near the start of the trail, explains that the first sign is 10 paces away, and gives the signal to begin tracking. No one may track independently; anyone who finds a trail must notify the others to save them from fruitless searching. Moreover, establishing the direction of the trail makes further searching easier. Eventually, the patrol reaches the announced sign marking the end of the trail. The scraps must be collected. This way, the patrol leader can see how many of the scattered trails were missed and who collected the most.

The paper scraps should be 6–10 cm long and 1 cm wide. Instead of scraps, colored threads or cotton (more difficult trails) can be used, or agreed-upon chalk marks can assist.

**b)** Similar tracking can be organized as a competition between several patrols. For each patrol, a color of scraps and a chalk mark are assigned, e.g., for Patrol 1: blue scraps and a cross; for Patrol 2: green scraps and a circle; for Patrol 3: brown scraps and a squiggle. All colors should have the same intensity, meaning they should be equally easy or difficult to spot.

Three Scouts set out and scatter the trails. At first, they walk together, then separately but close to one another. At a certain point, they split up, each taking a route of equal length and heading toward a visible distant meeting point. Upon reaching it, they walk together again, only to separate once more after a while. After covering several kilometers, they hide and mark their hiding place with three scraps placed together. Each Scout should have the same number of scraps, lay them out roughly the same distance apart, and pass through terrain of equal difficulty for tracking. The paper trails should be interspersed with chalk marks. The leader accompanying the Scouts ensures the trails are laid out correctly and fairly.

Half an hour after the departure, the three patrols set out from a point about a dozen paces away from the first trail. The patrol that finds the hidden Scouts not in the shortest time, but by collecting the highest percentage of the scattered trails, wins. If the tracking is timed, usually only the fastest one tracks, and the rest blindly follow. It is good to place the hiding spot on a hill from which the tracking patrols can be seen.

During tracking, it is forbidden to touch another patrol’s trails, nor should one deliberately lead another patrol to their own trail for personal gain. The exercise is exceptionally engaging.

**c)** Three patrols can also track in the same way, not necessarily each having three different trails.

There is only one trail, but each patrol sets out separately every 15–20 minutes. (Of course, the trails must not be collected.) In this case, however, the terrain should be chosen so that the previous patrol is not visible to the next. The last patrol collects the trails.

Organizing such tracking is easier.

A variation of the described games can be the announcement that, upon reaching the destination, a description of the route taken will be required. This forces the trackers to pay attention to the surrounding terrain, interesting features encountered, changes in direction, etc., while simultaneously following the trail.

**d)** Tracking can be combined with another game, such as setting ambushes, of which the trackers are informed. Along the trail, individual Scouts hide. The trackers must not only follow the trail but also detect these ambushes. A hidden Scout, called out from a distance of, say, 30 paces, becomes a prisoner, as does the tracker if called out by the hidden Scout from 20 paces.

Prisoners continue to participate in the game (it is difficult to interrupt it halfway)—some keep tracking, others wait in ambush for the next patrol. After the exercise, it will be clear which patrol suffered the fewest losses, which can be considered in the evaluation.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: False Trails
body:
It is possible to make tracking more difficult by laying false trails. Specifically, branches are created from the true trail, marked with scraps of paper of the same color, but ending at a certain distance with an agreed-upon sign indicating that the trail is false (e.g., a clearly visible chalk cross).

![img-1.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-127-img-1.jpeg)

Fig. 31.

Additionally, branches can be made that later reconnect with the true trail, meaning they are genuine but lead a longer route to the destination than the true trail.

As a result of such trail arrangements, the scout patrol must split up at every fork in the trails, because if the entire patrol follows a false trail or takes a side trail instead of the true one, they will unnecessarily cover extra distance and waste time.

In this exercise, patrols can be sent out one after another every 15 minutes, with the winner being the one with the best time—or all patrols can be released at once. With rivals close behind, scouts of the same patrol then communicate with each other using agreed-upon shouts or signals to inform their own group whether they have found a good or bad trail, and on the other hand, to mislead the competitor following the patrol’s search and lead them onto a false trail. Much often depends on the cleverness and ingenuity of those tracking. Collecting or destroying trails is, of course, not allowed.

Where suitable terrain exists, the described tracking exercises can also be adapted by marking trails with irons attached to the soles of shoes. Such an iron leaves a trace that is distinctly different from ordinary footwear marks (a circle, several crosses, a bird drawing, etc.).

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Behind the Straw Bundles
body:
For many, it is an interesting matter to find out whether the trail they laid has been discovered. This can be combined with laying another kind of trail. A stick about 30 cm long is split at one end, and a handful of twisted, knotted straw is inserted into the split. Such sticks are made, for example, 50 in number, and 10 scouts each take 5 sticks, marking their name or their sign at the spot where they have cut a bit of the bark with a knife. Now the trails are laid out, each 20–30 paces apart, either by driving the sticks into the ground or by hanging them on trees at arm’s reach height. Each tries to place their stick in a spot difficult to find. The patrol leader oversees the correct laying of the trails.

The tracking begins. Each searches on their own; a found trail is their prize, but they must loudly announce to everyone where they found the given trail. The last stick (appropriately marked) reveals the hiding place where the tracked scouts have concealed themselves. Who will collect the most sticks, and from whom? Who will reach the hiding place first?

A rule can be added that no trail may be skipped, meaning that a stick cannot be taken until the previous one has been found. The sticks are therefore marked with sequential numbers.

If two patrols compete, one lays the trails while the other searches. The search time is recorded, and then the patrols switch roles.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Tracking in the Snow
body:
In winter, 2 or 3 scouts set out across clean snow, while the rest follow their trail 15–25 minutes later. The fugitives, weaving through not very open terrain (quite extensive but with defined boundaries), try to mislead the trackers to gain time. If they are not caught within the set time, they win. For example, they may split up and cross their own tracks repeatedly, then reunite—erase their footprints behind them with a branch—alter their trail by tying a strap to a boot—exploit every patch of ground, fence, or bridge where no tracks are left (allowed for no more than 50 paces)—walk backward—step into their own tracks so that three become two or one, possibly creating a different mark by leaning on a stick, etc.—as long as it delays the pursuit.

The more cunning the fugitives display, the more tricks they use to deceive the pursuers, the greater their chances of winning.

Eventually, the fugitives hide in some thicket, where their pursuers catch up with them.

One restriction: it is forbidden to join other trails—if encountered, they must be immediately crossed.

A battle can also be added to this game. The fugitives, in their hiding place, prepare a pile of snowballs and begin pelting the pursuers. The latter do not hesitate to retaliate, and the fight rages in earnest. One accurate hit kills an attacker, while a fugitive requires two hits.

The outcome can then be decided as follows: the fugitives win if they are not found within the set time and also win the battle, i.e., kill half of the attackers. The attackers win if they reach the fugitives on time and kill them without losing half their own people. Any other result is a draw.

This game can also be played on skis.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Hey, After the Fox!
body:
The fox glides on skis. Wherever it encounters more ski tracks, it drops small scraps of colored paper. Fifteen minutes later, the hounds set off in pursuit of its trail. The fox zigzags, finally hiding in a den from which a convenient escape is possible. There, the hounds catch up to it, flush it out of the den, and try to corner it. Whoever touches it with their hand kills it.

It is important to skillfully choose the fox’s route. This route should lead through varied terrain with difficulties adjusted to the scouts’ age and skiing abilities. It should not be precisely marked out, as that would overly restrict the fox’s freedom of movement; instead, an area should be designated where it is allowed to roam. This terrain should be chosen so that its layout forces the trackers into various, more or less difficult, skiing maneuvers.

A stronger skier is chosen to play the fox.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Treasure Hunt
body:
a) The treasure — a pocketknife, a matchbox, or similar object — is well hidden, and the patrol must find it by following a series of hidden clues, discovered one after another. The patrol is set on the trail by being given the first and only clue. For example: *"Go north. After several hundred paces, you will reach a hill with three solitary pines. Stand beneath them, and you will see a white cottage. On one of its walls, there is an arrow. Follow the direction of the arrow for 50 paces, and you will find a stone beneath which lies the next clue."*

The patrol sets off. There may be several white cottages and many stones. Eventually, they find a note. It reads: *"Stand by the southern wall of the cottage, and you will see a haystack with a pole stuck in the middle. Position yourself so that the pole exactly covers the western edge of the house. Walk in that direction until you reach a road, where you will find a pile of stones. Fifteen paces from it, in the fork of a tree marked with a cross, is another note with clues."* The next clue says: *"Go northwest, and you will find a hut with hollyhocks in the garden. Stand on the woodpile near the hut (note: this is a trap, as there are two piles, but it is not specified which one), and you will see a tree stump (note: three stumps are visible). When you stand on it facing south, you will see spruces. One of them is tied with thread; near it, under a stone, is the third note."*

In this way, the patrol follows the trail from one hiding place to the next. In one, they may find an order to locate three trees marked with crosses, with the note hidden in the triangle they form. The trail to the next hiding place may be marked with shreds of yarn, etc., and they often encounter deliberately set traps, forcing them to think hard before finding the next hiding spot, until they finally reach the hidden treasure.

The more cleverly the hiding places are chosen and the more wittily they are described, the greater the scouts' interest in this excellent exercise. When placing the notes, the patrol leader should start from the treasure and work backward, hiding the notes in reverse order, not the other way around. Otherwise, the patrol leader would have to return from the second hiding place to the first to place a note there, from the third to the second, from the fourth to the third, etc. This is because a note can only be written and hidden in the previous hiding place after familiarizing oneself with the terrain details around the next one.

This exercise can be turned into a competition between several patrols. In this case, patrols set off one after another every 15 minutes, and it will be clear which one reaches the treasure in the shortest time. The same can be done with a single patrol, dividing it into groups of two scouts each.

However, all groups can also be sent simultaneously if the scouts have already developed a certain self-control. In this case, whoever finds a note must remove it discreetly so that no one notices, read it, and then hide it again just as carefully, before disappearing with their companion to avoid leading others onto the trail.

In such competitions, it is especially important to order that each note be hidden again exactly as it was found and in the exact same place. The last patrol collects all the notes. Sometimes, the leader places the notes the day before the exercise. In that case, they should be wrapped in pieces of tinfoil to protect them from moisture.

Depending on the number of hiding places and whether the whole setup is very simple or intricate and full of traps, the game can be easy or very difficult, lasting half an hour or even four hours.

b) The treasure, containing cards with the names of all the patrol’s scouts, is not found by following a series of discovered clues, as before, but by following a more or less precise description of the route leading to it. This route must first be walked by the patrol leader, who then describes it based on direct observation. For example: *"500 paces along the road, then cross the small forest northwest, along the boundary between oats and clover until the stream, follow the left bank of the stream to the hut, jump to the right bank, and march northwest until the forest, along the edge of the forest to the clearing, through the clearing, head toward the factory chimney, and upon reaching a solitary oak, 25 paces north, etc., until you reach the treasure."* Whoever finds it takes their card and brings it to the designated meeting point. This point is predetermined, easy to spot, and located near the treasure. Who will bring their card within the prescribed time?

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: After the Night Dew
body:
On a quiet, clear evening, a scout patrol gathers on a small hill. Each scout, in complete silence, strains their ears to catch all the rustles and sounds coming from every direction and to determine their origin. There are many and varied: the call of a bird or the bark of a dog, the footsteps of a person, the rumble of a cart, the rustling of trees, the whisper of falling leaves, the splash of a stream, the sound of conversation, and so on. Everyone listens intently. Suddenly, the name of one of the scouts is called softly. The scout responds with two words and points in the direction from which the sound comes. The others remain silent if they agree with his opinion; otherwise, they correct the mistake as briefly as possible. Soon, another name is called, and so on.

The patrol is now deeply engaged in listening, so two scouts step away, stand at a distance of several dozen (later several hundred) paces, and signal with a whistle that they are ready. Soon, a sound produced by them reaches the group (e.g., a stone falling to the ground, a branch rubbing against a trunk, a stick breaking over a knee, a cough, a hiss, a creak, water being poured onto the ground, footsteps, crawling, etc.). Each scout catches the sound and notes its probable cause on a piece of paper. These sounds occur at intervals of 1–2 minutes, in an order predetermined by the patrol leader. The patrol leader and the scouts in the field have a list of these sounds. Since other, unplanned sounds from the surroundings may intermingle, the patrol leader, after each produced sound, alerts the scouts with the word «attention».

After the exercise, it is checked who made the fewest mistakes. The exercise will be all the more engaging the more tools are prepared for producing sounds and the greater the variety of those sounds.

It is also possible to try listening by pressing an ear to the ground (on calm, dry days).

---
