author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Cat’s Step
body:
One scout has their eyes tightly blindfolded, and a small flag is stuck into the ground about 10 paces away from them. The blindfolded scout must not know where the flag is. The others stand scattered around at a distance of several dozen paces. Absolute silence is required. The scout designated by the patrol leader approaches the flag stealthily, avoiding any noise,

![img-2.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-136-img-2.jpeg)

*Fig. 32.*

in order to pull it out and carry it away to a distance of 10 paces. Whoever succeeds earns a mark. The blindfolded scout listens intently and follows every sound; if they hear something, they stretch out their hand in the appropriate direction and shout: «Stop!». The patrol leader decides whether the observation is correct and either corrects it, and the game continues, or orders the one who was detected to step back, and the next scout begins to sneak forward. After each successful attempt, the listener is changed, and the flag is placed in a new, unknown location.

If there are more players, several can be instructed to approach simultaneously, but from a distance of 10–15 paces from the flag, only one should approach, as it is otherwise sometimes difficult to determine who actually made the rustling sound.

The exercise works equally well on smooth ground as on ground covered with twigs, leaves, pebbles, etc.; one can walk, crawl on all fours, or slither; it is also possible to set a time limit for reaching the flag.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Like a Snake in the Grass
body:
Some scouts sit on the ground with their eyes blindfolded, forming a circle, each spaced 6–10 paces apart. In the center of the circle, scouting equipment is placed: hats, walking sticks, small shovels, canteens, etc. The rest of the scouts must, by stepping, crawling, or creeping, sneak into the center of the circle and, in the same manner, carry away one of the objects lying there. They should sneak in one at a time, not in a group, as one clumsy scout in the center could betray everyone. The guards may point out a suspicious rustle at their side or in the center of the circle, and the patrol leader checks the validity of the observation and removes the one discovered. A point is awarded to whoever completes the task. Then the roles are switched.

To ensure the game runs smoothly, the sneaking is done on the patrol leader’s signal. He may, by raising his hand, stop the one sent for a few moments, or then point to another, etc., so that there is always only one scout in the center of the circle. If someone is discovered, the patrol leader calls out: *"break"*, during which everyone remains in their places, and the discovered scout is removed.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: By the Clock
body:
A string is stretched between two trees, and a pocket watch is hung from it. One Scout has their eyes blindfolded and is then led near the watch. The rest surround them and keep them within a circle during the game. Guided by hearing alone, the blindfolded Scout must find the watch.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Who is Closer?
body:
A sentinel stands on a hill clearly visible even in the evening. Scouts approach from all sides, each trying to get as close as possible. When a scout believes they are close enough, they make a sign to indicate they have reached that spot. Then, they carefully retreat (or reveal themselves, if ordered to do so). However, the sentinel listens intently, and if they hear a suspicious rustle, they whistle. Everyone freezes, and the patrol leader checks whether an enemy is indeed hiding in the spot indicated by the sentinel. The leader then either excludes the scout, measuring the distance from the sentinel, or signals for the others to continue advancing.

After the designated time has passed or a signal is given that everyone has completed their task, it is checked whose sign is closest to the sentinel. Additionally, it is noted whose signs are no farther than 10 meters from the sentinel, as this is considered a good performance.

Scouts should approach one at a time and from all sides, not in a group, as it can be difficult to determine who is at fault in such cases.

If two patrols are competing, the opposing patrol provides the sentinel, and the results are compared afterward. Alternatively, scouts from both patrols may approach simultaneously, with one of the patrol leaders acting as the sentinel. When awarding victory, the leader considers both the number of those eliminated and which patrol, overall, got closer.

A good variation of this game is to give the sentinel an electric torch to illuminate the playing area. In this case, the approaching time is set, for example, to 15–20 minutes, after which a signal is given to end the game. Everyone remains in their place, and it is determined how many were discovered and who got closest.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: At the Whistle
body:
When it is sufficiently dark, one scout moves away from the patrol and, winding his way, hides in a place unknown to anyone. From there, he whistles once. The rest, standing in a group, determine from which direction the whistle came and from what distance, and each sets off separately in the direction he has chosen, then stops at the spot which, in his opinion, is closest to the hidden scout (one may also stick a branch at that point as proof of his presence and return). Now, a threefold whistle from the patrol leader calls the hidden scout to reveal himself, after which it is determined who came closest to him.

A certain variation of this game involves one scout hiding and whistling from time to time, while the rest search for him. Whoever finds him wins. It is also possible to allow the hidden scout to change his hiding place at an opportune moment, which makes the search more difficult. Of course, the hidden scout whistles or changes his hiding place only when he does not thereby risk being discovered.

There may also be several hidden scouts, each with a whistle of a different pitch. In this case, everyone may search for all the fugitives, or each group may search only for its own fugitive.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Pursuit in the Dark
body:
On a limited, enclosed space, one is to catch a Scout who, every minute, either whistles once or lights a match for a duration of 5 seconds. The pursuit is thus guided by both sight and hearing. If the pursuer does not catch the runner within the designated time, another takes over his role.

A signal and a meeting place for the assembly must be established.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Eavesdropping
body:
A scout patrol lies in a single line on the ground, each scout 15 paces apart from the next. The patrol leader is in the middle. Opposite them, at a distance of 20–25 paces, another patrol lies in the same manner. The patrol leader gives a single sentence to the scouts on his right and left in a normal voice, e.g., *"The cross on the chapel, under the little forest."* These scouts pass it along until it reaches the ends of the line. The opposing patrol listens in, and each scout in that patrol writes down what they heard.

If the sentence is passed without error all the way to the end, every scout who wrote it down correctly earns a point. If the sentence reaches the end in an altered form, it is determined who made the mistake in passing it along, and in the second patrol, every scout who noted the sentence with that error earns a point.

Then the patrols switch roles, and the patrol with the higher number of points wins. The distance between scouts and between patrols can be increased or decreased depending on the players' skill.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Learning to Hide
body:
Over a distance of 1–2 km, scouts hide on both sides of the road, no more than 50 paces away from it. Each scout uses ground depressions, rocks, bushes, etc., to better conceal themselves. After 10 minutes, the patrol leader walks along the road, and if he discovers anyone, he signals them to stand up and join him.

Each scout hides in secret from the others, but if someone notices another’s hiding place, they must not reveal it.

If the patrol leader does not find everyone after walking the road, on his return he orders one of the scouts to search for the remaining ones. This can only be the scout who swears he does not know the hiding places of the others. The winner is the one who is discovered last.

During the search, no one is allowed to leave the road.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Hide and Seek
body:
This exercise shares the same characteristic as the previous one: one person hides while the others search, or all the White Patrol hide while the Red Patrol search. One party must wear distinctive badges. It is essential to clearly mark the boundaries of the area where hiding is permitted (on a map, by pointing out the limits from an elevated vantage point, or by partially walking the perimeter), as well as the duration of the exercise. The area may cover several square kilometers, and the exercise may last several hours. It should also be determined how many found within a given time constitute a win. A "prisoner" is taken by touch (or by calling out from a distance of 15–20 paces).

A rule may be in effect that once a hiding place is chosen, it cannot be changed, or that in case of danger, one may leave it for another. After the exercise, those who remain undiscovered must report who they saw near their hiding place.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Learning to Approach Stealthily
body:
a) The terrain abounds in various small cover: uneven ground, bushes, stones, etc. The patrol leader stands in the middle; everyone scatters in different directions to a distance of 500 paces and drops to the ground, concealing themselves behind cover. On a given signal, the scouts approach the patrol leader as closely as possible, unnoticed, and presenting the smallest possible targets (i.e., staying low to the ground and using the terrain’s unevenness), while keeping their eyes on him the entire time.

Meanwhile, the patrol leader performs various movements (the sequence of which he has previously written down on a piece of paper): now he wipes his forehead with a handkerchief, now he sits down, turns around, removes his hat, spreads his arms, kneels, shields his eyes, etc. Despite their stealthy approach, all scouts must follow his movements and try to memorize them. Naturally, there should not be too many movements, nor should they follow one another too quickly.

After the allotted time has passed, everyone stands up on the patrol leader’s signal, and it will then be seen who has approached the closest. Approaching completely unnoticed becomes generally impossible if the patrol leader constantly looks around and watches the scouts’ movements; one or another may disappear from his sight only for a short time. This could only be achieved in completely covered terrain, but then the patrol leader would also be invisible. However, the purpose of this exercise is different: namely, to test whether the scout makes use of the terrain’s cover, presenting the smallest possible target, whether he avoids careless movements, does not unnecessarily expose himself, and whether, while approaching, he continuously observes the one being approached. Therefore, even if the patrol leader spots a scout, he does not consider it a mistake. Only when he notices a truly incorrect approach does he give a whistle signal. Everyone remains motionless, and the one indicated by hand (or with a flag) stands up. On a repeated whistle, the exercise continues.

Three whistles signal the end of the approach. Now comes the examination. Each scout reports what he observed during the approach, and the patrol leader records each observation next to the scout’s name. Who now followed best, as he noticed the most? Since it may happen that one scout approached the closest, while another saw the most, the patrol leader adjusts the rankings, moving one back and another forward, as the exercise was intended to test both skills equally.

b) An exercise somewhat different from the previous one. The terrain is the same; the scouts are at a distance of 150–200 paces from the patrol leader. He behaves like a sentry: he stands still, then slowly takes a few steps and stops, facing a different direction, etc. All movements are performed slowly.

Each scout takes advantage of this: whenever the sentry is not looking in his direction, he quickly moves from cover to cover, ensuring he is already hidden when the sentry turns his gaze toward him. If the sentry spots someone during movement, or if a scout, failing to hide in time, is seen on open ground, the sentry orders him to stand up. Who will approach the closest?

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: On the Covert Trail
body:
From opposite directions, at a distance of 2–4 km, two scout patrols approach each other. Both set out at the same time. The route is chosen such that they must meet; specifically, a meeting point is designated, which each patrol must reach, as well as two points they must pass.

Since each patrol knows it will encounter the opponent along its path, and the route passes through mixed terrain—partially covered, offering many concealments that facilitate stealth—they advance in a dispersed formation, with a "lookout" at the front.

The patrol moves cautiously, utilizing all unevenness of the terrain and all cover to advance unnoticed, while sharpening their eyesight to spot the approaching opponent. The side whose patrol leader first sees the opposing scout wins, and as proof, they must blow a whistle and raise a flag. However, if a single scout spots the opponent, this does not decide the matter; the patrol leader must be informed of the sighting, verify it, and only they have the right to blow the whistle. All scouts must therefore maintain constant "contact" with their patrol leader so they can inform them of any sighting at any moment and indicate the point where the enemy is located.

A judge with a white armband on their hat is positioned along the route. Upon hearing the signal, the judge verifies the accuracy of the sighting. From the moment the whistle is blown until the decision is made, everyone must remain in place and in hiding, as the sighting may have been deceptive, and the exercise continues after three whistles from the judge.

During this approach, all manner of tricks are permitted: climbing trees, sneaking behind or on a cart, etc., except for disguising oneself.

After the exercise is completed, it is repeated with the patrols moving in opposite directions. If a time limit is set for the patrols to reach the destination, it should be long enough to allow them to take full advantage of all favorable conditions for stealth.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Dispersion
body:
a) After the assembly point is designated, in case of dispersion, the patrol goes on reconnaissance, using the terrain for concealed movement. Suddenly — at the patrol leader’s whistle — dispersion occurs. Each scout vanishes from sight as quickly as possible. The patrol leader swiftly proceeds to the assembly point and from there observes how and when the scouts arrive, using cover and terrain irregularities to approach unseen. Who performs this task most skillfully? Then, an assessment of proficiency follows.

b) The White patrol moves along a precisely marked route, with a specific task to perform at a certain point. From the opposite direction, along the same route, the Red patrol advances. When they spot each other, at the patrol leader’s signal, both patrols disperse. The patrol leaders deliberately separate from their patrols, move quickly forward, and wait in concealment along the designated route for their scouts. Each leader reveals their presence to their arriving scouts. How quickly and effectively do the scouts regroup with their patrol leader? A patrol that has dispersed must always (unless an assembly point has been designated) regroup along the line of march, primarily to complete its task rather than chase the opponent. Therefore, scouts must always know this route.

After regrouping — a discussion of the adventure and identification of mistakes made.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Along the Polygon
body:
A scout patrol travels along a path forming a closed polygon, aiming to traverse it entirely and return unnoticed to the starting point. The path is 3–4 km long and should be covered in 1½–2 hours. The patrol knows that during the march, they will encounter an enemy, whom they must pass without drawing attention while observing them closely. They may deviate from the marked path, but no more than 30 paces to the side. Each scout who passes the enemy unnoticed must record who the enemy was, as well as where and under what conditions they were encountered. If both enemies notice each other, they must retreat until they are out of each other’s sight. Each scout moves separately unless the patrol leader has given other instructions.

A second patrol is sent along the same path in the opposite direction, but the first patrol does not know the time of their departure—whether they have already set out or are yet to do so. It is the leader’s responsibility to arrange the departure times so that the scouts meet on the section of the path most suitable for stealth.

Scouts from both patrols who reach the destination within the specified time must present their notes to the leader, from which it will be clear who managed to pass unnoticed and observe the enemy.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: On the Trail of the Enemy
body:
A patrol is heading to a destination, one hour's march away, following a strictly designated route and having several tasks to complete during the march at specified locations, e.g., two halts, measuring the width of a river, signaling with a semaphore from two hills, etc. At the destination, they are to set up camp. However, they are unaware that a second patrol has the task of tracking them without revealing their presence. Can the second patrol reach the destination unnoticed and observe the first patrol setting up camp? Can they accurately report the activities the first patrol performed during the march? Conversely, will the first patrol notice they are being followed, and if so, can they evade the tracker, mislead the pursuit, and set up camp undetected?

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Misdirecting the Pursuit
body:
At a destination, one hour’s march from the starting point, a flag is deliberately planted in a fairly visible spot by an appointed person. The White patrol heads there, while the Red patrol follows their trail. Only the Whites know where the flag is planted. The goal is to evade the pursuers’ eyes or mislead the chase so that neither the destination is revealed nor the flag is reached unnoticed. How can this be done when both patrols start from the same place?

As a binding rule, it is accepted that a Red, once called out by a White, may not proceed further until the White loses sight of them. Now, the field is open for a whole series of ruses. The Whites may hide and let the Reds pass, then quietly take another route to the destination; they may split into two or three groups, with one or two groups attempting to lead the opponent off the correct trail while the rest, taking advantage of this, hurry to the flag; they may scatter, designating a meeting point, with the understanding that anyone who is pressed too hard will not go there but instead lead the enemy astray, and so on. Ultimately, the Whites win if at least half of them, along with their commander, reach the flag unnoticed, pull it up, and hide it, then go to meet the Reds and show it to them. The Reds win if they are not deceived and can indicate where the flag was and what it looked like. (Therefore, the flag must be appropriately altered, e.g., by adding a ribbon, a tuft of leaves, etc.).

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Terrain Reconnaissance
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

Terrain reconnaissance is the act of personally verifying whether a given section of terrain is suitable for a specific purpose. It is conducted because maps do not contain all details (which, moreover, are subject to constant change), and the terrain itself changes in appearance depending on the season, weather conditions, etc. Additionally, for certain purposes, it is necessary to gather data that a map simply does not provide.

When practicing terrain reconnaissance, avoid complicated tasks; instead, assign simple, concrete tasks. The goal is for the scout to learn to focus their attention on the specific details that need to be identified in a given situation.

A reconnaissance report primarily consists of creating a cartographic sketch, marking the elements that were to be investigated, with a supplementary description providing further clarification. Such a report should be clear and concise. During reconnaissance, a map should be used; if it cannot be taken along, at least "study" the map before the march, which will not only make navigation easier but also help in locating the necessary points and terrain details.

In many of the exercises provided, this "reconnaissance" of the terrain is a component part.

However, terrain reconnaissance itself can also be a separate exercise or the most important part of one.

As with any other type of exercise, the difficulty of reconnaissance should be graded for the scouts.

a) Scouts first complete a sketch of a terrain section based on a map, then supplement it in the field by drawing in all the relevant details, marking some with conventional symbols, and adding a "legend"—i.e., an explanation and verbal supplement to the sketch. This is done under the supervision and guidance of the leader, who provides precise instructions each time on what and in which direction to investigate.

![img-2.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-154-img-2.jpeg)

*Fig. 36.*

b) Next, scouts practice sketching using various methods. Once they have gained some proficiency, they are given different terrain reconnaissance tasks to complete independently, such as investigating a railway line, road, river and its fords, bridges, forest, swamp, settlement as a potential quarters location, terrain for a camp, or an ambush site, etc. (Relevant manuals provide detailed guidance on what details to pay attention to in these cases). All scouts may receive the same task, each completing it separately, after which the results are compared and discussed.

c) Finally, there are exercises in terrain reconnaissance where the patrol provides protection for the sketch artist. This task for the patrol comes to the forefront, especially when the investigator is not stationary but moves across the entire area being surveyed. In such cases, the patrol's duty is to guard the investigator against danger throughout the process. To create realistic conditions, an opposing patrol is deployed in the vicinity of the surveyed terrain. Their orders might be: "A patrol is moving around area X, likely reconnoitering the terrain. Investigate what they are doing and prevent them from completing their task." Now, a simple terrain reconnaissance turns into a more complex exercise. The white patrol, which is protecting the investigator, hides from the red patrol, continues the reconnaissance when the danger passes, and avoids engagement, as the primary goal is to survey the terrain. In short, they strive not to reveal their presence, communicating quietly with signals; if the enemy gets on their trail, they attempt to mislead and divert them. The red patrol also tries to fulfill its orders—one tracks, the other hides, and the winner is the one who completes the assigned task within the specified time.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: At the Bivouac
body:
At the designated bivouac site, the White patrol is stationed. Around it, 4–5 sentries, each a single scout, are positioned at a distance of several dozen paces from the bivouac. The terrain is not very open, allowing for stealthy approach.

At the appointed hour, various activities begin in the bivouac, carried out precisely in the order prescribed. For example: assembling backpacks in a specific place and order, setting up a certain type of field kitchen and lighting a fire, digging a pit for waste, striking camp, etc. Some tasks are to be performed simultaneously if so instructed.

Meanwhile, the Reds, who know the bivouac’s location, approach it individually in stealth. Whoever succeeds in getting close observes who is doing what and when. After ½ to ¾ of an hour (depending on how long the bivouac activities are to last), they withdraw and write reports on what they have seen, bringing them to the assembly point.

The obstacle in this reconnaissance is the sentries, who, upon spotting a scout, may challenge him («Halt!») from a distance of 20–25 paces, thereby taking him prisoner. If they spot the scout from a greater distance, they drive him off. The scout must then retreat, as he may be captured if a sentry approaches within 25 paces.

After the game ends, an evaluation is made to determine who brought the best report.

If a competition between Whites and Reds is to be held, the roles are reversed, and victory is awarded to the side that lost fewer people, provided they also delivered a good report. Otherwise, the other side wins, as in this case, a good report is more important.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Sketch of Outposts
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

The white outposts stand in a semicircle, each 100–200 paces apart. Each consists of 2–3 people. Between the outposts, in places offering a view of the nearest surroundings, several neutrals with white armbands are stationed. The reds sneak up to scout the arrangement of the outposts. Each of them must draw a sketch on a piece of paper, marking their positions. If any red is spotted, a whistle sounds from the relevant outpost. Then, the nearest neutral goes to the scout indicated by the outpost, taking a path that does not reveal the outpost’s location, and removes the discovered scout’s shoulder badge, also taking their sketch. The exercise continues in the meantime. Who discovered how many outposts, and was there anyone who sketched all of them without being noticed by the whites?

The duration of the exercise is specified.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Raid on a Bivouac
body:
a) The White patrol receives an order to launch a sudden raid on the Red patrol, which is bivouacked. If this exercise is not connected to another (e.g., the "step-by-step pursuit of the enemy" march, p. 72), meaning the Whites do not know the Reds' location, the leader designates a fairly large section of terrain within which the Reds are bivouacked.

The Whites must therefore scout out the bivouac site. To do this, they send out individual scouts, who then bring back or send word—either verbally or in writing—possibly accompanied by a situational sketch.

The patrol then approaches stealthily from the side that allows them to get close without being noticed. If the Reds have not posted a guard, the raid may succeed, and the Whites will plant their flag in the middle of the bivouac as proof of victory. However, if there are guards and the sentinel sounds a whistle in time to warn the bivouacked Reds, the Reds will either quickly withdraw from the threatened point or take up a well-organized defensive position—and in that case, the raid has failed.

The sentinel may indeed give the signal, but too late, in which case his badge will be torn from his arm (see general rules of encounter), and similarly for a few separately approaching scouts. The Whites may still manage to plant their flag in the Reds' unabandoned camp despite the warning.

Hence the lesson: a patrol should bivouac in a concealed location with a clear view of the surroundings, and it should always be surrounded by guards.

This exercise can also be conducted on a clear evening, by moonlight; defense is then more difficult, and the raid easier, but locating the patrol is much harder.

The Red patrol must not know about the impending raid; the leader bivouacs with this patrol and decides the outcome in favor of one side.

![img-3.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-158-img-3.jpeg)

*Fig. 37.*

b) The raid can also be organized differently. Here, the Reds are three times stronger than the Whites. The Whites know the threat they face, and the Reds know the Whites' bivouac location, as it has been marked on a map for them.

The Reds win if they manage to surround the bivouac and simultaneously attack the Whites with all their groups. They must be divided into groups: two groups of one patrol each and two groups of half a patrol each (no smaller). A loud signal marks the start of the raid.

The Whites (who have the strength of one patrol) win if they manage to attack a group weaker than themselves before the signal, as this is considered to have broken the encircling ring. They must retreat if facing a group of equal strength.

Of course, impartial observers must confirm whether the signal for the raid was given only when the bivouac was actually surrounded.

Since it is difficult to determine from a distance the size of the group one is dealing with, the Reds must raise a flag during a White raid: a red flag if it is a full patrol, or, for example, a yellow flag if it is only half a patrol.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Withdrawal from a Threatened Point
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

The White Patrol set up camp on a clear evening. They surrounded themselves with guards, knowing the enemy is nearby, and are prepared to abandon the camp if alarmed. Indeed, the enemy approaches and disturbs the guards. (The Red Patrol does this intentionally, thereby revealing their own position). The patrol leader then alerts the camp in the greatest silence and withdraws without a sound from the threatened location. The goal is to, as it were, vanish into the earth so that the Reds do not realize where the Whites have gone or where they have set up a new camp. Then the Whites win. Various methods of misleading the enemy and leading them onto a false trail may be used. (For example, sending one scout in a different direction who acts carelessly—either by stomping loudly or pretending to converse with a comrade—draws the pursuit, only to suddenly disappear and rejoin the patrol, etc.).

This is the task of the Whites. The Reds, on the other hand, must not lose contact with the Whites, must not be deceived, and must follow their trail step by step; or, if they fail to do so, within a specified time (not too short!) they must locate the new camp.

In this exercise, the task of one side can be made easier or more difficult. For example, it will be easier for the Whites to withdraw if the Red Patrol approaches as a whole, since the enemy’s location will be known—more difficult if the Reds are allowed to scatter and use various tricks. For instance, guards may surround the camp from three sides, while the fourth side is openly disturbed. No matter which way the Whites go, they will encounter a Red who will not reveal their presence but may later signal to their comrades. Will the Reds find them in time, or will the Whites, upon noticing a pursuer, use a method to drive them off (e.g., by threatening to break their staff, which can be established before the game as a rule for encounters applicable only to the Whites), and in the meantime disappear? Or, suspecting they are being tracked, will they set up camp only for a moment, then vanish again and set up camp in a third location?

Another rule can be added: the Whites must retreat whenever they encounter at least 2 (or 3) Reds together. Such a condition, of course, also makes the Whites’ task more difficult.

The exercise area must be limited, and the time must be specified. A designated meeting place for the end must also be indicated.

If the exercise is not done in the evening but during the day, it should be made easier for the Whites, and above all, it should be conducted in terrain that is not very open, with varied topography and ground cover.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: After the Retreat is Cut Off
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

A patrol of Whites is returning from reconnaissance to their unit in X. The path winds through a forest, which is difficult to traverse. Since the patrol must deliver important information, they have been ordered to avoid encountering a stronger enemy. The banner carried by the unit signifies forces twice as large as their actual numbers.

From the opposite direction, along the same path, a patrol of Reds with a banner is advancing. They have been ordered to patrol along the road and drive off the enemy, and if possible, take them prisoner.

The time should be calculated so that the opponents meet on the forest path. The Reds immediately launch an attack — but what about the Whites? This will show whether they quickly assess the situation and whether they have not neglected to issue the necessary orders in advance. For they should scatter at the patrol leader’s whistle. But what next? Will they regroup and how quickly at the assembly point, from which the entire patrol will return to X? Has the assembly point been designated, or will each scout individually make their way back to X?

Taking into account the march route, the scattering, the regrouping, and the final return, it is easy to determine whether the Whites’ patrol has completed the task well and in good time, or whether they have done it incorrectly and at the wrong time.

As always, the exact departure time for both patrols must be precisely marked, and these times do not have to be the same.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Ambush
body:
A patrol should, as far as possible, not return by the same route it took to go on reconnaissance. This is one of the principles of conducting reconnaissance. Why? The following exercise provides the answer.

The White patrol receives an order to reach point N, investigate whether there is a small bridge over the stream at that location, and send a report about it. Then, it must examine the width of the stream, its bed, banks, etc., over a distance of 300 paces, and return to M, from where it set out. (Note: the order may be different). The route passes through mixed terrain, which is in places impassable. After the Whites have left, and without their knowledge, the Reds receive an order to set up an ambush on the M—N route for both the returning messenger and the entire White patrol. It is rare for the messenger not to return by the same, already known, and thus most convenient route, and he will certainly fall into the ambush. The same will happen to the White patrol if it does not choose a different return route. Part of the patrol will be captured (there are more Reds), and the rest will be scattered. (Capture can be done by touching with the hand; the captured person is not allowed to escape). In what way and where will they regroup? Was a meeting point designated? Did the patrol leader control the situation, give the signal to scatter, and withdraw skillfully from the ambush? Did the Whites, walking carelessly without a guard, fall into the ambush, or did they discover it in time?

![img-0.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-163-img-0.jpeg)

Fig. 38.

All of this will be the subject of a discussion, and at the same time, it will make both the messenger and the rest of the Whites more cautious in the future.

In general, an ambush can be used in various other exercises as a variation, where the patrol may know about the ambush but not its location, or it may be a surprise for the patrol.

Usually, the following rule is given for encounters: the ambush has failed if it is discovered in time, and conversely, the patrol loses if it is unexpectedly surrounded.

In such cases, hand-to-hand combat, involving the removal of the "combat ribbon," should be avoided, as it leads to chaotic tugging and confusion, in which it is also difficult to determine who has won.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Scouts Sneaking Past the Enemy
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

A patrol sets out on reconnaissance without a map and must, based solely on a general explanation and description, locate a specified point in the terrain. For example: *"At a distance of 2–3 km in the NW direction, there is a marshy depression in the terrain. A stream flows through it, which has a footbridge in only one place. What does the footbridge look like and what is its condition? Bring the information to point X."*

It will take some time to find the footbridge. After thoroughly inspecting it, the patrol leader opens an envelope previously given to them (it must not be opened earlier!) and learns from it that the path to point X is cut off by the enemy. They then explain to everyone the appearance and condition of the footbridge, order the patrol to scatter, and command each scout to sneak past the enemy line individually.

Meanwhile, the leader, considering the distance to the footbridge and the time needed to find it, sends two patrols toward the footbridge with orders to catch the messengers carrying the information—or at least to drive them off, delay them, or prevent their return. Although one should generally avoid running across fields, in this exercise—where the goal is to drive off the messengers—this may be permitted.

The terrain should not be too extensive; it must have defined side boundaries. The patrols are to catch the messengers but must not occupy point X. The conditions for capturing and forcing a retreat are established according to the general rules of encounter.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Between Outposts
body:
a) In the evening, three outposts, each consisting of 3–4 men, are stationed in front of the village, spaced 100–300 paces apart (the distance depends on the quality of the terrain between the outposts and the degree of darkness). The outposts are marked with lanterns, and their positions must not be changed—each has a judge stationed with it.

Five patrols, each composed of 5–10 men, must sneak through to the village between the outposts, with the rule that a patrol may not split up. A whistle blown by an outpost indicates that a sneaking patrol has been spotted. The judge verifies the matter, and if the patrol was indeed discovered within 10 paces before or after the line connecting the outposts, the judge takes it captive. (The judge does this because the outpost must not move from its position.) If no patrol is present, then for a false whistle, the sneaking patrol—provided it is within a maximum of 30 paces from the line—passes through to the village without hindrance. (The judge checks this discreetly so as not to reveal a patrol hidden nearby.) Three whistles signify that a given patrol has reached the village (flag or lantern). The task can be made more difficult by ordering the patrol to reach the lantern and then return to the starting point.

b) The same exercise can also be conducted in such a way that the outpost positions are not marked with lanterns. In this case, each patrol is allowed to send one or two scouts to reconnoiter the positions of the two neighboring outposts, after which these scouts guide the entire patrol.

c) Another variation involves stationing one patrol in a line or semicircle with intervals of several dozen paces, while a second patrol sneaks through the gaps between the sentries, with each scout doing so individually and on their own. The positions of the individual guards may be completely unknown—only their line may be known. Alternatively, their positions can be revealed to scouts, or marked with small flags (a stick with a white handkerchief), or even lanterns. In this way, the difficulty of the task is adjusted. The procedure is the same as before.

The duration of the exercise is predetermined. The exercise can also be done with a smaller number of scouts.

d) Yet another variation involves placing outposts at a somewhat greater distance from each other and allowing patrols of 2 scouts to move between the outposts. The opposing side, divided into 2 groups, is stationed on both sides of the outpost line, several hundred paces away from it. This creates sneaking in both directions, which significantly complicates the task for the patrols guarding the line. A scout has successfully sneaked through if they reach the lantern, which is placed at the starting point of both groups.

Patrols capture opponents by shouting "Halt!" from a distance of 10–15 paces, and they are allowed to chase the enemy to this distance, unless the enemy is already more than 50 (100) paces away from the outpost line.

If the outposts or patrols capture a specified number of enemies, they win.

*Games involving sneaking can, of course, also be practiced during the day. Instead of lanterns, small flags are used, and the distance between outposts is increased, with terrain chosen that allows for concealment and covert movement.*

Sometimes, the use of all kinds of tricks (e.g., disguises) that could facilitate moving between outposts may be permitted.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Through Three Lines
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

An exercise similar to the previous one. The sides of the area through which one is allowed to sneak are precisely defined, e.g., by a road on the left and the edge of a forest on the right. Within this area, there are three lines of guards. Guarding is carried out by a small number of fixed outposts (2 people each), but mainly through patrolling. Patrols are not allowed to roam the entire area; they may only move along one line from the road to the forest, parallel to the outposts. The number of patrols assigned to each line (1–3) depends on the width of the area through which the sneaking takes place. The blockade, of course, cannot be too dense. One line of guards is positioned 200–300 paces from the next.

10–20 scouts sneak through the enemy lines to reach lantern X, placed 200–300 paces beyond the third line (the boundary).

The guards capture those sneaking by (by tapping them with a hand), but they are not allowed to chase them more than 10 paces in front of or beyond their own line.

![img-1.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-167-img-1.jpeg)

*Fig. 39.*

The sneaking scouts win if, after the designated time (1–2 hours), at least 2 out of every 10 have made it past the boundary, i.e., to the lantern.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Siege of the Fortress
body:
A fortress is a wall of snow, perhaps semicircular, perhaps closed in a circle—it may be a solid snow wall, and it may have loopholes. Inside the fortress, the Whites are stationed with a supply of ammunition—snowballs.

The Reds must locate and capture this fortress. They receive clues about its location, more or less precise, such as: *"Go in the direction of Z until you reach the roadside chapel surrounded by birches; the fortress is located a few hundred paces from it."* They may also follow the Whites' trail, either fresh tracks in the snow, which their leader directs them to, or an artificial one (colored paper scraps). In any case, after some time, they discover the fortress. A council is held on how to conduct the attack, and ammunition is gathered.

The battle begins. Any attacker hit twice (or three times) is considered dead (the fight is overseen by impartial judges). A defender is killed with a single hit. The fortress is captured when 1/3 (or 1/4) of the "living" attackers breach the wall. The dead on both sides (marked with a badge!) prepare snowballs for the fighters.

If the fortress is not circular, it may only be attacked from the front. A truce may be called (with an agreed signal and mutual consent) for rest, making snowballs, or repairing the fortress.

---

*Source scan: [Polona / National Library of Poland](https://polona.pl/item-view/0782bd3a-4d20-41be-86f8-bcdfc65555c5?page=0), marked "Public domain". [View scan — PDF page 168](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/harcerz-w-polu.pdf#page=168).*

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: For the Flags
body:
The exercise terrain is uneven, full of trees, bushes, etc., and is divided by a clear natural boundary, such as a road, path, or a row of trees, etc.; its natural side boundaries should also be marked (which must not be crossed during the exercise). However, this is rarely possible. Therefore, it is usually necessary to mark the dividing line with flags, with the outermost flags indicating the side boundaries.

The Whites and the Reds stand facing each other on either side of the central boundary and, in their respective areas, plant 3 flags each at a distance of 80–120 paces from the boundary, spaced 40 paces apart. The flags are placed in a line parallel to the boundary. The Whites attempt to sneak across the boundary, seize the flags, and bring them back to their camp.

Each scout may bring back only one flag per sortie. A raider may be taken prisoner. Since the Reds have the same task, both sides send some of their scouts beyond the boundary, while others remain in camp to defend their own flags. These defenders may stand no closer than 20 paces from a flag; otherwise, they are excluded from the game. The side that collects 5 flags in its camp wins. A captured flag is not planted in the ground unless it replaces a missing one.

Capturing a prisoner is done by touching them with a hand. A prisoner may only be taken within one’s own camp, never beyond the boundary in the opponent’s camp. The prisoner is then led to a designated prison area.

What will the course of the exercise be under these rules? For example, the Whites post guards near their flags. After a moment, a Red appears, crawling toward one of them. A guard spots him and blocks his path to force a retreat. The Red withdraws, leading the White away, while two more Reds emerge from the side. Before the guards can deal with them, the first Red reaches the flag (which the White is not allowed to approach). However, surrounded on all sides, he cannot seize it—he is neutralized for now. But since it is difficult to both guard and constantly watch for new enemies hiding behind bushes or rocks, the guards are caught off guard when two Reds suddenly appear and rush toward the nearest flag. The attack turns out to be a feint, but the surrounded Red takes advantage of it and escapes with the flag.

However, halfway back, he encounters two Whites who, hidden, form a second line of guards; they capture him and take the flag. Since the rule states that a flag taken within one’s own camp must be planted where it was captured, not on the original line, the Reds lose a man but bring the enemy flag closer to their camp, extending the Whites’ flag line and making their defense more difficult. This increases the chances of capturing more flags.

In this way, flags pass from one side to the other—one disappears, another is planted in its place—while at every step, one may encounter a lurking enemy. Thus, each scout sometimes crawls cautiously, using every cover to survey everything before taking another step, or sprints at full speed to reach a flag or, with a feigned attack, to help their comrades get to it.

New plans for real and feigned attacks constantly arise, where boldness and cunning triumph. Ultimately, one side has its 3 flags planted and 2 captured—and wins.

Each side has a judge to resolve disputes. It is advisable to plant twigs in the ground 20 paces from the flags to mark how close guards may approach.

Flags should not be hidden from the enemy. However, this is done (by planting them behind bushes, not in thickets) once scouts have gained sufficient experience in the game.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: In Search of the Letter
body:
In a forest or terrain with clearings, many scattered trees, overgrown ground, thickets, hollows, etc.—where it is easy to hide and move unnoticed—the leader hides a letter, marking the hiding spot in a visible manner.

Then, he gathers both patrols, the whites and the reds, and after giving them the boundaries of the area within which the exercise will take place, he informs them in general terms about the letter’s hiding place. For example: *"There is a tree, tied with a white thread at waist height; 5 paces away from it, under a stone, lies the letter."* This is the letter the scouts must retrieve.

Both patrols then assemble at opposite ends of the terrain near a flag marking the camp location, and at a given signal, they set off to search for the letter.

The search must be conducted as inconspicuously as possible to observe the opponent’s movements without drawing their attention, and with great caution to avoid falling into an ambush. The terrain should be spacious to minimize encounters. However, since it is impossible to avoid them entirely when searching in different directions—and direct encounters may occur—the conditions for such meetings must be strictly defined (based on the general guidelines provided) and all participants must be familiarized with them before the exercise begins.

For example: if a scout’s armband (a colored thread) is torn off, he is taken prisoner and must, without hiding, go directly to the enemy’s camp. (Thus, anyone who does not feel strong enough to fight or sees the enemy’s advantage should step aside—or, if hidden and wishing to remain in place, stay silent without revealing their hiding spot.) If an encounter occurs at a distance of 15–20 paces, the smaller group must retreat before the opponent if the opponent demands it (though the opponent is not obligated to use this right and may instead attempt to surround the smaller group to take them prisoner).

The party that retrieves the letter wins. The opposing side can nullify this victory by capturing at least half of the patrol. However, before counting prisoners, an exchange must take place, as the opposing side may also have captives.

From the above description, one can imagine the course of the exercise. The patrol leader of the whites (or reds) divides the entire terrain among the scouts, providing them with methods of communication, such as signals for: *"Help!"*, *"I found it!"*, *"The enemy is on the letter’s trail!"*, *"The enemy has seized the letter!"*, etc. Each scout searches their assigned section, with scouts sometimes moving alone, sometimes in pairs, separating and then regrouping. Since retrieving the letter is far more important than capturing prisoners, encounters are generally avoided. The opponent is only forced to retreat or ambushed (possibly with called-for reinforcements) if they interfere too much and hinder the search. The reds do the same.

Eventually, someone discovers the letter’s hiding place. At that point, they either take it, avoiding all encounters and seeking support from their comrades, or, if the enemy’s presence prevents taking the letter, they notify their friends and, with their help, carry it away. Ostentatiously taking the letter may lead to its loss, as the enemy could tear off an armband, in which case the letter must be surrendered. A direct encounter may even occur near the hiding spot, and during the skirmish, someone might manage to snatch the letter and flee with it.

Even after taking the letter, the scouts must not destroy the marks made by the leader.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Across the Border
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

 a) Not every terrain is suitable for this exercise. It must be undulating, in places overgrown, full of hollows, bushes, clusters of trees, etc., to facilitate concealment and stealth. A border runs through its center (a road, stream, long ravine, or a row of trees, etc., or a series of planted flags), dividing the white team’s territory from the red team’s. Both sides gather at the border, then separate, each moving deep into their own section until they lose sight of each other.

The opponents now occupy observation points from which at least part of the border is visible, and from which they can survey the enemy’s territory. The number of these points and their permissible distance from the border are predetermined. These points are occupied cautiously, in a manner invisible to the enemy, and are manned by 1–2 scouts each.

Half an hour after separating, the actual exercise begins. This time is needed to set up outposts, devise a plan of action, and assign tasks. The objective for each side is to cross the border undetected into the enemy’s territory and bring back precise information about the location of their observation points. Accordingly, the leader assigns some to guard the border, ordering them to patrol it continuously, while others are tasked with sneaking across the border to gather the necessary intelligence.

Behavior upon encountering an opponent may vary. For example: a scout, upon spotting an enemy sneaking up, may allow them to approach, then suddenly leap forward at the last moment, tear the ribbon from their arm, and thus take them prisoner. Alternatively, they may allow the enemy to come within 15–20 paces, then, while hidden, shout "Halt!"; the opponent is then captured and must withdraw from the game, tying their scarf around their cap. Or, if the enemy is interfering with their work, they may call out to them from a greater distance, in which case the enemy must retreat and disappear from sight, etc. Therefore, the method of procedure should be established before the exercise according to the previously given rules of encounter (see the general section) and all scouts should be informed of it.

Anyone who has ever participated in scout exercises will easily understand how much variety, surprise, and charm this exercise contains. Ingenuity, quick exploitation of a given situation, patience in waiting for the right moment to act, personal agility, etc.—all these qualities achieve great triumphs.

And the task is not easy. First, the enemy has chosen observation points that are difficult to locate; second, one can encounter the enemy at every step; and finally, it is not enough to gather information—it must also be carried back across the border to a designated point marked by a flag. Therefore, only great vigilance, even greater self-control, extreme caution, and above all, patience can yield positive results.

After 1½–2 hours, a signal is blown, and a joint assembly is held. Then, both leaders report what their scouts have discovered and how many prisoners were taken, and the instructor awards victory to one side.

The border dividing the terrain should be long enough to prevent it from being entirely guarded by permanent sentries. If, with a short border, both sides were to do this, the entire exercise would be impossible. If the border is long, permanent sentries will likely work to the disadvantage of the party that sets them up; better results will be achieved by crossing the border.

b) A simpler variation of the previous exercise is when only one side sneaks in for reconnaissance—of course, in terrain that allows it. The whites then occupy a space of several dozen paces in length and width, which can only be observed from a short distance. Here, they position themselves in various ways: in one place, a single scout is stationed; 10 paces away, a group of 4 scouts; after a larger gap, 2 scouts; in the center, a flag is planted; elsewhere, a tripod made of sticks, etc. No one is allowed to leave their assigned position.

The reds approach from a distance of 500–1000 paces. Their task is to get as close as possible and determine which points are occupied by the enemy, what their formation is, what lies beyond it, etc. If someone is discovered and a white scout calls out to them, e.g., from a distance of 40–50 paces, that person becomes a prisoner. The gathered information is reported to the instructor standing by the flag between the two parties.

After the designated time (1–2 hours), the value of the reds’ reconnaissance and the whites’ vigilance are assessed. Taking into account the quality of the terrain—whether it was easy or difficult to approach—and the fact that the reds had the more difficult task overall, victory is awarded to one side.

The whites can also be arranged in a single line, and reconnaissance can be allowed from the front and sides, but not from the rear. The success of this exercise depends mainly on choosing the right terrain.

A few impartial observers ensure the game proceeds correctly.

c) Another variation involves the whites setting up outposts at locations designated by the instructor, with the reds having these locations marked on their maps.

The goal is for the reds to sneak between the outposts (each 300–500 meters apart) in groups of at least 2 scouts, which is made more difficult by the constant patrols circulating between the outposts.

In the rear, beyond the outposts, a flag is planted where those who manage to sneak through are to gather.

Only sentries can take prisoners (tearing off ribbons, calling out, etc.—see the general section: rules of encounter). The reds win if they reach the flag in the designated number.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: From the Nest
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

The leader points out to one scout the place where he must hide the flag. No one knows this location. The scout sets off from point A, taking a winding path through varied terrain to make tracking difficult, but he carefully marks his route with agreed-upon signs. With him go three neutrals, who, after the flag is hidden, establish a boundary around the hiding spot with a radius of 100 to 300 paces. They do this by making rough sketches in which they mark the surrounding noticeable terrain features, and where necessary, they mark this boundary, e.g., with chalk on the door of a hut standing there. The entire area should be suitable for concealment and stealth.

Three quarters of an hour later, two scouts from each patrol set off, following the marked trail to find the flag. Each pair tracks for themselves, and cleverly, so as not to make the work easier for rivals from other patrols. Whoever reaches the flag must not take it; instead, they take only a card with the name of their patrol (there is a card for each of the seekers at the flag) and tries to deliver it to the leader, who waits for this at a location known to all, point B, several hundred paces away from the hiding spot.

Meanwhile, the patrols follow at a distance behind the trackers, keeping them in sight from afar. It is not allowed to pass members of one’s own patrol, but it is allowed to pass others. They do not necessarily follow the trail, as this might show the way to others—however, they always move in such a way as not to lose sight of their own.

![img-4.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-178-img-4.jpeg)

Fig. 42.

When they reach the boundary, which they are no longer allowed to cross, they receive the sketches from the neutral who waits for them there. Anyone who crosses the boundary during the exercise has their badge torn from their arm and is excluded from the exercise.

Now the actual exercise begins. Each patrol tries to catch the envoys of other patrols when they are on their way back to the leader (of course, after they have passed the boundary, as patrols are not allowed to cross it). By doing so, they eliminate their rivals’ own messengers, thus making it easier for their own to win. A captured envoy must surrender the card taken at the flag.

Of course, individual patrols move along the boundary, set ambushes for the sneaking opponent, block their path, etc., as long as they prevent the delivery of the card to the leader (the method of taking prisoners should be established based on the rules of the encounter).

However, one must not interfere with the capture of one’s own messengers or rescue them; likewise, one must not take prisoners other than enemy messengers. On the other hand, one may warn their own, inform them of enemy positions, point out a clear path, etc.

The patrol that brings the most cards within the designated time wins.

Those searching for the flag must have special badges, different for each patrol.

The boundary around the hiding spot can be closer or farther from it, depending on the scouts' proficiency.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Breaking the Railway Line
body:
The road is a railway line that the scout patrol must break. The exercise takes place in the evening.

The Whites guard this road. Patrols of several men walk back and forth along it. (A patrol may stop briefly at a certain point, but it is not allowed to permanently occupy the line.)

Since breaking such a road requires remaining on it for some time, the Reds are given a task that will keep them on the line. The Whites do not know what this task is. For example, the Reds may be ordered to dig a hole of 1 m² next to the road, to the depth of a spade’s blade, or to drive a dozen or so stakes in a single row to the same depth (not on the road! — they are removed later), or to stretch three ropes across the road above human height, etc. The Reds, in groups of two, sneak under the line and begin work. If a patrol approaches, they hide so as not to reveal the start of work at that spot. When the patrol passes, they finish the work as quickly as possible.

![img-5.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-180-img-5.jpeg)

*Fig. 43.*

If the Whites spot the Reds, they drive them off the road (if they manage to get within 10 (15–20) paces of the Reds, they take them prisoner) and, if they figure out what the Reds were doing, they destroy their work. After completing the work, the Reds place a prearranged sign on it; the Whites are not allowed to destroy work marked with such a sign.

If the Reds find a particular spot too hot because they have drawn the enemy’s attention, so that all their patrols are now especially watching that section of the line, they may abandon the work and start it in another place. Pursuit is not allowed.

The Reds win if, within the designated time, at least one of their groups completes its work; the Whites win if they prevent this.

The railway line should be long enough in proportion to the number of scouts so that both sides have equally difficult tasks.

The game time should be sufficiently long.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: The Aviator
body:
In the forest, an aviator has crashed and lies helpless. It is not known where he fell or to which side he belongs. Both the Whites and the Reds, encamped on opposite sides of the forest at a distance of 1–3 km from each other, receive this news simultaneously. Both sides set out at the same time to search for the aviator, so that upon determining which side he belongs to, they may either take him prisoner or defend him from the enemy and escort him to their own camp.

The aviator, wearing a distinct insignia on his shoulder, remains passive throughout the exercise as a wounded man. If he has no companion (White or Red) with him, he must not move from his spot. Depending on whether the terrain is easy or difficult to search, the leader hides him in a more or less hard-to-find hiding place. In any case, the aviator must not reveal his hiding place to his friends, as this would give one side an unfair advantage over the other.

This leads to a whole series of surprises and varied situations. For example, the Whites, whether individually or in small groups, scour the entire forest in search of the aviator. Upon encountering a Red, they may hide from him (since finding the aviator is more important than capturing an enemy), or they may force him to retreat, suspecting that the aviator is hidden in that very area. Someone finds the aviator and quietly leads him away (the wounded aviator can only walk at a slow pace). However, if they feel threatened, they order the aviator to lie down on the ground and rush for help. But then three Reds arrive and take the aviator with them. A White sees this but cannot retake him alone, so he follows their trail and, with a prearranged vocal signal, alerts his comrades that he is on the trail of the captured aviator. The Whites gather, learn what has happened; a brief council is held, and they all disappear. The forest is ending, so the Reds will soon be in their camp, but it turns out that the Whites are waiting for them in an ambush. A sudden raid—the aviator is recaptured, two are killed. The exercise continues. Finally, one side brings the aviator to their camp and wins.

As seen in the example, the exercise offers room for a variety of ideas; it requires, on the one hand, thoughtfulness and deliberation in actions, and on the other, often great cunning and dexterity. To orient oneself in the situation, seize the right moment and method of action, and, if the circumstances change, maintain presence of mind and quickly make a new decision—all of this puts the Scout to a severe test. If the exercise fails, it is usually due to a lack of patience and a strange eagerness to hastily resolve every situation, even when there is time to think. For instance, a Scout who finds the aviator may take him away on his own, only to immediately fall into enemy hands. Would it not be better, if there is no immediate danger, to find another hiding place and, at the right moment, move the aviator there, gradually getting closer to his own camp, while notifying his comrades along the way and requesting clever and cautious assistance and protection?

This game will only succeed if the players do not cluster around the found aviator to defend him, but rather keep their distance, entrusting only one person with his escort, while drawing the enemy’s attention to themselves. If they do not do this, a fight will soon break out, and the game will stall.

Since this exercise often involves encounters between individual Scouts or groups, the conditions for such encounters must be clearly established before the exercise begins, based on the rules provided in the introduction (preferably without removing armbands).

Any number of Scouts may participate in the exercise. Neutral observers with white armbands on their caps should move through the forest to resolve any doubts that arise.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Spies in the Camp
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

From each patrol participating in the exercise, two scouts are selected. These, as the *reds*, play against the remaining *whites*. The whites set up a camp with very visible boundaries and surround it with sentries. Half of the reds leave the camp, while the other half remain inside. Each patrol knows that there is one enemy among them, but no one knows who it is—especially since the reds do not reveal themselves. Only the exercise leader knows, as they secretly designated the reds before the exercise began.

The reds outside the camp (acting as scouts of the besieging force) attempt to sneak in to deliver a letter to the leader. Each carries one copy of the letter. If a red is caught inside the camp, they are searched, and the letter is confiscated if they have not managed to destroy or hide it.

Of course, a scout who has successfully infiltrated the camp cannot directly hand the letter to the leader (who remains impartial throughout the exercise) without risking almost certain capture, as the whites are vigilant and aware of the danger. Instead, they try to communicate with one of their hidden allies inside the camp and use them as an intermediary to deliver the letter. Before the exercise, the reds agree among themselves on methods of communication and coordinated actions. This agreement and the leader’s designation of the reds must occur before the exercise is announced, as the whites, knowing the objective, would either prevent communication or quickly identify the hidden enemies.

If the leader receives 2 letters within the specified time (3 if more than 5 patrols are camping), the reds win. If the reds fail, the whites win.

The camp should be set up in a location conducive to sneaking in, should be spacious with clearly visible and known boundaries to all, and the sentries should not be densely posted. Otherwise, the exercise cannot be carried out. The whites are not allowed to search the camp to find any hidden reds.

From the description, it is clear how difficult the reds’ task is. Infiltrating the camp is already challenging, and that is only half the task. Where to hide, and how to draw attention to oneself while the whites are alert to every suspicious movement or sound? And how to approach a comrade without revealing oneself, since the whites are watching each other and any action may seem suspicious? Only great self-control, immense patience, immediate decision-making at the right moment, along with cunning and ingenuity, can succeed. Much also depends on good prior coordination.

There can be countless ideas, changing with the situation. For example, one red might act clumsily in the camp to draw suspicion, then try to hand over a fake dispatch, creating a distraction to help another red deliver the letter to an intermediary. (This can only be done if they are certain someone is already hidden in the camp and simply lacks a way to receive the letter. This shows that even the disguised reds should have ways to communicate with each other.) A captured red might also carry a fake dispatch, and once in captivity, later deliver the real one—well hidden—to an intermediary. Similarly, a red sneaking in might deliberately attract the guard’s attention to help a comrade infiltrate the camp, and so on. Hundreds of ideas, adapted to the situation, but above all, *cold blood*—that is the first condition for success.

The camp should host various camp activities ordered by the leader. There should be normal movement, because if everyone sits and watches each other suspiciously, nothing will work. The leader should also change their position in the camp—in short, everything should proceed normally.

It should be added that a scout who has slipped past the guards must not be chased inside the camp; the guard may only signal danger with a whistle.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Bandits and Gendarmes
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

A gang of 4–5 bandits, led by a chief, hides in the forest. The gendarmes conduct a manhunt. To this end, several of their patrols set out simultaneously from several points on the perimeter of the designated exercise area, moving toward the center to meet at an agreed location. Each patrol must search a specific section of the terrain and capture the bandits. If a gendarme encounters a bandit and manages to approach within 15 paces, he shouts "Halt!" and thereby takes him prisoner. The gendarmes have a password and a response, by which they recognize each other from a distance, as the bandits are dressed the same as the gendarmes.

The exercise is very simple but requires great cunning, extreme vigilance, quick orientation, and decisiveness from the bandits. All tricks are allowed, as long as they can slip through the net. If the bandits manage to obtain the password, they thereby increase their chances of success. They can, for example, eavesdrop on it if a gendarme, unable to distinguish the person he meets, demands the password, and the encountered individual—who is also a gendarme—provides it from a distance. Or a bandit, pretending to be a gendarme, asks for the password from afar, and upon receiving it, when asked for the response in turn, flees. Once the password is known, the response can also be learned, as a bandit, when questioned, gives the password and in return demands the response to confirm that he is dealing with a gendarme and not another bandit, etc. The more cunning the bandits, the easier it is for them to mislead the gendarmes.

The gendarmes win if, within the designated time, they capture the bandits, with at most one (or possibly two) escaping, and the chief is not among them. Otherwise, the bandits win.

The exercise terrain should be spacious and have clearly defined boundaries. It should also offer great variety in its layout, with thickets, many ravines, etc. The leader positions the patrols, indicates each patrol’s starting point and assembly point. The patrol leaders coordinate among themselves regarding the division of the search sections. Of course, each patrol is free to turn back if necessary, but the bandits can exploit this to their advantage.

Since the bandits are selected from the patrols after they have dispersed, no patrol knows all the bandits. The leader should draw attention to this important circumstance.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: The Merchant with Goods
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

From north to south, through dense forests, ravines, gorges, etc., a merchant travels accompanied by 6 men. From the west, a gang of Whites lies in wait for him; from the east, a gang of Reds. Both sides want to capture the merchant, but they are hostile toward each other and not only do they refuse to help one another, but on the contrary, when they meet, they attack each other, seeking to either destroy or at least drive each other off and prevent the other from capturing the merchant. The merchant takes advantage of this rivalry and slips through stealthily to the designated place.

Both the Whites and the Reds know the hour at which the merchant departs, his starting point, and his destination. The finish line, toward which he is heading, is neutral within a radius of 200 paces; neither the Whites nor the Reds are allowed to cross it. The distance the merchant must cover is several kilometers. The starting positions of the Whites and Reds are located to the right and left, each 1 km away from the center of this area. No one is allowed to move from their position before the designated hour.

If the merchant reaches the finish line accompanied by at least 3 men, he wins. If he is captured, the patrol that captures and brings him to their starting point wins. Even if the merchant reaches the finish line, the side that captured more opponents can still claim a partial victory.

The Whites and Reds face equally difficult tasks. They must focus primarily on capturing the merchant and only drive off the opponent if they hinder their efforts; however, they must never lose sight of their main objective. Both sides may split into small groups to confuse the opposing side, set obstacles, or delay their search, but they must always keep track of the merchant’s location. Then, one part attacks and captures him, while the other holds off any potential pursuit. Breaking a thread signifies killing an opponent; other meeting rules are established based on the general guidelines provided in the introduction.

The merchant (who wears an armband) and his companions (who wear no insignia) are not allowed to fight. However, they may use all means to slip past the Whites and Reds. The merchant must always be accompanied by at least 3 men. The other three serve as scouts and to mislead the enemy.

The area where the exercise takes place, whose boundaries must not be crossed, must be clearly marked.

---
