author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Relay Post
body:
During many exercises, a relay post is set up for the rapid transmission of messages, as if a single messenger could do it. Scouts are positioned in a single long line every 50–150 paces, and a note, handed to the last scout, passes sequentially from hand to hand until it reaches the recipient. The note is marked with the speed of delivery using one, two, or three crosses. One (X) means a brisk march, two (XX) a normal run, three (XXX) a fast run.

The relay post is set up quickly and should operate efficiently. This can be practiced by combining such a setup with an exercise. For example: There are three patrols of 8 scouts each and 3 patrol leaders. The scouts will act as messengers, the patrol leaders as scouts. I need to verify whether the bridge over the river in the direction of Pn is occupied by the enemy. From the map, I calculate the distance to be 840 m. The first patrol sets out and, every 120 paces (60 double paces), leaves one scout behind. Each stands in concealment. The relay post is set up over a distance of 840 m. The patrol leader writes: *‘Bridge clear, the second patrol is to set up a relay post to village A in the direction of Z and report that the post is ready (X)’*. The note passes from hand to hand, each scout moving at a brisk pace; the last one hands the note to the second patrol leader. He calculates the required spacing for the messengers, sets up a new line, and a message returns to the front of the first line: *‘Second relay post to village A ready (××)’*; this time, the messengers carry the note at a run. The third message reads: *‘I am withdrawing the first line; the third patrol is to extend the second line as far as the forest beyond village A; await further orders (××)’*. After the first line is withdrawn, I send a fourth note: *‘Withdraw the entire second line, assemble at the original location (××)’*. The second line is withdrawn, the three patrols gather together, and the exercise is discussed.

The sign of three crosses is used exceptionally when the fastest possible transmission of a very important message is required. During the same exercise, it may be used at most twice, provided the distance between two scouts does not exceed 100 m and there is time for rest.

Scouts who serve in front of the relay line must always know where its beginning is.

A dispatch may also be passed verbally. In that case, we also have an exercise in properly receiving a report.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Attack on the Relay Post
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

At the assembly point, one white scout remains, while the entire patrol sets off in a designated direction toward a specified goal, located an hour's march away. The march takes place partly along the road and partly across off-road terrain. Every 10–15 minutes, individual scouts (or pairs) are left in good hiding spots, thus creating a chain of intermediate relay stations through which dispatches will be sent to the receiving station. Eventually, the patrol leader arrives at the goal with a few remaining scouts. From there, at intervals (every 10–20 minutes), a courier is sent with a dispatch. This courier must locate the nearest station and relieve the scout hidden there, who will then carry the dispatch further to the next station. Dispatches must be numbered and signed by the patrol leader—they are carried in the shirt pocket.

So far, the task is simple and easy. However, from the assembly point, 20 minutes after the white patrol departs, the red patrol sets off. They only know that couriers with dispatches are moving in the area and that a relay post exists. But which route does it follow, and where are the individual stations? The reds must try to obtain this very information, for the goal is to intercept the dispatch, and even more so, to break the chain and prevent the transmission of messages.

Now it becomes clear how difficult the task is for the whites, for if even one hiding spot is discovered and the scout hidden there is captured, every approaching courier will fall into a trap. Moreover, instead of searching the area, the reds can discreetly follow the white patrol’s trail and thus discover the location of the stations. And what to do if the chain is broken—how to warn the others? Difficult situations may arise, and there is no end to them; one must be prepared for every surprise and immediately find remedies.

It will then become apparent whether the whites have their wits about them. Above all, each hiding spot must be well chosen, i.e., known to all couriers and easy to find, while also providing both adequate concealment and a good view of the surroundings. In this way, the courier will know what is happening not only around him but also near the previous and next stations (a hiding spot can even be in a tree).

Furthermore—all couriers should have established signals and always send them from cover so as not to reveal their presence. These do not need to be flag signals, i.e., conveying entire words (though that is also possible); simple signs will suffice, indicating the interruption of the post with the number of the destroyed station, the interception of a dispatch, an impending danger, the relocation of one station to another place due to the discovery of a hiding spot, etc. There should not be many such signals, but they must be clear.

Not all stations can see each other, as the terrain does not always allow it. Therefore, each courier must cautiously sneak toward the next station, using all possible cover, and approach it carefully, waiting for a signal that the way is clear, for he might walk into an ambush. Anyone who has had to leave the line must notify the previous station, or at least warn the approaching courier—in short, every important event must be communicated to the others.

The whites can more easily overcome all these difficulties if, instead of leaving one scout at each station, they leave two: one to relay the messages, the other to mend broken links. This is also how the exercise should be organized from the start.

A courier is taken prisoner by being stopped with the word: «Halt!» from a distance of 10 (15) paces (it is also permissible to allow direct capture by tearing off the badge from the shoulder, as both sides wear badges). The whites win if, within the designated time, they deliver two-thirds of the sent dispatches to the first assembly point. The number of dispatches is predetermined. A courier must not destroy a dispatch or refuse to hand it over.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Breaking the Telegraph Line
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

A road with telegraph poles runs through terrain that is perfectly suited on both sides for stalking and sudden attacks.

The Whites, with a strength of 2 patrols, occupy the road, stationing one scout at each pole; the rest remain in reserve. Their commander will decide whether to man all the poles or to station scouts at some of them in small groups.

![img-1.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-194-img-1.jpeg)

*Fig. 45.*

The Reds, with a strength of 1 patrol, must break the telegraph line. They succeed if they manage to wrap one pole with three ropes or scarves. However, the White defends the pole and can "kill" a Red by tearing the wool armband from their arm.

How does the exercise unfold under these general rules? The Whites, expecting an attack but not knowing from which direction it will come, send scouts in both directions. Each scout diligently reports their observations to the command: where the Reds are gathering or where they are heading. Based on this, the commander stealthily sends part of the reserve to the threatened points, where they wait for the enemy or force them to retreat with their numerical advantage, thus preventing the attack.

But the Reds are not idle either. They try to mislead the Whites, feigning false attacks, etc., so that at the right moment they can strike in the least expected place and wrap an unguarded pole. A whistle—rush to the rescue—but it is already too late. They also dare to attack a guarded spot: while one Red distracts the White, skillfully avoiding having their armband torn off, a second or even a third wraps the pole in the meantime. And who knows if the entire raid, though noisy and requiring the sacrifice of three, just to draw as much of the enemy as possible, is not also a feint? For suddenly, two Reds appear at a distant spot and wrap the undefended poles.

As can be seen, nothing here can be done independently. Everyone must be in constant contact; everything must be carried out according to a plan: lightning-fast assessment of the situation and lightning-fast action. And yet, they must not let their guard down, for after a failed attack, the next one might succeed.

Whoever completes their task within the designated time wins: the Reds if they wrap the poles as prescribed, the Whites if they prevent this.

This exercise can be varied in many ways; it can also be made more difficult for one side or the other. For example:

- The defense will be more difficult if the exercise is set on such a long stretch of road that it is impossible to station a defender at every pole. Or:

- The Reds can be declared the winners even if, in one raid, they wrap a pole only once or twice, and only on the third attempt do they wrap it three times. Or:

- The task can be to wrap not one but three poles (each with one rope), and not simultaneously, but at any intervals. Or: "killing" occurs by touching a Red with the hand (easier than tearing off the wool armband). Or: it is allowed to untie a rope from the pole if it has not been wrapped three times, etc.

Only the defender can "kill," but a rule can be added that the Reds must cease their work and retreat if the Whites appear at a given point in greater numbers.

Outside the road, the Reds retreat before the Whites, or vice versa: the Reds retreat if the Whites are equal in number, while the Whites retreat if the Reds have the advantage. However, it is also possible to allow mutual tearing of armbands on this terrain (but not on the road), etc.

Of course, a scout without an armband does not participate further in the exercise. With cleverness and some experience, the game can proceed very smoothly and develop in an engaging manner.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Courier
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

The terrain on which the exercise takes place has precisely defined boundaries. A courier must cross it and deliver a dispatch to a designated point (there may be several such points).

The courier is the white patrol leader, who, in addition to his patrol badge, wears another badge on his shoulder. He is escorted by 1–2 scouts, while the rest of the patrol facilitates his journey by scouting the terrain, giving early warnings of danger, driving off the reds, etc. Before the exercise, the patrol leader must explain to everyone the route he will take and how they are to assist him along the way. If he is forced to change his original route, he must inform his patrol, so he must maintain constant contact with them. In case of great danger, he may hand the dispatch to one of his escorts, but in such a case, he must also hand over his courier badge. The dispatch must be kept in the blouse pocket; it must not be destroyed or hidden elsewhere.

The reds, who have twice as many patrols as the whites, attempt to intercept the dispatch or at least prevent its delivery within the specified time. In that case, the game will be undecided. They are not allowed to occupy the points to which the dispatch is to be delivered.

The evaluation of results can vary. One may award 6 points for delivering the dispatch — 3 points for intercepting it — 1 point for capturing an opponent. Alternatively, both delivery and interception may be counted as 3 points each if the whites have a clear advantage in skill.

The exercise can also be made more difficult for the whites by prohibiting the courier carrying the dispatch from handing it to a comrade.

During the exercise, the rules for encounters with the enemy, based on general regulations, apply.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Two Passwords
body:
Towards a forest glade, located in the middle of the terrain where the exercise takes place, scouts creep forward, each positioned singly around the area:

The exercise begins as follows: all participants (after receiving cards, the contents of which must not be revealed to anyone) form a circle and then disperse along radii to a distance of 500–800 paces, after which they hide and wait for the signal to start the game.

Half of them are conspirators, who have a password and a response (e.g., *Warsaw — Castle*). The other half are gendarmes tracking them, who have also been given their own recognition signs (e.g., *Vistula — Wawel*). No one knows who is a conspirator and who is a gendarme, for everyone has a band of the same color tied around their left arm, but each carries a card in their pocket, given to them by the leader. (On the card, for example: *Bandit. Password: Warsaw — Response: Castle*.)

Since the side that has the most members on the glade at the end of the game with their band still on their arm wins, each tries to neutralize as many enemies as possible by tearing off their bands, while also saving themselves. But whose band should one tear off? First, one must ask for the password, for what if it is a friend? But by doing so, one might reveal oneself. And what then?

There is a rule: the one who first asks for the password from a distance of 15–20 paces has the right to demand it from the other. Therefore, one must cautiously sneak up to the observed person or lie in wait on their path in order to have the right to ask.

And many complications can arise in the process. For example, the question is asked: *Password?* The answer is: *Warsaw!* Then the one asked, in turn, asks for the response to confirm whether they are indeed dealing with a friend. What if the questioner was a gendarme and does not know the conspirators' response? Then, either they attack the opponent to tear the band from their arm, or, not wanting to expose themselves, they flee after learning the enemy’s password. Part of the secret is revealed. Now, if this gendarme later encounters someone else, they deliberately do not ask for the password, and when asked, they give the wrong one: *Warsaw*. If they also encounter a gendarme, that one will certainly attack or flee; then they quickly correct themselves, giving the proper password *Vistula* and receiving the response *Wawel* in return. Two friends have recognized each other, and now two know the conspirators' password. If, however, it was a conspirator, they will certainly, upon receiving the password *Warsaw*, reveal their response *Castle* to the gendarme. This information is extremely valuable for the gendarme: they approach the conspirator, who suspects nothing, and suddenly tear off their band! The enemy is neutralized, and their password is known. The gendarme is now somewhat in control of the situation, but not absolutely, for one of the conspirators might have similarly deceived the gendarmes and, in turn, also misled them.

There can be countless such tricks as the one above. From this single example, one can see how much presence of mind is required to avoid being deceived by anyone, how vast the field is for various ideas, and how many different stratagems are needed to outwit the enemy and gain the upper hand. Those who recognize each other explain who among the rest are friends and who are enemies, and often begin joint action.

At first, it is difficult to encounter anyone, but the closer one gets to the glade, the easier it becomes. Yet, no one knows whom to trust or whom to guard against, whether it is better to enter the glade (for once someone enters, they are not allowed to leave it) or to try their luck further to tip the scales of victory in favor of their own side. And the edge of the glade may also be occupied, and suddenly a question about the password may be asked, leading to a hopeless self-revelation! Finally, at the designated hour, on the signal to assemble, everyone enters the glade, and after revealing themselves, they count the number of "killed." One side has won. It should also be added that once a band is torn off, it is not allowed to be tied back on, even if it was torn off by mistake.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Transport
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

The White Patrol escorts a cart, which must be delivered to a designated location several kilometers from the starting point. The cart is a type of stretcher made from scout staves. Specifically, two staves are connected by a crossbar, covered with tent canvas, a cape, etc., and everything is securely tied. At one end of the stretcher, a rope is attached, by which it is pulled: the front end is raised, while the rear end drags along the ground.

![img-2.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-200-img-2.jpeg)

Fig. 46.

Three enemy patrols—Red, Blue, and Green—know where and when the White Patrol departs and where it is heading, but they do not know the route it will take. They therefore try to track the Whites’ path so they can ambush them at the right moment and seize the cart.

The Whites, however, do not forget they are moving through enemy territory and what dangers await them. Thus, part of the patrol escorts the cart, while another part scouts the terrain and reports any threats to the patrol leader, who then takes all defensive measures, even changing the route to avoid dangerous areas.

The Whites move along various paths, sometimes advancing quickly, sometimes retreating; but since three patrols lie in wait for them, they will sooner or later encounter an ambush, and it is doubtful whether they can avoid an attack. At least they have the consolation that the enemy patrols are not allowed to join forces, so they are only ever threatened by one patrol at a time.

What happens in case of an attack? The attackers, say the Reds, will capture the cart if they manage to throw their flag onto the stretcher. However, all scouts wear a woolen armband of their patrol’s color around their left arm, and anyone who has it torn off is considered killed—whether defender or attacker. Additionally, if the scout carrying the flag is even touched by one of the defenders, the attack is considered repelled along the entire line (judge’s whistle), and it can only be repeated in another location. Thus, both defenders and attackers suffer losses during an attack, and after a successful defense or a successful attack, it becomes harder for both sides to defend against the remaining patrols.

If the Reds manage to throw their flag onto the stretcher, the judge blows a whistle to signal that the attack succeeded (the judge, wearing a white armband, always accompanies the transport patrol—ideally, there should be two judges). The Reds then take over the role of the escort and attempt to deliver the cart to the destination despite attacks from the Blues, Greens, and even the Whites, who may try to retake it.

Ultimately, the patrol that succeeds in delivering the cart to its destination wins.

This exercise provides an opportunity, on one hand, for skillful and cautious terrain reconnaissance (since each scout on reconnaissance may fall into an ambush), for rapidly assessing the situation in case of an attack, and for making quick decisions amid constant surprises. On the other hand, it allows for tracking the escort’s march, using the terrain for cover and ambushes, and continuously adapting to changes in the transport’s route by maintaining constant contact with it.

All tricks are permitted except disguising oneself, as long as the flag is thrown onto the cart.

This exercise requires scouts to demonstrate particular discipline. Since hand-to-hand encounters occur, any scout whose armband is torn off must immediately withdraw from the exercise: they place their scarf on their shoulder and proceed to the assembly point, which is the destination where the transport is heading. Judges must strictly enforce the rules and compliance with the encounter regulations.

The rules can also be modified slightly. For example:
- After capturing the cart, the defeated patrol may be eliminated from the exercise;
- The destination may be known only to the transport patrol, which, if the cart is taken from them, reveals it to the victor and then withdraws;
- The cart must be delivered within a specified time, etc.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Camp in the Forest
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

The exercise takes place on a clear evening. The Whites are camping in the forest; guards are posted around. The camp consists of a planted flag with a few scouts by a campfire or, if fires cannot be lit, by a lantern. The area in front of the forest is scouted by patrols from the direction where the Reds are expected to approach.

The Reds are stationed at point A, and having learned of the Whites’ camp in the forest, they send two patrols in the directions m—n with orders to search the area and locate the Whites’ position.

Sooner or later, the opposing patrols will encounter each other. The Reds’ primary task is to locate the camp, so they will avoid combat, the outcome of which is uncertain; instead, they will try to evade the Whites’ sight. The Whites, on the other hand, aim to prevent the Reds from entering the forest, so upon confirming the presence of an enemy patrol, they will attempt to cut off their path and set an ambush. If the Reds spot a White, they will follow him closely, as he may lead them to the camp, and if circumstances are favorable, they may even attack him. The White will return not by the shortest route but by a roundabout path to avoid revealing the camp.

Since the Whites have three patrols (one at the camp, one on guard duty, one on reconnaissance) and the Reds have two or three, and the exercise takes place in the evening, one side must wear distinguishing badges on their caps or shoulders (in addition to the colored armbands), and both sides must have their own challenge and password. The patrols may be small, consisting of just a few scouts.

The Reds must send reports to point A, behind the line m—n. Additionally, the rule is that the Whites change their roles at regular intervals (every ½–1 hour), meaning that those on patrol go to the camp or on guard duty, and others take their place.

If the guards raise an alarm (not before), the Whites are allowed to change the camp’s location (always within a designated area), making it harder for the Reds to find it. However, they should leave one or two scouts behind to explain the situation to returning patrols.

Everything is done quietly; the Red patrols in particular try to move as silently as possible and conduct reconnaissance as cautiously as possible to avoid detection. However, since the exercise takes place in the dark, a series of surprises will inevitably arise.

At a set time, the exercise ends with an agreed signal. Locating the camp or preventing its discovery constitutes victory.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Avoiding the Enemy
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

A scout with one signal flag indicates an outpost; with two, a larger unit. Both sides are aware of this.

Along a stream, 3 white outposts are stationed, with the middle one occupying the bridge. (If there is no stream, a road is chosen.) The white patrol must scout the area in front of the outposts, reach settlement A, and check if it is occupied by the reds. Reports must be sent to point B, located behind the middle outpost.

The red patrol, having left their unit in A, sets out to inspect the bridge. If the situation allows, they are to wait for their unit near the bridge.

The leader sends both patrols at such a time that they meet in the middle of the space between the bridge and settlement A. When the reds encounter the whites, they should not engage in any skirmishes but rather avoid them, as their task is to inspect the bridge. However, they are puzzled by the presence of an enemy patrol in this area, so they send a report about encountering the enemy at that location and continue onward. At the bridge, they notice the presence of an outpost—this is already more important information, as it reveals the enemy’s position. Therefore, a second report is sent, but since it is very important and the whites are lurking behind them, it is dispatched via two messengers on different routes. The patrol then locates the positions of the remaining outposts and, given the changed situation, decides not to wait for their own unit but instead to go toward A to personally report the new developments.

The whites, upon encountering the reds, should also not be distracted from their proper task: verifying whether the red unit is in A. They will therefore send a messenger with news of the encounter with the reds and continue on their way. However, they should assume that messengers will be sent to A by the reds and do their best to intercept them.

Will both patrols carry out all of this? Or will a chase begin, with the original task forgotten—the very task that must be fulfilled above all? The leader will assess the conduct of both sides and award priority to the one that, having recognized the changed situation, chose the best course of action.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Without an Opponent
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

The exercise takes place in the evening. The white patrol receives the order to reach point A to determine whether it is free of reds. They must proceed very cautiously, and if they encounter the enemy either on the way to this point or on the return, they must bypass them and reach point B unnoticed, from which they set out.

After their departure, two white patrols, each consisting of 4–6 people, take up positions at the edge of the forest at points m and n, 200–400 paces apart, while a third patrol serves as a communication link between them, patrolling along the forest’s edge; all have the order to repel red patrols and prevent them from entering the forest. Reports are sent to point B.

Meanwhile, there are no reds at all; only four white patrols are participating in the exercise. However, the guards are unaware of this and constantly expect the enemy from the direction of A.

Now, interesting situations may arise. The first patrol cautiously approaches A, checks that there are no reds there, and returns even more cautiously, convinced that they will encounter them at any moment.

![img-2.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-207-img-2.jpeg)

Fig. 49.

Thus, they reach the forest and observe it before entering deeper. They notice one or another outpost or a patrol moving along the forest. In the darkness, it is difficult to distinguish who they are dealing with, and since the order states that they must pass unnoticed to B, they take advantage of the opportunity and, at the right place and moment, sneak into the forest. In this way, they may reach point B, still convinced that they have broken through the red line. The leader gives the signal to assemble, and then everything becomes clear: the carelessness of the guards and the unnecessary sneaking through their own line instead of first determining who is defending the forest. A lesson for the future.

It may also happen that an outpost or patrol notices the approaching group and either drives them away or sets an ambush, etc. However, it is only later (if at all) that they realize they were dealing with a friend, that they have taken part of their own into captivity, or scattered some of them in all directions. Whatever happens, such an experience teaches that not every approaching figure must be seen as an enemy.

All wear armbands of the same color. The guarding patrols must be kept unaware of whether and where the first patrol has gone and what color it is.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: With the Enemy at Your Back
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

The White patrol moves from point B towards A, occupies the bridge over the river (i.e., the point marked by two flags on the road), and observes whether the Reds are approaching A, where they are currently stationed. Upon reaching the bridge, and then regularly every quarter of an hour (or 20–30 minutes), they must send reports to B about what they have observed, and finally, after one hour (or 1½ hours), return.

Meanwhile, the Red patrol, which is secretly positioned at point O (unknown to the Whites) and is heading towards B, learns that the Whites have occupied the bridge and are constantly sending reports to B, to which they will also return. (The Reds should arrive at point B roughly at the same time the Whites reach the bridge). Therefore, they decide to intercept the reports and even set an ambush for the White patrol during its return. In turn, they must send a message to A about what they have learned and what they intend to do. The Red messenger can only go to A via the bridge.

The Whites do not know that they have an enemy behind them and that this enemy is intercepting their messages. Unless their messenger is alert and cautious and manages to escape or at least signal a warning of danger. If the Whites hear a warning signal, since they cannot abandon their post and do not know what it means, they should send the next message by two routes with two people, so that at least one of them reaches the destination. When the entire patrol returns, they should proceed with the utmost caution.

Now, the scouts' efficiency will be tested—their ability to orient themselves in the situation and make the right decisions. The leader observes the exercise and this will give him a basis for an instructive discussion of the whole. Did a warning signal sound? Did the messenger try to lose or destroy the report? (It may only be carried in a breast pocket). Did a signal for dispersal sound during the attack on the returning patrol? Did the part of the patrol that escaped gather at the designated assembly point (if one was assigned at all)? Did the warned patrol cleverly avoid the ambush and reach B by another route? etc. If the patrol does not keep its wits about it, of course, all messengers in turn and the entire patrol will be captured.

Taking into account the behavior of both sides and the fact that the Reds have an easier task, the leader will award victory to one side. Among the Reds, only one messenger will have a tough nut to crack and room to shine: to sneak into A via a route occupied by the enemy. (It is assumed that the river can be forded 20–30 paces to the left and right of the bridge).

In A and B, reports are received by designated impartial scouts, standing by a planted flag.

---

*Scan source: [Polona / National Library of Poland](https://polona.pl/item-view/0782bd3a-4d20-41be-86f8-bcdfc65555c5?page=0), marked "Public domain". [View scan — PDF pages 208–210](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/harcerz-w-polu.pdf#page=208).*

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Unaware of Danger
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

Two white patrols are sent towards the river to check if bridges m and n are free of the enemy.

![img-3.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-210-img-3.jpeg)

Fig. 51.

Written reports about this should be sent to point B, then the river crossings should be occupied, and any approach of the reds should be reported.

After the whites have left, and secretly from them, the leader positions two red patrols at points 1 and 2 and orders them to report in writing to A that the white unit is at B. (Both at point A and B, a scout with a flag stands to receive the reports).

The red messengers are sent 15–20 minutes after the whites have left (when it is assumed that the whites have already taken the bridges and sent reports to B). Twenty minutes after them, both red patrols set out towards the bridges, one to the right bridge, the other to the left, in order to reach their unit at A. (If there are no bridges, the river can be replaced by a road, on which two flags are planted at two sufficiently distant points to indicate that patrols may only cross the road there).

In this way, both sides are unaware that the enemy is active in their vicinity or has taken a position behind their backs. This will lead to various surprises.

Thus, on the one hand, the white messengers returning from the bridges will easily fall into the hands of the reds; on the other hand, the red messengers will even more easily be captured by the whites in an ambush before or beyond the bridge. Will all four be taken prisoner? Or will one of them manage to slip through the enemy position and deliver the message?

The red patrols heading towards A will also fall into a trap if the whites hide well and spot them in time, or if they previously capture a red messenger and deduce from this that the entire patrol will soon arrive.

However, it is also possible that the reds will be warned in time by their messenger, who managed to retreat from the dangerous point, or they will orient themselves in the situation and then either reach the other side with losses or join the second patrol to force a crossing through one of the bridges with combined forces.

The leader will award victory to one side not based on the number of prisoners, but based on an assessment of how the side behaved in the changed situation and whether it took the most appropriate steps at the given moment.

Before the exercise, the rules of encounter are established, whether it is tearing off armbands, or the smaller number retreating before the larger, etc. Special attention should be paid to distances and adjusting the timing of sending messengers and the march accordingly.

The terrain should be uneven and non-transparent, which is less necessary if the exercise takes place in the evening.

---

*Source of scan: [Polona / National Library of Poland](https://polona.pl/item-view/0782bd3a-4d20-41be-86f8-bcdfc65555c5?page=0), marked "Public Domain". [View scan — PDF pages 210–212](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/harcerz-w-polu.pdf#page=210).*

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Between the Hammer and the Anvil
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

One patrol of Whites plays against three patrols of Reds. The Whites receive the order: «Reconnoitre the road section M—N—O—P and wait in P until hour X for their own unit (i.e., a scout with a flag), which will travel along this road. If they encounter the enemy, report this to M and ascertain where the enemy is and what they are doing».

![img-4.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-212-img-4.jpeg)

Fig. 52.

(Reconnoitring the road covers only certain details, e.g., its width, curves, gradients, and obstacles that prevent moving off to the sides. Point O is to be subjected to such examination so that the patrol must stop there for 5–10 minutes).

The three Red patrols are dispatched from A: Patrol I towards N, Patrol II towards O, and Patrol III towards P. They receive the order to observe the road and report to A about the appearance of the Whites and their activities. The departure time is regulated so that the White patrol reaches O at the same time as the Red Patrol II.

The exercise may proceed without any complications: one side reconnoitres the road, while the other reports on their work, and that is the end of it. However, complications of various kinds may arise if the patrols become aware of the situation and show some initiative.

For example, Patrol II, which first spots the Whites, observes them and concludes that the enemy is reconnoitring the road, which likely means their unit will travel this way. Will the Whites turn back, or will they proceed towards P? Therefore, on the one hand, they must notify the command at A, and on the other, Patrols I and III at N and P. Perhaps one of them, forewarned, will set an ambush and attack the Whites?

Meanwhile, the Whites have noticed the Reds, for instance, near O, from which they conclude that the road is under observation. Therefore, they must report this to M. However, it is possible that there are more Reds, and they might encounter them elsewhere, so they must warn the messenger about this and decide: either to return once more to N to check if there are enemy patrols there as well, and then return, or to continue reconnoitring the road all the way to P.

If the Whites turn back, Patrol II may set an ambush for them near N; if they proceed further, they might be surprised by an attack from Red Patrol III. Or perhaps they will spot the Reds near P? In that case, they will send a new messenger or messengers via a detour to M, while they themselves will wait in hiding for their own unit, posting guards well. Or perhaps they will manage to launch an attack on the Reds? etc. The events can unfold in the most varied ways, as the situations can change.

After the exercise, a debriefing follows. Victory is not decided by capturing a prisoner, but by whether, at a given moment, a good decision was made and whether, despite an unfavourable outcome, it was the best possible decision in that situation.

The road section is 2–3 km long. In the case of an ambush attack, the rules given for other exercises of the same type apply.

In this, as in any other exercise, the leader may omit all further explanations if the scouts are experienced and he wants them to assess the situation and make decisions independently; he may also provide even more detailed explanations than those given in the exercise.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Difficult Reconnaissance
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

White patrols guard the railway line against destruction by the reds and report their observations via relay post — the reds must uncover the white’s protective arrangements.

A designated section of a road running through a forest represents the railway line. Along it, from the center toward the ends of the section, two white patrols (each of 4–5 people) walk. This forms one line of guards. Two other patrols guard in the same manner along the edge of the forest, approximately 1 km away from the railway line, thus forming a second line of guards. In the forest between these two lines, two flags are planted, and two people are stationed at each — these are the positions of the units that sent patrols to the forest’s edge. Beyond the railway line is station S, which collects all reports, and from there, a relay post leads further back to the main headquarters.

The forward patrols must send written reports to the flags, from which they are then forwarded to the collection station; the patrols guarding along the railway send them directly to the station.

The reds, with a strength of one squad (8–12 people), are only told that the railway line is guarded by the whites and that the flags mark the positions of the units. They do not know whether there is one

![img-5.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-215-img-5.jpeg)

Fig. 53.

or more lines of guards, nor how the white line is guarded. They are ordered to sneak up to this line, uncover the positions of the units and the method of guarding. A point is also designated for them to send their reports, and a relay post can also be arranged to their headquarters.

If it is difficult to find a road through a forest with an edge at the appropriate distance for this exercise, a road through another type of terrain can be chosen, provided it is not easily visible and facilitates stealthy approach. The length of the railway line must be precisely marked, as well as the forest’s edge along which the patrols are to move.

The reds, whether in groups of two or three or individually, try to sneak into the forest and reach the line to determine how it is guarded and where reports are sent. Some will realize that they must first penetrate the first line of patrols; others will later spot the flags and confirm that they are the first stations collecting reports. However, this information must then be carried back out of the forest, meaning they must sneak through again. All of this is a very difficult task, requiring great patience and skill, the exploitation of all terrain conditions, and above all, great presence of mind. The whites must not be attacked or taken prisoner.

The whites have an easier task. They only monitor the movements of the reds and drive them away from the line, and they may take individual enemies prisoner. However, they do this only when the opportunity arises, as their primary task is to guard the line and not leave the designated path.

A prisoner is taken by calling out to them from a distance of 10–15 paces. If the distance is greater, the called-out person must retreat a few hundred paces until they are out of sight. This makes it difficult for the opponent to observe one’s own actions. The white patrols are not required to constantly walk back and forth; they may stop for a moment at a certain point, but they must not split up to cover the entire line.

If a red scout penetrates the first line and this is noticed, the patrols must be even more vigilant about their return, so that if it is not possible to take them prisoner or turn them back, at least their return can be delayed. The reds win if, within the designated time, they provide an accurate description of how the whites guard the line and the locations of their units. Otherwise, the whites win.

---

*Scan source: [Polona / National Library of Poland](https://polona.pl/item-view/0782bd3a-4d20-41be-86f8-bcdfc65555c5?page=0), marked "Public domain". [View scan — PDF pages 214–216](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/harcerz-w-polu.pdf#page=214).*

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Behind Enemy Lines
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

One patrol of the Whites is to set up outposts at points m—n—o; another, after they are placed, is to search the terrain (non-transparent) in front of them, drive off the enemy if encountered, and then join the outposts; in any case, they must inform their own unit, stationed at M behind the outposts (a flag planted in the ground, with a scout beside it).

The patrol of the Reds, stationed at N, is to reach point M, check whether it is occupied by the Whites, and return to N.

The leader should arrange the departure times of the Whites and Reds so that the Reds pass the line m—n—o before it is occupied by the outposts.

If the Reds perform their task well, moving stealthily and in concealment, they will see the Whites passing by. Then they will ask themselves: what does this mean? Could the Whites have abandoned point M? And if so, where are they going? Both questions must be verified. Thus, a difficult task begins. On one hand, they must reach M; on the other, they must not lose sight of the enemy. They will realize that the Whites’ unit is at M because the flag is planted, so they must return. They will further check that the Whites have set up three outposts, so they must slip through between them. Perhaps they should scatter the patrol, after first informing everyone of the situation and what they must report? In any case, they attempt to slip through. Some are captured, others succeed. But even those who succeed may encounter the Whites’ patrol searching the terrain in front of the outposts, of whose presence they were completely unaware. This is a second obstacle, and the question is how to overcome it. As can be seen, all manner of interesting incidents may occur.

The Whites, meanwhile, set up outposts without knowing that the Reds are behind them. They report the placement to M. The messenger may fall into the hands of the Reds, or the Reds may deliberately let him pass to avoid revealing their presence, as this is more important. The Whites expect the enemy from the front, but suddenly one or another Red slips through the outposts. This must not be allowed; they must be captured, and the patrol in front of the outposts and their own unit must be informed.

But could it happen that no one notices anything, and the patrol reports that there are no Reds and joins the outposts? Then, after the exercise, to their surprise, they will learn that the Reds not only observed everything but also returned unharmed to N.

Only a well-trained scout patrol can play the role of the Reds. Before the exercise, the conditions of the encounter must be established based on the already provided regulations.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Alliance of the Allied Forces
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

The Reds, divided into two parts, stand 2–4 km apart. A White detachment separates them, positioned in the middle. Both sides are of equal strength. The Reds must unite while avoiding contact with the Whites, as each Red detachment alone is weaker than the Whites, whereas the Whites must prevent this union.

The terrain must be bounded and cover 2–4 km²—depending on the number of scouts. The smaller it is, the more difficult the Reds' task becomes. Furthermore, it should be mixed, mostly covered, with only occasional open areas; certain elevated points should provide a view of the immediate surroundings.

The exercise begins. Both Red detachments must first agree on a joint action. If each acts independently, it could happen that, for example, one detachment sneaks through on the left flank while the other moves in the opposite direction on the right, and still no union occurs—only their positions change.

A council is held, a crossing plan is devised, methods to deceive the enemy are established, etc., and scouts are sent with the agreed plan to the opposing side. Of course, other means of communication can be used, such as signaling. What could be simpler than finding a point from which the opposite terrain is visible, sending the word "wait," and receiving a sign that it is "understood"? Admittedly, the enemy might intercept this word and realize from which side the opponents are sneaking, but one cannot sit idle. And if this communication fails, scouts remain. However, it must be remembered that the opposing side may also send their own scouts with a different plan—and then whose plan should be followed? This circumstance must also be anticipated, and the dispatch should specify whose plan will be executed in such a case. But what if both sides make the same reservations, as that is also possible? And how can one be certain the dispatch arrived? For it might contain a request to confirm receipt by signaling, but could not the enemy, having intercepted the dispatch, give such confirmation—and then one would fall straight into a trap! It is clear from all this that even the first phase of the exercise presents no small difficulties and dangers.

But what could be foreseen has been, and the scouts set out. Those carrying the dispatch (there may be two or even three, taking different routes) know the responsibility they bear and that the success and victory of the detachment depend on their skill, presence of mind, and resourcefulness. A considerable challenge awaits them, for the enemy’s primary goal is to prevent mutual communication. Here, boldness alone is not enough; cunning may be required. For example, one scout might carry a false dispatch while another, with the real one, follows. The first moves as if clumsily (but not too clumsily, or it will arouse suspicion!) and is eventually captured, drawing the entire pursuit onto himself—the second takes advantage of this and slips away unnoticed. The first pretends to want to destroy the dispatch, the enemy prevents this and triumphantly leads the prisoner away—while the second, who escaped, has already reached the destination and informed everyone. Should scouts be given ideas? Can they not think of hundreds themselves and devise them? Need it be added that under no circumstances can the real dispatch be allowed to fall into enemy hands?

Finally, success is achieved—a joint plan of action is established, along with the time to begin (this is important!—even deadlines for individual actions may be set if the plan is complex). Now the second phase of the exercise begins.

According to the plan, this phase can take many forms. In one or two places, the Reds make feigned attempts to cross to the side of their second detachment, while in a third, that detachment actually crosses to their side, and the union of both occurs. Or only part of it crosses (retreating if in danger and later seeking a free passage elsewhere), and thus the reinforced detachment checks the Whites to facilitate the passage of the rest, etc.

Various additional rules can be introduced for the exercise, such as allowing each side to send no more than 4 scouts individually (each separately), while the rest must cross in groups of at least 6–10 people, etc.

And what do the Whites do during all this time? Their task becomes more difficult once the Reds have communicated. They must first establish a headquarters from which they can quickly send aid if called by the guards. These guards should be placed at points with a good view of the surroundings; they must report all important observed events through messengers. Furthermore, the Whites must keep the entire border under continuous surveillance, both by guards and patrols, and must send scouts in both directions to gather information, etc. If the exercise demands a great deal of ingenuity from the Reds, the Whites also have an equally difficult task: to prevent all surprises and not be deceived by false trails.

If the border is too long, the Whites should be given a numerical advantage; otherwise, they will not be able to fulfill their task. The Reds know what they must do, while the Whites are often unprepared for the Reds' actions until the last moment. There is another solution: the rules of engagement can be adjusted in favor of the Whites to balance the chances of both sides. For example, a Red is taken prisoner if a White calls out to them from a distance of 10–15 (or 15–20) paces—they must retreat if the call comes from a greater distance; a group of Reds must retreat if the Whites show a numerical advantage of even one person in an encounter. Or: any White may remove a Red’s armband and thus "kill" them, but Reds may not do this—except for scouts; only groups of at least ¼ of the total number of Reds may cross, etc. Depending on the scouts' training, the leader selects these or other general engagement rules and communicates them to everyone before the exercise. In any case, the information must be given separately to both Red detachments (after the detachments are separated and before the exercise is announced) to avoid any possible collusion.

The duration of the exercise must also be determined. It cannot be too short. From experience, I know that untrained scouts once completed the exercise in a quarter of an hour, crossing to the other side without much effort and with no prior preparations. However, I have also witnessed the same exercise with others lasting over 4 hours without ending.

It should also be established how many prisoners or "killed" scouts would nullify a victory, even if the two detachments unite.

Many variations of this very good but also difficult exercise can be created. It can be performed with a small number of participants (even just 3 patrols) or with the involvement of several hundred people. The only requirement is that the length of the border must be well-adjusted to the number of players if crossing is allowed at any point. It is better for it to be too short than too long.

However, less attention should be paid to the length of the border and more to the number of roads and paths if the rule is introduced that only these roads may be used by compact groups, e.g., of 10 or more people, while scouts may sneak through at any point. This will also result in the rule that a smaller group must retreat before a larger one, but then the Whites must be much more numerous than the Reds.

A simpler variation of the exercise is to designate only one Red detachment and give it the task of crossing to the other side of the border, which lies behind the Whites. In this case, the first phase of the described exercise is omitted. Both sides are of equal strength.

Whatever form is chosen, all rules must always be defined as precisely as possible, as the exercise can become very complicated. There must also be a sufficient number of neutral parties to resolve any disputes and clarify doubts.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Obstacles
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

The Whites are assigned a route they must traverse within a specified time, for example, 4 km per hour. Alternatively, two routes can be marked over a certain area of the terrain, and the marching party may freely choose one as better or safer. The route passes through unknown, largely impassable terrain, giving the Reds many opportunities to set an ambush.

The Reds, half as numerous as the Whites, know the time and starting point of the Whites' march, as well as their destination, but not the exact route they will take. The Reds' task is to ambush the Whites or at least hinder their march so that they cannot reach the finish line on time.

As a result, the Reds will first and foremost try to obtain information about the Whites' direction of march. They will therefore send strong scouts in groups of 2–3 toward the Whites to set up an ambush in the most suitable location based on the reports received. The scouts must maintain constant contact with the enemy once discovered, as the Whites may change their route at some point, which would also require the Reds to adjust their plans. If the Reds manage to approach the Whites undetected to within 40–50 paces, with at least a quarter of the marching force, and launch a sudden ambush, the ambush is considered successful. If they are discovered in time, they must retreat before the Whites if the Whites' detachment is twice as strong.

Thus, the Whites do not march without security; instead, they send scouts to the sides and forward to ensure the safety of the route. If an ambush is detected, they either force the Reds to retreat or change their direction of march, switching to another allowed route, thereby disrupting the Reds' plans. The Reds must then abandon the ambush site, outmaneuver the Whites, and attempt an attack elsewhere. This, in any case, delays the Whites' progress.

The Reds can use various stratagems to achieve their goal. They may stage false attacks or ambushes here and there; discovering and neutralizing them takes the Whites a lot of time. They may set two ambushes close to each other, so that when the Whites eliminate one, they fall into the other, and so on. All of this can be effective, provided that all Red groups maintain constant communication and coordination, and that the operation is so organized that orders can be sent to the right place at any moment and executed efficiently.

Let us add the rule that scouts (not detachments) can be "killed" by tearing the armband, and both Whites and Reds can do this. Thus, either side can ambush the other, surround them, etc., making it not so easy to find the hiding Reds, and many a scout from either side may fall into a trap, followed by the entire detachment.

The Reds' task will be much more difficult if the Whites are only given a starting point and a finish line, which they can reach by any route.

At the beginning of the exercise, the two parties are not placed at opposite ends of the designated terrain. The Whites stand at the starting point, and the Reds are positioned at a relatively short distance from them, as it would be a waste of time to have them march unnecessarily toward each other.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Towards the Flag
body:
The Whites set up outposts in a semicircle. There are at least four of them, each consisting of several people. They are well concealed, and if the terrain in front of an outpost is impassable, it sends out two-man scouts ahead. Small patrols move back and forth between the outposts, making it even harder to slip through to the flag, which is planted a few hundred paces behind.

Each outpost occupies a fairly elevated position, where it is possible to both hide well and see a large stretch of terrain ahead. This terrain should be uneven rather than flat, thus facilitating stealthy approach. There may be completely impassable sections on it.

The Reds, who are fewer in number than the Whites, must slip between the outposts and reach the flag, which represents an important object that must be destroyed. They are not allowed to go around the known side boundaries agreed upon by both sides.

The Whites can take Reds prisoner, and they do so by calling out from a distance of 15–20 paces. The called-out Red must not flee—they must place a white band on their cap and go to the flag, where they remain until the end of the exercise.

Since the Whites are well concealed and do not reveal their hiding places, and since they can spot a Red from afar, determine the direction they are heading, and notify an approaching patrol, the Reds' task is difficult. Behind every tree, behind every boulder, an enemy may be hiding, and at any moment—even with the most cautious approach—one might stumble upon them. Therefore, one cannot proceed blindly. Everyone must strain their eyes to see if an enemy is visible somewhere; one moment of inattention from the Whites, one careless movement, and the Red knows where to slip through. The movement of patrols can also indicate where the outposts are, provided one keeps their eyes open and patiently waits for the right moment. If things are going very badly, one Red, sacrificing themselves to reveal an outpost, can make it easier for the rest to slip through. Thus, it is not always the case that everyone acts on their own. In the process, one may use ruses (except for disguises) to get closer, whatever one can think of.

No one from the outposts is allowed to leave their position to block the path of someone slipping through—only patrols may do this, but even they can only drive the opponent away, not pursue them.

If at least half of the Reds (excluding those taken prisoner) reach the flag, the Reds win.

The outposts are spaced 200–400 paces apart. If there are fewer scouts, the outposts can be moved closer together, and patrols can be dispensed with.

If the designated number of Reds reach the flag within the specified time, they win.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Destruction of the Battery
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

In this exercise, of the same type as the previous one, the Reds have a more difficult task to accomplish. The terrain is similar, the procedure and meeting conditions are the same, but in this case, the Whites' outposts form part of a chain encircling the besieged camp of the Reds, rather than their own forces as before. Additionally, behind each outpost, at a distance of 400–800 paces, flags are planted in visible locations. These are, let us assume, batteries, each guarded by 1–2 scouts.

The Reds must break through the line of outposts and reach one of the batteries to destroy it. The Whites guard the line, and in case of an alarm, they rush to the flag to repel the attacker.

The Reds, therefore, divide into patrols of 2–4 scouts and agree among themselves on which flag the attack will be directed, by which route they will sneak through, and at what time the attack will take place. They must also establish signals for communication. Finally, they slip between the outposts in the manner described in the previous exercise, with the possible additional rule that the outposts are farther apart, and at least two scouts must always move together.

Some Reds are discovered and forced to retreat, some are captured, but the rest manage to sneak through to the designated flag. Now, the goal is to take the guard captive so that he cannot report the attack. This is done by touching him with a hand. Therefore, the attackers must surround the guard (or guards) so that he cannot slip through the gaps. If this succeeds, all remain hidden around the flag for a predetermined time (as many minutes as it takes to reach the outpost and return), and then, after removing the flag as proof of their presence, they disperse to sneak back to their own camp. If, after toppling the flag, at least three return to the camp within the specified time (e.g., within 2 hours), the Reds win. If they fail to attack the flag or are captured during the retreat, the Whites win.

The Whites know what threatens them, so they guard the line of outposts carefully and search the area between the outposts with the help of dispatched patrols. If these patrols cannot capture a Red due to the great distance, at least a few men move toward him to force a retreat. Additionally, they must have a plan for coming to the aid of the flag in case of an alarm: how many people, from where, and to where. The guard (or guards), forced to retreat from the flag by the attack, cannot take anyone captive, as he himself would risk capture; he is also not allowed to give any signals. He must simply retreat before the attack and hurry with the news to the nearest outpost. The designated men then rush to assist and force the Reds to retreat, driving them back beyond the line of outposts (according to the previously given rules, only the Whites can take prisoners). In this way, the attack is thwarted because the flag is not removed after the prescribed time has elapsed.

The Reds can prepare two attacks on two flags. They can also exploit the confusion caused by the alarm and sneak through a less-guarded section to launch a second attack elsewhere after the first is repelled, etc. The more cunning the plan, the greater the chances of success.

If one wishes to make the task easier for the Reds, only the first part of the exercise is carried out: the attack on the flag and remaining there for a certain time, without requiring a return to the camp.

As before, the outer boundaries of the outposts are marked, beyond which it is not permitted to sneak.

A larger number of scouts can participate in the exercise. The more scouts there are, the larger the arc of outposts and the more flags, but the Reds are always far fewer in number than the Whites.

At the flags, there are neutral observers with white armbands who monitor the time the Reds spend at the flag.

---

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: In Constant Contact with the Enemy
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

This exercise is intended to demonstrate proficiency in maintaining contact with a once-located enemy and in transmitting information about them under changing tracking conditions.

One or two white patrols receive an order to set up camp and surround it with guards at a location several (4–7) kilometers away from the red headquarters. The order specifies the exact time to remain in camp

![img-0.jpeg](https://jfpio.github.io/harcerz-w-polu/book/assets/page-231-img-0.jpeg)

*Fig. 56.*

in camp, the hour to break camp, the route the unit should take afterward, the points where it should stop, and what to do at each location.

For example, at point A (according to the map), the unit must set up camp, deploy 4 outposts, light campfires, and remain until 4:00 PM; at that time, they must break camp, march in a secured formation through locality B to point C, and reconnoiter the bridge over the river. At 5:00 PM, they must move on through D to point E, remain hidden there, and send out scouts to determine if there are any enemies nearby. If enemies are detected, the unit must try to disappear from their sight (without scattering) in such a way that, by circling, they reach point F unnoticed, no later than 6:00 PM. If they arrive there undetected, they must remain hidden until 6:30 PM, then proceed to point G, where they will halt until 7:30 PM, at which time the exercise ends. If, however, they are discovered at point F, they must scatter, and each scout individually must reach point G stealthily and remain hidden there until the end of the exercise, i.e., until 7:30 PM.

The white unit receives such a written order. The leader who issued it can verify whether the information brought by the reds corresponds to the actual state of affairs, whether it is precise and accurate, or whether it reveals deficiencies. Apart from the moment of breaking contact with the enemy, the subsequent unnoticed passage, and possibly scattering and regrouping in hiding at the final point, the whites behave rather passively. The active and proper role in the exercise falls to the reds.

The reds receive a more laconic order. In this case, it would read as follows: *"At a distance of 5 km in the direction of Z, near the village of X, there is a white unit. Locate its position, maintain constant contact with it, and regularly report all its actions to the headquarters at point Y. Organize the transmission of information in stages, in various forms."*

What, then, do the reds do? First, they send reconnaissance patrols to locate the enemy (there are 2–3 times as many reds as whites, as many people must serve as messengers). These patrols are given several (1–2–3) points to which they must send reports. From these points backward, toward the main headquarters, relay posts are set up, converging at one location. Here is a station that collects incoming messages by post and forwards them along a single line to the road. On the road, there is a cyclist station, which again transports dispatches in stages to the main headquarters. (Fig. 56).

In addition to foot messengers, signal stations can also be organized. One or two are located at the front, and the receiving station is together with the post-collecting station.

When the whites move from their location, the postal lines are also shortened, either by withdrawing the forward posts or by reducing the distances between individual posts. In any case, the reconnaissance patrols must always know where to send the information they have gathered, i.e., know the relay line and, if necessary, the sign by which the start of the post can be found. Similarly, the signal stations gradually retreat.

Thus, some of the reds serve as messengers, while others are tasked with closely monitoring the whites' actions, never losing sight of them throughout the entire time (which may not be easy given the whites' previously assigned task), and immediately transmitting every observation to the main headquarters.

The entire exercise is not difficult and will show whether the scouts can organize a communication service and whether it will function smoothly. Given the strict definition of the whites' actions, no mistake will go unnoticed; it will always be known when and where an error occurred. A discussion of the exercise, citing dispatches and simultaneously emphasizing what the whites were doing at any given time, will be a very good lesson.

The leader should very precisely define the route, type, and timing of the whites' actions, and the whites must execute all orders as strictly as possible. To save time and distance, the exercise can begin halfway between the whites' camp and the reds' headquarters: patrols go forward, and the postal line is set up behind.

Neutral observers are needed to ensure that the timing of each action is strictly followed.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Attack on the Railway Line
body:
The Whites are to guard the railway line from damage, while the Reds are to destroy it—these are the tasks of both parties.

The leader selects a road passing through impassable terrain and marks it with flags at the points where the line must be broken. The length of this road (1–3 km) depends on the number of participants and must be carefully measured so that it is not too long (which would make defense impossible) nor too short (which would eliminate the possibility of an attack). Similarly, the number of flags should not be too large (3–6). In any case, there must be at least twice as many Whites as Reds. One or two judges must constantly patrol the road (preferably by bicycle) to observe events as they unfold.

Suppose there are 20 Reds and 40 Whites. The Reds win if they manage to gather 10 of their number at one of the flagged points and remain there for 5 (or 5–8) minutes—the time needed to destroy the line. If, before this time elapses, the Whites arrive in greater numbers than the Reds at that point, the attack at that location has failed. Both sides are permitted to cross the road throughout the exercise.

Given this, the Whites must protect the threatened points with outposts (which must maintain constant contact with one another), while keeping their main forces hidden in several well-chosen locations so they can quickly reach any endangered spot. Additionally, they must send scouts along both sides of the road to locate the Reds, track their movements, and thus determine their intentions. The Whites’ commander must organize matters so that all information reaches the Whites’ positions as quickly as possible.

The Reds, in turn, must also locate where the Whites are concentrated and then, with a sudden attack, seize one point on the road in such a way that no witness of their success can escape and summon enemy reinforcements within the prescribed time.

If the road’s length is well chosen and the number of attack points is appropriate, ensuring both sides have equal chances, the task is difficult for both. The initiative lies with the Reds, who may use all manner of deception to mislead the Whites about their intentions. They can stage feints, retreat before advancing Whites, attempt an attack at one point, lure the Whites away from the true target, and then, with a sudden movement, seize it in such numbers that the Whites cannot gather the necessary forces in time to repel the assault. The more the Whites are kept in the dark about the enemy’s whereabouts, the more opaque the Reds’ plans, and the more cunning their ruses, the easier their victory will be. And since the Whites also depend on uncovering the Reds’ plans, both sides must constantly maneuver, conceal themselves from each other, and continually adjust their movements to those of the opponent.

Acting alone will lead to nothing. Every piece of intelligence must be delivered at once to the proper hands. Only coordinated teamwork can bring victory.

During this exercise, opponents of unequal numbers will often meet, so to avoid confusion and disputes, the rules of engagement must be clearly defined.

For example, an opponent may be "killed" by removing the cord from their left shoulder (a "killed" player then ties a handkerchief to their cap and goes to a designated location; they must not reveal the movements of either side). This is only permitted when one or two isolated opponents meet; with larger groups, the attackers must have at least a two-to-one advantage, and it is not allowed at all if the attacked group consists of at least 10 people. In the latter case, the weaker side must retreat, even if only by a single person. Depending on the scouts’ skill level, the leader may choose other general rules of engagement.

Judges must perform their duties with great discretion—for example, their prolonged absence from one point must not raise suspicions that something serious is happening elsewhere.

The road should be winding so that it cannot be easily surveyed. It must be emphasized again that the exercise can only succeed if the road’s length is proportionate to the number of defenders. The goal is to prevent the Whites from stationing enough men at all points to make a Red attack impossible.

If the Whites’ task proves too easy compared to the Reds’, it can be made more difficult by not marking the points where the railway line can be broken with flags. In that case, the Reds may destroy the line at any point.

author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
sourceTitle: Harcerz w polu: zabawy i gry terenowe
title: Free Shooters
body:
> **Game marked with an asterisk in the book:** more suitable for older scouts.

The Whites must capture the hidden bands of "free shooters" (the Reds), while the Reds must evade the encirclement.

The terrain should be as varied as possible—hilly and mixed, with both open and obscured spaces. The area covers several square kilometers (expanding if more participants are involved), and its boundaries, which must not be crossed, should be clearly defined by roads, rivers, forest edges, etc. A fairly large number of scouts (100 or more) take part, with the Whites outnumbering the Reds four- or fivefold.

The White party occupies one or two elevated points offering a wide view and posts guards there to monitor the Reds’ movements; signalers may also be added to these points. The entire terrain is divided into sections, and the search begins from a corner section. The goal is to detect the Reds, drive them forward, and force them toward the opposite edge of the terrain, where they are to be captured.

To this end, the Whites divide into patrols (with the strongest central patrol led by the commander) and advance evenly, with scouts at the front, searching the first section. Patrols maintain "contact" with one another and send messages to the commander, who, if necessary, dispatches reinforcements to the right or left. Above all, the Whites must ensure that once a group of Reds is detected, it cannot slip through to the other side. After the first section, they proceed to the next, and so on. From every open spot, attention is paid to the guards on the hills, as important clues may come from there.

If, during the encirclement, a Red occasionally slips between patrols, the Whites should not alter their plan but continue as before. However, if a fairly large group of Reds escapes, the commander may change the original plan and turn back, as capturing this group could decide the victory. Such a change of plan (previously communicated to all patrols) can be difficult, and in obscured terrain, even very difficult. Therefore, the Whites must maintain contact with one another and have established signals for "halt," "advance," "assembly," "watch the right (left) flank," etc. Otherwise, confusion may arise, which clever Reds could exploit.

Meanwhile, the Reds have divided into small groups, each acting independently to evade the encirclement. They primarily seek hiding places, posting well-concealed guards to warn of approaching enemies. If danger arises, they either remain hidden if there is a chance of staying undetected, or stealthily slip away or retreat, waiting for a better opportunity to move between the Whites. If the danger is very serious, they scatter; then, each individually, using all available terrain cover, sneaks toward a prearranged meeting point designated by the group commander. There, they hold a council to decide their next steps. It is permissible to deceive the enemy—for example, someone may deliberately sacrifice themselves and allow capture if it diverts the Whites from a critical point and facilitates their comrades' escape.

It is forbidden to hide in buildings on the exercise terrain. Before the exercise, as always, the rules governing encounters for both sides must be established. For example, it may be stipulated: Only the Whites may take prisoners; this is done by calling out to the Reds from a distance of no more than 10–15 (or 15–20) paces, or simply by touching them with a hand. Thus, there is no need for colored armbands; instead, badges are used to distinguish the sides.

The Whites win if, after two passes across the terrain from one side to the opposite (a turn counts as a pass), they capture more than half of the Reds—otherwise, the Reds win.

Alternatively, the duration of the exercise may be set in advance, during which the Whites must capture a prescribed number of prisoners, leaving the method of searching the terrain to their discretion.

The more scouts participating, the better the exercise can succeed.

---
