author: L. Ungeheuer
title: For Further Watch
body:
Night approaches...

You will stand on the watchtower of our troop’s camp. Let the clear, starry sky mark the time for you.

You will wake me for the next watch.
summary: Night approaches... You will stand on the watchtower of our troop’s camp. Let the clear, starry sky mark the time for you. You will wake me for the next watch.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: The Silent One
body: I bind your mouth with tape. Your patrol is near. Only they can free you from the tape. Only a voice obtained by skill can lure them; shouts will not help. Take this knife and this log from me! Obtain a voice by skill, a sign by skill!
summary: I bind your mouth with tape. Your patrol is near. Only they can free you from the tape. Only a voice obtained by skill can lure them; shouts will not help. Take this knife and this log from me! Obtain a voice by skill, a sign by skill!

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: On Reconnaissance
body:
Go to the town and find a red-haired man. Learn about him:

1) his age
2) whether he is married
3) his profession
4) what he intends to do today
5) where he lives.

— answer in 3 hours.
summary: Go to the town and find a red-haired man. Learn about him: 1) his age 2) whether he is married 3) his profession 4) what he intends to do today 5) where he lives. — answer in 3 hours.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: What Song
body: Play me the song you sing most often. Have no instrument? On anything, make your own instrument—flute, cymbals, whatever you like—but play.
summary: Play me the song you sing most often. Have no instrument? On anything, make your own instrument—flute, cymbals, whatever you like—but play.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: The Hunt
body: Take a photograph of your troop leader (a photo, sketch, or caricature) without them noticing.
summary: Take a photograph of your troop leader (a photo, sketch, or caricature) without them noticing.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Foolish Thomas
body: ...and now free yourself from these bonds and tell me with what knot I bound your hands.
summary: ...and now free yourself from these bonds and tell me with what knot I bound your hands.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Mistake
body: There is a printing error on this newspaper page. Find it and state in minutes how long you searched. — Naturally, without a watch. — Begin.
summary: There is a printing error on this newspaper page. Find it and state in minutes how long you searched. — Naturally, without a watch. — Begin.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: By what trick?
body:
Here you have a 25-meter rope. You may not walk on the ground. Nor from branch to branch—only along the rope. From this tree here, you must reach that third one.

By what trick will you do it? — I’ll see!

The distance between these trees is at most 2 meters.
summary: Here you have a 25-meter rope. You may not walk on the ground. Nor from branch to branch—only along the rope. From this tree here, you must reach that third one. By what trick will you do it? — I’ll see! The distance between these trees is at most 2 meters.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Bowl
body: From this lump of clay, you will make a durable bowl to serve your troop on the night of your vigil.
summary: From this lump of clay, you will make a durable bowl to serve your troop on the night of your vigil.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Underground
body: On the glade, whose sketch I give you, I will arrive promptly at 3 p.m. along with your patrol leader, who will attempt to find you within one minute. Your task: by 3:01 p.m., you must lure the patrol leader toward you with your voice from a distance of less than 20 paces. You have 3 hours, a small shovel, and a hatchet — farewell.
summary: On the glade, whose sketch I give you, I will arrive promptly at 3 p.m. along with your patrol leader, who will attempt to find you within one minute. Your task: by 3:01 p.m., you must lure the patrol leader toward you with your voice from a distance of less…

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Disrupt the Troop Meeting
body: Tonight at 6 o'clock, the Buffalo Patrol of your troop is to hold its meeting. Without causing the slightest harm to any of the Buffaloes, you shall endeavor to ensure that the meeting follows a completely different program than originally intended.
summary: Tonight at 6 o'clock, the Buffalo Patrol of your troop is to hold its meeting. Without causing the slightest harm to any of the Buffaloes, you shall endeavor to ensure that the meeting follows a completely different program than originally intended.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Cat
body:
Do you have a cat at home? No? — all the better, for I need a cat just for a moment. Bring me a cat from wherever you can, without harming it in any way.

You’ve brought one! Well done, scout. Now pay attention, for I am letting it go free, and you must quickly sketch the path it now takes as it heads home.
summary: Do you have a cat at home? No? — all the better, for I need a cat just for a moment. Bring me a cat from wherever you can, without harming it in any way. You’ve brought one! Well done, scout. Now pay attention, for I am letting it go free, and you must…

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Dead Branches
body: To the north of here you will find an old pine. Lead the way to it. — That’s the one. Do you see those lower dead branches? — Set up your camp beneath it. You will have firewood and everything else from those old branches, but you must not touch the trunk. This rope is quite strong and is about 20 meters long.
summary: To the north of here you will find an old pine. Lead the way to it. — That’s the one. Do you see those lower dead branches? — Set up your camp beneath it. You will have firewood and everything else from those old branches, but you must not touch the trunk.…

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Two Fir Trees
body:
Look: on both sides of this ravine, two fir trees grow, almost of the same age. — How old do you think they are? — They stand no more than three paces apart.

From one to the other, you can only reach using this rope.
summary: Look: on both sides of this ravine, two fir trees grow, almost of the same age. — How old do you think they are? — They stand no more than three paces apart. From one to the other, you can only reach using this rope.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Gathering
body: Do something that will draw the entire troop to the clubhouse or another place. Then, arrange something there so that the troop will not regret coming.
summary: Do something that will draw the entire troop to the clubhouse or another place. Then, arrange something there so that the troop will not regret coming.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Along the Rope
body: There is only one way down to that ravine—along a rope. Search the bottom of the ravine thoroughly and report back to me at once. Here is a piece of bread, some sugar, and tea. There is water at the bottom.
summary: There is only one way down to that ravine—along a rope. Search the bottom of the ravine thoroughly and report back to me at once. Here is a piece of bread, some sugar, and tea. There is water at the bottom.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Defense of the Fire
body: Do you know that broken tree by the road to Borek? North of that tree is a clearing. The snow there is deep, up to the knees. In that clearing, light a fire at three o'clock and keep it burning until I arrive. I will be there at 3:15. Hidden enemies will try to extinguish it. Defend it.
summary: Do you know that broken tree by the road to Borek? North of that tree is a clearing. The snow there is deep, up to the knees. In that clearing, light a fire at three o'clock and keep it burning until I arrive. I will be there at 3:15. Hidden enemies will try…

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Troop Reconnaissance
body:
You will cleverly find out about the "Eagles" patrol of the neighboring troop: when the Eagles hold their meetings,
where,
what happened at their last meeting,
what they plan to do at the next meeting,
how many are in the patrol,
what the troop leader’s opinion of them is,
whether they have an agreed-upon writing system (alphabet, cipher),
what their alarm plan looks like,
what inventory they have,
and whether they have, and what they have, in their corner of the troop’s room.
I give you 3 days to do all this.
summary: You will cleverly find out about the "Eagles" patrol of the neighboring troop: when the Eagles hold their meetings, where, what happened at their last meeting, what they plan to do at the next meeting, how many are in the patrol, what the troop leader’s…

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Along the Line into the Abyss
body: Do you see that branch on this beech tree—yes, the one 5 meters above the ground? Beneath this tree, I place a full mess tin of water. Take this rope and do as I command. Bring that water up to that height immediately, without spilling a drop from the mess tin, and then bring the water back down, keeping the mess tin always with you. He who is bold will succeed!
summary: Do you see that branch on this beech tree—yes, the one 5 meters above the ground? Beneath this tree, I place a full mess tin of water. Take this rope and do as I command. Bring that water up to that height immediately, without spilling a drop from the mess…

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: What is there?
body: What is the exact distance from you to that old pot standing on the other side of the stream? — You say 7 steps, but how many meters? Check it precisely, and then, without crossing the river, find out what substance is inside that pot. Here is a 15-meter rope.
summary: What is the exact distance from you to that old pot standing on the other side of the stream? — You say 7 steps, but how many meters? Check it precisely, and then, without crossing the river, find out what substance is inside that pot. Here is a 15-meter rope.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Birds, Trees, Stones
body:
For half a day, you will come with me. We will go into the forest.

You will identify three birds — and describe them.

You will identify three trees — from each tree, a leaf, a piece of bark, and a lump of resin.

You will identify three different stones — break them and describe them.
traits: Tracking their life; knowledge of trees and inanimate nature
summary: For half a day, you will come with me. We will go into the forest. You will identify three birds — and describe them. You will identify three trees — from each tree, a leaf, a piece of bark, and a lump of resin. You will identify three different stones —…

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Leap
body:
Do you have the sports badge?

Can you jump three meters?

This stream is exactly three meters wide. — Jump!
summary: Do you have the sports badge? Can you jump three meters? This stream is exactly three meters wide. — Jump!

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Preserve the Ice
body: Tomorrow, precisely at 12 noon, you will receive from me on the hill at 435 meters northwest of the city a piece of ice. Do this—without leaving the hill—so that by 6 p.m. I receive from you the remainder of the ice. Your entire patrol will be waiting there. Be prepared!
summary: Tomorrow, precisely at 12 noon, you will receive from me on the hill at 435 meters northwest of the city a piece of ice. Do this—without leaving the hill—so that by 6 p.m. I receive from you the remainder of the ice. Your entire patrol will be waiting there.…

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Iron Burns
body: On this very stake, draw with a glowing iron the history of this trial.
traits: gathering impressions from the completed trial
summary: On this very stake, draw with a glowing iron the history of this trial.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: About the Document
body: In the Troop Command, there is a valuable document that you must retrieve. This letter is written by me to the Troop Commander on the 7th of March of the current year.
summary: In the Troop Command, there is a valuable document that you must retrieve. This letter is written by me to the Troop Commander on the 7th of March of the current year.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: By One's Own Industry
body:
Make, by your own industry, for someone dearest to you something both very beautiful and useful.

You shall complete the task and present the item on the last night of the vigil.
summary: Make, by your own industry, for someone dearest to you something both very beautiful and useful. You shall complete the task and present the item on the last night of the vigil.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: To the Mast
body:
Within 5 minutes, climb this mast to the height of the stork’s nest.

You may use the rope.
summary: Within 5 minutes, climb this mast to the height of the stork’s nest. You may use the rope.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Cut the Rope
body: Without using sharp tools, you will cut this rope into two parts within 5 minutes.
summary: Without using sharp tools, you will cut this rope into two parts within 5 minutes.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Barrel Run
body: You will run by rolling inside this large barrel for 25 meters. I will give the signal in a moment.
summary: You will run by rolling inside this large barrel for 25 meters. I will give the signal in a moment.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: In the Hay Bag
body:
Take your Scout uniform with you.

Here is your own camp hay bag.

Step inside it, like this. I will sew you into it for a period of 15 minutes. In a quarter of an hour, you will stand before me in your Scout uniform.
summary: Take your Scout uniform with you. Here is your own camp hay bag. Step inside it, like this. I will sew you into it for a period of 15 minutes. In a quarter of an hour, you will stand before me in your Scout uniform.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: The Mysterious Campfire
body: Here, on this beautiful glade, you will kindle a fire—but in such a way that afterwards no one will recognize that you were here and that a fire burned.
summary: Here, on this beautiful glade, you will kindle a fire—but in such a way that afterwards no one will recognize that you were here and that a fire burned.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: With a Stone
body: Enter this hayloft. I will fasten it. Stand up inside it. Now take this stake from me, carry it to that rock, no more than 100 paces from here. Drive the stake into the ground beneath the rock and await further orders.
summary: Enter this hayloft. I will fasten it. Stand up inside it. Now take this stake from me, carry it to that rock, no more than 100 paces from here. Drive the stake into the ground beneath the rock and await further orders.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Like an Eagle
body: On this very oak, you shall make your bed for tonight. Good night.
summary: On this very oak, you shall make your bed for tonight. Good night.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Find the Thought
body:
Tea ready? — Then let us sit here in a circle and drink. In this leaf, I have enclosed my thought.

Ask, and I will answer yes or no; find my thought.
summary: Tea ready? — Then let us sit here in a circle and drink. In this leaf, I have enclosed my thought. Ask, and I will answer yes or no; find my thought.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: The Nine
body: — Now, draw the Arabic numeral nine (9) on the ground so that the diameter of the circle in this number is 2 small steps, and the line is 10 steps long. Good, now run around the circumference of that circle for 100 steps, then along the straight line of the nine. — Go! On the double, march!!
summary: — Now, draw the Arabic numeral nine (9) on the ground so that the diameter of the circle in this number is 2 small steps, and the line is 10 steps long. Good, now run around the circumference of that circle for 100 steps, then along the straight line of the…

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Extinguish the Lamp
body: Put out this gas lantern, then quickly light it again, but in such a way that you are not caught doing so.
summary: Put out this gas lantern, then quickly light it again, but in such a way that you are not caught doing so.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: No One Will Hear
body: From this moment until the arrival of your watch, that is, for the entire day, no one shall hear your voice.
summary: From this moment until the arrival of your watch, that is, for the entire day, no one shall hear your voice.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Forged!
body: From this iron bar, make a camp knife, using fire, bricks, and an axe.
summary: From this iron bar, make a camp knife, using fire, bricks, and an axe.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Without Water, Without Bread
body:
Tomorrow at sunrise, set out on a hike
and until sunset you shall neither drink nor eat. —
At sunset, you will prepare your own supper.
summary: Tomorrow at sunrise, set out on a hike and until sunset you shall neither drink nor eat. — At sunset, you will prepare your own supper.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Literary Scout
body: Write something so engaging for our *"Skaut"* or another Scout magazine that it truly gets published in its pages.
summary: Write something so engaging for our "Skaut" or another Scout magazine that it truly gets published in its pages.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: The Hunted
body:
— Make yourself a bow and arrows. You must cook your own dinner from the potatoes that lie there on the rock, 5 paces away from us. Only the potatoes hit by 16 of your arrows will be yours.

Aim and strike!
summary: — Make yourself a bow and arrows. You must cook your own dinner from the potatoes that lie there on the rock, 5 paces away from us. Only the potatoes hit by 16 of your arrows will be yours. Aim and strike!

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Apple
body: I give you 17 minutes. Do you see that apple attached to the board? It is no more than 3 steps away. Take out your camping knife and cleverly ensure that the apple is no longer there from this distance.
summary: I give you 17 minutes. Do you see that apple attached to the board? It is no more than 3 steps away. Take out your camping knife and cleverly ensure that the apple is no longer there from this distance.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Guard the Flower
body: Take this wildflower and transplant it there beneath the rock, and see to it that when we come on the night of your vigil, we find it as fresh as it is now.
summary: Take this wildflower and transplant it there beneath the rock, and see to it that when we come on the night of your vigil, we find it as fresh as it is now.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: From the Scree Slope
body: No harm will come to you, even with your legs bound. Descend this sandy scree slope; at the bottom, free yourself from the bonds and make your way back here to face the next trial.
summary: No harm will come to you, even with your legs bound. Descend this sandy scree slope; at the bottom, free yourself from the bonds and make your way back here to face the next trial.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: How Will You Do It?
body: I give you a sheet of paper with this instruction: Make a hole in it so that you and your entire patrol can pass through it.
summary: I give you a sheet of paper with this instruction: Make a hole in it so that you and your entire patrol can pass through it.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Lantern
body: You will make a camp lantern from this bottle. It must have the advantage that even a strong wind cannot extinguish the candle placed inside it.
summary: You will make a camp lantern from this bottle. It must have the advantage that even a strong wind cannot extinguish the candle placed inside it.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: With Silent Step
body: In that hollow below, a wolf patrol is encamped. — Approach it with silent step, find out what is happening there, write everything down, and return to me. Be careful, for the jingles (bells) I have tied to your legs may easily betray you, and if they do, the wolves will give you a thorough thrashing.
summary: In that hollow below, a wolf patrol is encamped. — Approach it with silent step, find out what is happening there, write everything down, and return to me. Be careful, for the jingles (bells) I have tied to your legs may easily betray you, and if they do, the…

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: To the Rescue
body: — Tomek, get up! Alarm — look, there’s a fire. Run to the rescue.
summary: — Tomek, get up! Alarm — look, there’s a fire. Run to the rescue.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Arise
body: Lie down on this turf on your back, place your hands on your chest. — Very well, and now, without crossing your legs, arise!
summary: Lie down on this turf on your back, place your hands on your chest. — Very well, and now, without crossing your legs, arise!

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: The Touchstone
body: This stone weighs more than you. Roll this stone up this hill to the very circle, so that you may sit upon this stone for the next trial.
summary: This stone weighs more than you. Roll this stone up this hill to the very circle, so that you may sit upon this stone for the next trial.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Uphill
body: How much do you think this rock fragment weighs? 10 decagrams? Perhaps. Holding it continuously in your hand, roll it down this slope all the way to that spruce tree above the stream.
summary: How much do you think this rock fragment weighs? 10 decagrams? Perhaps. Holding it continuously in your hand, roll it down this slope all the way to that spruce tree above the stream.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: The Weight
body: Here you have a weight of 1 kg. Without a scale — tell me in a moment how much I weigh.
summary: Here you have a weight of 1 kg. Without a scale — tell me in a moment how much I weigh.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Three-Pronged Forks
body:
They say that three-pronged forks bring luck to the patrol. Such a forest talisman.

— Go and find such forks, but you must absolutely go for them at 12 at night, to find ones that possess the power of luck.
summary: They say that three-pronged forks bring luck to the patrol. Such a forest talisman. — Go and find such forks, but you must absolutely go for them at 12 at night, to find ones that possess the power of luck.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Thrift
body: We are going into the forest, but first you will go shopping. I give you 25 groszy. Buy with it enough food of such kind that it will suffice for both of us for breakfast.
summary: We are going into the forest, but first you will go shopping. I give you 25 groszy. Buy with it enough food of such kind that it will suffice for both of us for breakfast.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Wheel from the Cart
body: Place this wheel on the ground, sit on it, and do not let yourself be thrown off, even if the wheel tries to throw you off.
summary: Place this wheel on the ground, sit on it, and do not let yourself be thrown off, even if the wheel tries to throw you off.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Twin Stones
body:
Bring a stone similar to this one and place it on that old stump beside the waterfall.

— Here — I cover both with a scarf and, from under the scarf, I throw them into the water. Recognize both in the water, bring them back, and tell me which one you placed on the old stump.
summary: Bring a stone similar to this one and place it on that old stump beside the waterfall. — Here — I cover both with a scarf and, from under the scarf, I throw them into the water. Recognize both in the water, bring them back, and tell me which one you placed on…

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Such a Cart
body: Here you have a wagon wheel. From this single wheel, make a forest cart so that, sitting on it, you can travel along this road as far as the strongest man can throw a stone.
summary: Here you have a wagon wheel. From this single wheel, make a forest cart so that, sitting on it, you can travel along this road as far as the strongest man can throw a stone.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Sink the Bladder
body:
Inflate this bladder and tie it tightly, then measure the depth and current of this stream.

Can you swim? You say the water is waist-deep? Well, secure this bladder to the bottom without entering the water at all, nor using any string.
summary: Inflate this bladder and tie it tightly, then measure the depth and current of this stream. Can you swim? You say the water is waist-deep? Well, secure this bladder to the bottom without entering the water at all, nor using any string.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Facing the Sea
body: Stand facing the Polish sea without using any instruments.
summary: Stand facing the Polish sea without using any instruments.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: From a Book
body: I give you this book for 15 minutes. Find out what its content is, and when I return—you will tell me.
summary: I give you this book for 15 minutes. Find out what its content is, and when I return—you will tell me.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Backwards Boots
body: — Take off your shoes, then put the left one on your right foot and the right one on your left foot. Walk like this and find someone you know, behaving so that they do not notice the change. Then switch the shoes back to the correct feet and return as quickly as possible.
summary: — Take off your shoes, then put the left one on your right foot and the right one on your left foot. Walk like this and find someone you know, behaving so that they do not notice the change. Then switch the shoes back to the correct feet and return as quickly…

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Kayak Dash
body: Can you swim? — yes? and in a kayak? — then sit down and paddle down this stream. Stop at the bend by that broken tree. Without paddles. Be prepared!
summary: Can you swim? — yes? and in a kayak? — then sit down and paddle down this stream. Stop at the bend by that broken tree. Without paddles. Be prepared!

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Roll the Hoops
body: Take this hoop in your left hand and that one in your right, and roll them simultaneously along the path I show you—from here all the way to that post.
summary: Take this hoop in your left hand and that one in your right, and roll them simultaneously along the path I show you—from here all the way to that post.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Observe
body:
Do you remember who last passed by you?
Who was it? How were they dressed? Approximately how old were they? Describe.
summary: Do you remember who last passed by you? Who was it? How were they dressed? Approximately how old were they? Describe.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Three Nails
body: I have driven three nails of different lengths into this board with their ends exposed. With your hands tied behind your back, drive the nails into the board.
summary: I have driven three nails of different lengths into this board with their ends exposed. With your hands tied behind your back, drive the nails into the board.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Chop Along the Mark
body:
Just now, I made a mark with an axe on this branch.
With a single blow, cut through the branch, hitting my mark.
summary: Just now, I made a mark with an axe on this branch. With a single blow, cut through the branch, hitting my mark.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Chop
body: With one hand, chop a log from this very clearing. I will wait no longer than 5 minutes.
summary: With one hand, chop a log from this very clearing. I will wait no longer than 5 minutes.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: Coins
body:
Here is a handful of small coins. Put them in your pocket and, without looking, count how much money is there.

— Yes, and now check how much there actually is. — Declare the difference to the Scout Station.
summary: Here is a handful of small coins. Put them in your pocket and, without looking, count how much money is there. — Yes, and now check how much there actually is. — Declare the difference to the Scout Station.

author: L. Ungeheuer
title: The Black Hand
body: Immerse your left hand in this vessel. Black ink. No one may see this hand for a full day. You will return here tomorrow at this hour and show the black hand.
summary: Immerse your left hand in this vessel. Black ink. No one may see this hand for a full day. You will return here tomorrow at this hour and show the black hand.

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Arctic Expedition
body:
Each patrol makes a bob sleigh with ropes, harness, for two of their number to pull (or for dogs if they have them, and can train them to the work). Two scouts go a mile or so ahead, the remainder with the sleigh follow, finding the way by means of the spoor, and by such signs as the leading scouts may draw in the snow. All other drawings seen on the way are to be examined, noted, and their meaning read. The sleigh carries rations and cooking-pots, etc.

Build snow huts. These must be made narrow, according to the length of sticks available for forming the roof, which can be made with brushwood, and covered with snow.
summary: Each patrol makes a bob sleigh with ropes, harness, for two of their number to pull (or for dogs if they have them, and can train them to the work). Two scouts go a mile or so ahead, the remainder with the sleigh follow, finding the way by means of the spoor,…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Snow Fort
body: The snow fort may be built by one patrol according to their own ideas of fortification, with loop holes, etc., for looking out. When finished it will be attacked by hostile patrols, using snowballs as ammunition. Every scout struck by a snowball is counted dead. The attackers should, as a rule, number at least twice the strength of the defenders.
summary: The snow fort may be built by one patrol according to their own ideas of fortification, with loop holes, etc., for looking out. When finished it will be attacked by hostile patrols, using snowballs as ammunition. Every scout struck by a snowball is counted…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Siberian Man Hunt
body: One scout as fugitive runs away across the snow in any direction he may please until he finds a good hiding place, and there conceals himself. The remainder, after giving him twenty minutes' start or more, proceed to follow him by his tracks. As they approach his hiding-place, he shoots at them with snowballs, and everyone that is struck must fall out dead. The fugitive must be struck three times before he is counted dead.
summary: One scout as fugitive runs away across the snow in any direction he may please until he finds a good hiding place, and there conceals himself. The remainder, after giving him twenty minutes' start or more, proceed to follow him by his tracks. As they approach…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Scout Meets Scout
body:
### In Town or Country.

Single scouts, or complete patrols or pairs of scouts, to be taken out about two miles apart, and made to work towards each other, either alongside a road, or by giving each side a landmark to work to, such as a steep hill or big tree, which is directly behind the other party, and will thus insure their coming together. The patrol which first sees the other wins. This is signified by the patrol leader holding up his patrol flag for the umpire to see, and sounding his whistle. A patrol need not keep together, but that patrol wins which first holds out its flag, so it is well for the scouts to be in touch with their patrol leaders by signal, voice, or message.

Scouts may employ any ruse they like, such as climbing into trees, hiding in carts, etc., but they must not dress up in disguise.

This may also be practised at night.
summary: In Town or Country. Single scouts, or complete patrols or pairs of scouts, to be taken out about two miles apart, and made to work towards each other, either alongside a road, or by giving each side a landmark to work to, such as a steep hill or big tree,…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Despatch Runners
body:
A scout is sent out to take note of some well-known spot, say, the post office in a neighbouring town or district. He will there get the note stamped with the post mark of the office and return. The rest of the scouts are posted by their leader to prevent him getting there by watching all the roads and likely paths by which he can come, but none may be nearer to the post office than two hundred yards. The despatch runner is allowed to use any disguise and any method of travelling that he can hit upon.

In the country the game may similarly be played, the scout being directed to go to a certain house or other specified spot.
summary: A scout is sent out to take note of some well-known spot, say, the post office in a neighbouring town or district. He will there get the note stamped with the post mark of the office and return. The rest of the scouts are posted by their leader to prevent him…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Kim's Game
body:
Place about twenty or thirty small articles on a tray, or on the table or floor, such as two or three different kinds of buttons, pencils, corks, rags, nuts, stones, knives, string, photos—anything you can find—and cover them over with a cloth or coat.

Make a list of these, and make a column opposite the list for each boy's replies. Like this:

- List Adams Smith Long. Atkins Jones

- Walnut

- Button

- Black button

- Red rag

- Yellow rag

- Black rag

- Knife

- Red pencil

- Cork

- String knot

- Plain string

- Blue bead

Then uncover the articles for one minute by your watch, or while you count sixty at the rate of "quick march." Then cover them over again.

Take each boy separately and let him whisper to you each of the articles that he can remember, and mark it off on your scoring sheet.

The boy who remembers the greatest numbers wins the game.
summary: Place about twenty or thirty small articles on a tray, or on the table or floor, such as two or three different kinds of buttons, pencils, corks, rags, nuts, stones, knives, string, photos—anything you can find—and cover them over with a cloth or coat. Make a…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Thimble Finding
body:
(Indoors).

Send the patrol out of the room.

Take a thimble, ring, coin, bit of paper, or any small article, and place it where it is perfectly visible but in a spot where it is not likely to be noticed. Let the patrol come in and look for it. When one of them sees it he should go and quietly sit down without indicating to the others where it is.

After a fair time he should be told to point it out to those who have not succeeded in finding it.

[This ensures his having really seen it.]
summary: (Indoors). Send the patrol out of the room. Take a thimble, ring, coin, bit of paper, or any small article, and place it where it is perfectly visible but in a spot where it is not likely to be noticed. Let the patrol come in and look for it. When one of them…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Shop Window
body:
(Outdoors in town).

Umpire takes a patrol down a street past six shops. Gives them half a minute at each shop, then, after moving them off to some distance, he gives each boy a pencil and card, and tells him to write from memory, or himself takes down what they noticed in, say, the third and fifth shops. The one who sets down most articles correctly wins. It is useful practice to match one boy against another in heats—the loser competing again, till you arrive at the worst. This gives the worst scouts the most practice.
summary: (Outdoors in town). Umpire takes a patrol down a street past six shops. Gives them half a minute at each shop, then, after moving them off to some distance, he gives each boy a pencil and card, and tells him to write from memory, or himself takes down what…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Similar Game
body:
(Indoors).

Send each scout in turn into a room for half a minute; when he comes out take down a list of furniture and articles which he noticed. The boy who noticed most wins.

The simplest way of scoring is to make a list of the articles in the room on your scoring paper with a column for marks for each scout against them, which can then easily be totalled up at foot.
summary: (Indoors). Send each scout in turn into a room for half a minute; when he comes out take down a list of furniture and articles which he noticed. The boy who noticed most wins. The simplest way of scoring is to make a list of the articles in the room on your…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Spotting the Spot
body:
(Indoors—town or country).

Show a series of photos or sketches of objects, in the neighbourhood such as would be known to all the scouts if they kept their eyes open—such, for instance, as cross-roads, curious window, gargoyle or weathercock, tree, reflection in the water (guess the building causing it), and so on.

A pair of scouts can play most of the above competitions off between themselves, if they like, as a matter of practice.

Patrol leaders can match one pair of their scouts against another pair in the game, and thus get them really practised at it, and when they become really good he can challenge other patrols to compete against his.
summary: (Indoors—town or country). Show a series of photos or sketches of objects, in the neighbourhood such as would be known to all the scouts if they kept their eyes open—such, for instance, as cross-roads, curious window, gargoyle or weathercock, tree, reflection…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Follow the Trail
body:
Send out a "hare," either walking or cycling, with a pocketful of corn, nutshells, confetti paper or buttons, etc., and drop a few here and there to give a trail for the patrol to follow.

Or go out with a piece of chalk and draw the patrol sign on walls, gateposts, pavements, lamp-posts, trees, etc., every here and there, and let the patrol hunt you by these marks. Patrols should wipe out all these marks as they pass them for tidiness, and so as not to mislead them for another day's practice.

The other road signs should also be used, such as closing up certain roads as not used, and hiding a letter at some point, giving directions as to the next turn.
summary: Send out a "hare," either walking or cycling, with a pocketful of corn, nutshells, confetti paper or buttons, etc., and drop a few here and there to give a trail for the patrol to follow. Or go out with a piece of chalk and draw the patrol sign on walls,…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Scouts' Nose
body:
(Indoors).

Prepare a number of paper-bags, all alike, and put in each a different smelling article such as chopped onion in one, tan in another, roseleaves, leather, aniseed, violet powder, orange-peel, etc. Put these packets in a row a couple of feet apart and let each competitor walk down the line and have five seconds' sniff at each. At the end he has one minute in which to write down or to state to the umpire the names of the different objects smelled, from memory, in their correct order.
summary: (Indoors). Prepare a number of paper-bags, all alike, and put in each a different smelling article such as chopped onion in one, tan in another, roseleaves, leather, aniseed, violet powder, orange-peel, etc. Put these packets in a row a couple of feet apart…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Far and Near
body:
(For town or country.)

Umpire goes along a given road or line of country with a patrol in patrol formation. He carries a scoring card with the name of each scout on it.

Each scout looks out for the details required and directly he notices one he runs to the umpire and informs him or hands in the article if it is an article he finds. The umpire enters a mark accordingly against his name. The scout who gains most marks in the walk, wins.

Details like the following should be chosen, to develop the scout's observation and to encourage him to look far and near, up and down, etc.

The details should be varied every time the game is played; and about 8 or 10 should be given at a time.

    Every match found 1 mark.

    Every button found 1 mark.

    Birds' foot tracks 2 marks.

    Patch noticed on stranger's clothing or boots. 2 marks.

    Grey horse seen 2 marks.

    Pigeon flying 2 marks.

    Sparrow sitting 1 mark.

    Ash-tree 2 marks.

    Broken chimney pot 2 marks.

    Broken window 1 mark.
summary: (For town or country.) Umpire goes along a given road or line of country with a patrol in patrol formation. He carries a scoring card with the name of each scout on it. Each scout looks out for the details required and directly he notices one he runs to the…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Track Memory
body: Make a patrol sit with their feet up so that other scouts can study them. Give the scouts, say, three minutes to study the boots. Then leaving the scouts in a room or out of sight let one of the patrol make some footmarks in a good bit of ground. Call up the scouts one by one and let them see the track and say who made it.
summary: Make a patrol sit with their feet up so that other scouts can study them. Give the scouts, say, three minutes to study the boots. Then leaving the scouts in a room or out of sight let one of the patrol make some footmarks in a good bit of ground. Call up the…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Track Drawing
body: Take out a patrol; set them on to one foot-track. Award a prize to the scout who makes the most accurate drawing of one of the footprints of the track. The scouts should be allowed to follow up the track till they get to a bit of ground where a good impression of it can be found.
summary: Take out a patrol; set them on to one foot-track. Award a prize to the scout who makes the most accurate drawing of one of the footprints of the track. The scouts should be allowed to follow up the track till they get to a bit of ground where a good…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Smugglers Over the Border
body: The "Border" is a certain line of country about four hundred yards long, preferably a road or wide path or bit of sand, on which foot-tracks can easily be seen. One patrol watches the border with sentries posted along this road, with a reserve posted further inland. This should be about half-way between the "border" and the "town," the "town" would be a base marked by trees, buildings, or flags, etc., about half a mile distant from the border. A hostile patrol of smugglers assembles about half a mile on the other side of the border. They will all cross the border, in any formation they please, either singly or together or scattered, and make for the town, either walking or running, or at scout's pace. Only one among them is supposed to be smuggling, and he wears tracking irons, so that the sentries walk up and down their beat (they may not run till after the 'alarm'), waiting for the tracks of the smuggler. Directly a sentry sees the track, he gives the alarm signal to the reserve and starts himself to follow up the track as fast as he can. The reserve thereupon co-operate with them and try to catch the smuggler before he can reach the town. Once within the boundary of the town he is safe and wins the game.
summary: The "Border" is a certain line of country about four hundred yards long, preferably a road or wide path or bit of sand, on which foot-tracks can easily be seen. One patrol watches the border with sentries posted along this road, with a reserve posted further…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Games and Competitions in Deduction
body:
Get some people who are strangers to the boys to come along as passers-by in the street or road, and let the boys separately notice all about them; and after an interval ask each for a full description of each of the passers-by as to appearance, peculiar recognisable points, and what he guesses his business to be; or let each boy have two minutes' conversation with your friend and try to find out what he can about him in that time by questioning and observation.

Set a room or prepare a piece of ground with small signs, tracks, etc., read aloud the story of the crime up to that point and let each boy or each patrol in turn examine the scene for a given time and then privately give each his solution of it.

The very simplest, most elementary schemes should be given at first, and they can gradually be elaborated. For instance take a number of footmarks and spent matches by a tree showing where a man had difficulty in lighting his pipe, etc.

For a more finished theme take a mystery like that in "Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes" called "The Resident Patient." Set a room to represent the patient's room where he was found hanging, with footprints of muddy boots on the carpet, cigar ends bitten or cut in the fireplace, cigar ashes, screw-driver and screws, etc. Put down a strip or "stepping stones" of stuff, handkerchiefs, or paper on which the competitors shall walk (so as not to confuse existing tracks). Let each scout (or patrol) come in separately and have three minutes in which to investigate. Then to go out and give in his solution, written or verbal, half an hour later.

Let one patrol make tracks by carrying out such a series as that which D'Atagnan elucidated. The other patrol then acts as detectives and endeavours to unravel the mystery from the tracks and other sign.
summary: Get some people who are strangers to the boys to come along as passers-by in the street or road, and let the boys separately notice all about them; and after an interval ask each for a full description of each of the passers-by as to appearance, peculiar…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Scout Hunting
body: One scout is given time to go out and hide himself, the remainder then start to find him, he wins if he is not found, or if he can get back to the starting point within a given time without being touched.
summary: One scout is given time to go out and hide himself, the remainder then start to find him, he wins if he is not found, or if he can get back to the starting point within a given time without being touched.

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Despatch Running
body:
A scout is told to bring a note into a certain spot or house from a distance within a given time: other hostile scouts are told to prevent any message getting to this place and to hide themselves at different points to stop the despatch carrier getting in with it.

To count as a capture two scouts must touch the despatch runner before he reaches the spot for delivering the message.
summary: A scout is told to bring a note into a certain spot or house from a distance within a given time: other hostile scouts are told to prevent any message getting to this place and to hide themselves at different points to stop the despatch carrier getting in…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Stalking
body:
Instructor acts as a deer—not hiding but standing, moving a little now and then if he likes.

Scouts go out to find and each in his own way tries to get up to him unseen.

Directly the instructor sees a scout he directs him to stand up as having failed. After a certain time the instructor calls "time," all stand up at the spot which they have reached and the nearest wins.

The same game may be played to test the scouts in stepping lightly—the umpire being blindfolded. The practice should preferably be carried out where there are dry twigs lying about, and gravel, etc. The scout may start to stalk the blind enemy at 100 yards distance, and he must do it fairly fast—say in one minute and a half—to touch the blind man before he hears him.
summary: Instructor acts as a deer—not hiding but standing, moving a little now and then if he likes. Scouts go out to find and each in his own way tries to get up to him unseen. Directly the instructor sees a scout he directs him to stand up as having failed. After a…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Stalking and Reporting
body: The umpire places himself out in the open and sends each scout or pair of scouts away in different directions about half a mile off. When he waves a flag, which is the signal to begin, they all hide and then proceed to stalk him, creeping up and watching all he does. When he waves the flag again, they rise, come in, and report each in turn all that he did, either by handing in a written report or verbally as may be ordered. The umpire meantime has kept a look-out in each direction, and, every time he sees a scout, he takes two points off that scout's score. He, on his part, performs small actions, such as sitting down, kneeling up, and looking through glasses, using handkerchief, taking hat off for a bit, walking round in a circle a few times, to give scouts something to note and report about him. Scouts are given three points for each act reported correctly. It saves time if the umpire makes out a scoring card beforehand, giving the name of each scout, and a number of columns showing each act of his and what mark that scout wins, also a column of deducted marks for exposing themselves.
summary: The umpire places himself out in the open and sends each scout or pair of scouts away in different directions about half a mile off. When he waves a flag, which is the signal to begin, they all hide and then proceed to stalk him, creeping up and watching all…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Lion Hunting
body:
A lion is represented by one scout who goes out with tracking irons on his feet, and a pocketful of corn or peas, and six tennis balls. He is allowed half an hour's start, and then the patrol go after him, following his spoor, each armed with one tennis ball with which to shoot him, when they find him. The lion may hide or creep about or run just as he feels inclined, but whenever the ground is hard or very grassy, he must drop a few grains of corn, every few yards to show the trail.

If the hunters fail to come up to him neither wins the game. When they come near to his lair the lion fires at them with his tennis balls, and the moment a hunter is hit he must fall out dead and cannot throw his tennis ball. If the lion gets hit by a hunting tennis ball he is wounded, and if he gets wounded three times he is killed.

Tennis balls may only be fired once; they cannot be picked up and fired again in the same fight.

Each scout must collect and hand in his tennis balls after the game. In winter if there is snow, this game can be played without tracking irons, and using snowballs instead of tennis balls.
summary: A lion is represented by one scout who goes out with tracking irons on his feet, and a pocketful of corn or peas, and six tennis balls. He is allowed half an hour's start, and then the patrol go after him, following his spoor, each armed with one tennis ball…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Plant Race
body: Start off your scouts, either cycling or on foot, to go in any direction they like, to get a specimen of any ordered plant, say a sprig of yew, a shoot of ilex, a horseshoe mark from a chestnut-tree, a briar rose, or something of that kind, whichever you may order, such as will tax their knowledge of plants and will test their memory as to where they noticed one of the kind required, and will also make them quick in getting there and back.
summary: Start off your scouts, either cycling or on foot, to go in any direction they like, to get a specimen of any ordered plant, say a sprig of yew, a shoot of ilex, a horseshoe mark from a chestnut-tree, a briar rose, or something of that kind, whichever you may…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Night Patrolling
body: Practise scouts to hear and see by night by posting some sentries, who must stand or walk about, armed with rifles and blank cartridges, or with whistles. Other scouts should be sent out as enemies to stalk and kill them. If a sentry hears a sound he fires, calls, or whistles. Scouts must at once halt and lie still. The umpire comes to the sentry and asks which direction the sound came from, and, if correct, the sentry wins. If the stalker can creep up within 15 yards of the sentry without being seen, he deposits some article, such as a handkerchief, on the ground at that point, and creeps away again. Then he makes a noise for the sentry to fire at, and when the umpire comes up, he can explain what he has done.
summary: Practise scouts to hear and see by night by posting some sentries, who must stand or walk about, armed with rifles and blank cartridges, or with whistles. Other scouts should be sent out as enemies to stalk and kill them. If a sentry hears a sound he fires,…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Mountain Scouting
body: This has been played by tourists' clubs in the Lake District, and is very similar to the "Spider and Fly" game. Three hares are sent out at daybreak to hide themselves about in the mountains; after breakfast a party of hounds go out to find them before a certain hour, say 4 p.m. If they find them, even with field glasses, it counts, provided that the finder can say definitely who it was he spotted. Certain limits of ground must be given, beyond which anyone would be out of bounds, and therefore disqualified.
summary: This has been played by tourists' clubs in the Lake District, and is very similar to the "Spider and Fly" game. Three hares are sent out at daybreak to hide themselves about in the mountains; after breakfast a party of hounds go out to find them before a…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Games in Pathfinding
body: Instructor takes a patrol in patrolling formation into a strange town or into an intricate piece of strange country, with a cycling map. He then gives instructions as to where he wants to go to, makes each scout in turn lead the patrol, say for seven minutes if cycling, fifteen minutes if walking. This scout is to find the way entirely by the map, and marks are given for ability in reading, that is to say, each scout is given ten marks on starting, and one is deducted for every mistake that he makes. If he makes no mistake at all throughout the exercise, his ten small marks will count as one real scout mark towards a badge "of merit."
summary: Instructor takes a patrol in patrolling formation into a strange town or into an intricate piece of strange country, with a cycling map. He then gives instructions as to where he wants to go to, makes each scout in turn lead the patrol, say for seven minutes…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Star-gazing
body: Take out the scouts on clear nights and post them separately, and let each find the North Star and Orion, etc., and point them out to you as you come round.
summary: Take out the scouts on clear nights and post them separately, and let each find the North Star and Orion, etc., and point them out to you as you come round.

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Judging Distance
body: Take a patrol and station its members about in different directions and with different background, according to the colour of their clothes; then take another patrol to judge distance of these points. Two competitors are sent in turn to three different points. At the first point they are merely given the compass bearing of the next one, which is some three hundred yards distant, and so on in succession. At each point each pair of scouts notices regarding the enemy—first, how many visible; second, how far off; third, what is their compass direction; fourth, how they are clothed. The best answers win provided they are within the specified time. The time allowed should be one minute for observation at each station, and half a minute for each bit of running.
summary: Take a patrol and station its members about in different directions and with different background, according to the colour of their clothes; then take another patrol to judge distance of these points. Two competitors are sent in turn to three different…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Find the North
body: Scouts are posted thirty yards apart, and each lays down his staff on the ground pointing to what he considers the exact north (or south), without using any instrument. The umpire compares each stick with the compass; the one who guesses nearest wins. This is a useful game to play at night or on sunless days as well as sunny days.
summary: Scouts are posted thirty yards apart, and each lays down his staff on the ground pointing to what he considers the exact north (or south), without using any instrument. The umpire compares each stick with the compass; the one who guesses nearest wins. This is…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Dispatch Running
body:
A scout is given a dispatch to take to the headquarters of a besieged town, which may be a real town (village, farm, or house), and he must return with a receipt for it. He must wear a coloured rag 2ft. long pinned on to his shoulder. He must start at least four miles away from the town he is going to. Besiegers who have to spot him can place themselves where they like, but must not go nearer to the headquarters' building than three hundred yards. (Best to give certain boundaries that they know or can recognise.) Anyone found within that limit by the umpire will be ruled out as shot by the defenders at headquarters. The dispatch runner can use any ruse he likes, except dressing up as a woman, but he must always wear the red rag on his shoulder. To catch him, the enemy must get the red rag from him. Ten hours may be allowed as the limit of time, by which the dispatch runner should get his message to headquarters and get back again to the starting-point with the receipt. This game may also be made a life-and-death venture, in which case any scout who volunteers to risk his life (i.e. his scout's badge) in getting through with a dispatch, gains the badge "For Merit" if he wins; but if he fails, he loses his scout's badge (fleurs-de-lis), and cannot get it again, although he may still remain a member of the corps. The enemy win three marks each if they spot him, and lose three marks if he succeeds. To win a badge of merit there must be not less than two patrols out against him. A similar game can be played in a city, but requires modifications to suit the local conditions.

For Exploration Practice, see Appendix, Part VI., for imitating exploring expedition in Africa, Arctic regions, etc.
summary: A scout is given a dispatch to take to the headquarters of a besieged town, which may be a real town (village, farm, or house), and he must return with a receipt for it. He must wear a coloured rag 2ft. long pinned on to his shoulder. He must start at least…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: The Struggle
body:
Two players face each other about a yard apart, stretch arms out sideways, lock fingers of both hands, and lean towards each other till their chests touch, push chest to chest, and see who can drive the other back to the wall of the room or on to a goal line. At first a very short struggle is sufficient to set their hearts pumping, but after practice for a few days the heart grows stronger and they can go on for a long time.

The "Struggle" for Strengthening the Heart.
summary: Two players face each other about a yard apart, stretch arms out sideways, lock fingers of both hands, and lean towards each other till their chests touch, push chest to chest, and see who can drive the other back to the wall of the room or on to a goal line.…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Wrist Pushing
body:
"Wrist Pushing" by one man alone. Stand with both your arms to the front about level with the waist, cross your wrists so that one hand has knuckles up, the other knuckles down. Clench the fists.

Now make the lower hand press upwards and make the upper hand press downwards.

Press as hard as you can with both wrists gradually, and only after great resistance let the lower push the upper one upwards till opposite your fore-head, then let the upper press the lower down, the lower one resisting all the time.

These two exercises, although they sound small and simple, if carried out with all your might, develop most muscles in your body and especially those about the heart. They should not be carried on too long at a time, but should be done at frequent intervals during the day for a minute or so.

"Wrist Pushing" can also be played by two boys half facing each other, each putting out the wrist nearest to his opponent, at arm's length; pressing it against the other's wrist and trying to turn him round backwards.
summary: "Wrist Pushing" by one man alone. Stand with both your arms to the front about level with the waist, cross your wrists so that one hand has knuckles up, the other knuckles down. Clench the fists. Now make the lower hand press upwards and make the upper hand…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Doctoring
body: "Doctoring"—each scout in turn acts as an explorer or missionary, with a few simple remedies. Three patients are brought to him in succession to be treated, each having a different disease or injury. He has to advise or show what treatment should be carried out.
summary: "Doctoring"—each scout in turn acts as an explorer or missionary, with a few simple remedies. Three patients are brought to him in succession to be treated, each having a different disease or injury. He has to advise or show what treatment should be carried…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Knight Errantry
body: Scouts go out singly, or in pairs, or as a patrol. If in a town, to find women or children in want of help, and to return and report, on their honour, what they have done. If in the country call at any farms or cottages and ask to do odd jobs—for nothing. The same can be made into a race called a "Good Turn" race.
summary: Scouts go out singly, or in pairs, or as a patrol. If in a town, to find women or children in want of help, and to return and report, on their honour, what they have done. If in the country call at any farms or cottages and ask to do odd jobs—for nothing. The…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Risking Life
body: Call for volunteers for some dangerous enterprise, such as "Dispatch Running," or some other game made dangerous by the condition that if the scout selected to do the dangerous job fails he will lose his life; that is, will forfeit his scout's badge permanently. If he succeeds he may get up to 15 marks towards a badge of merit.
summary: Call for volunteers for some dangerous enterprise, such as "Dispatch Running," or some other game made dangerous by the condition that if the scout selected to do the dangerous job fails he will lose his life; that is, will forfeit his scout's badge…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Bowmanship
body: Crossbow shooting. Scouts should, if possible, make their own crossbows.
summary: Crossbow shooting. Scouts should, if possible, make their own crossbows.

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Longbowmanship
body: "Longbowmanship" as by the archers of the Middle Ages. Scouts to make their own bows and arrows if possible. Read Aylward's doings in "The White Company."
summary: "Longbowmanship" as by the archers of the Middle Ages. Scouts to make their own bows and arrows if possible. Read Aylward's doings in "The White Company."

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Quarter Staff Play
body: "Quarter Staff Play" with scouts' staves, as played by the yeomen and apprentices in old days.
summary: "Quarter Staff Play" with scouts' staves, as played by the yeomen and apprentices in old days.

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Dragging Race
body: A line of patients of one patrol are laid out at one hundred yards distance from start. Another patrol, each carrying a rope, run out, tie ropes to the patients, and drag them in. Time taken of last in. Patrols change places. The one which completes in shortest time wins. Knots must be correctly tied, and patients' coats laid out under their heads.
summary: A line of patients of one patrol are laid out at one hundred yards distance from start. Another patrol, each carrying a rope, run out, tie ropes to the patients, and drag them in. Time taken of last in. Patrols change places. The one which completes in…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Shoot Out
body: Two patrols compete. Targets: Bottles or bricks set up on end to represent the opposing patrol. Both patrols are drawn up in line at about 20 to 25 yards from the targets. At the word "fire" they throw stones at the targets. Directly a target falls the umpire directs the corresponding man of the other patrol to sit down—killed. The game goes on, if there are plenty of stones, till the whole of one patrol is killed. Or a certain number of stones can be given to each patrol, or a certain time limit, say one minute.
summary: Two patrols compete. Targets: Bottles or bricks set up on end to represent the opposing patrol. Both patrols are drawn up in line at about 20 to 25 yards from the targets. At the word "fire" they throw stones at the targets. Directly a target falls the umpire…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: French and English, or Tug of War
body: "French and English," or "Tug of War."—One patrol against another.
summary: "French and English," or "Tug of War."—One patrol against another.

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: The Storming of Badajoz
body:
One patrol (French) mounts on a very strong kitchen-table, or bank, and holds it against all comers. The British attack, and try to gain possession of the fortress by pulling the defenders off. Defenders may have half their number on the ground behind the "rampart." If the defenders pull a Briton over the rampart on to the ground behind he is dead. No hitting or kicking allowed.

[Badajoz was a Spanish fortress held by 5,000 French and Spaniards. It was attacked, and stormed, and taken by the British, who lost 3,500 in the assault, on March 17th, 1812.]
summary: One patrol (French) mounts on a very strong kitchen-table, or bank, and holds it against all comers. The British attack, and try to gain possession of the fortress by pulling the defenders off. Defenders may have half their number on the ground behind the…

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Relay Race
body: One patrol pitted against another to see who can get a message sent a long distance in shortest time by means of relays of runners (or cyclists). The patrol is ordered out to send in three successive notes, or tokens (such as sprigs of certain plants), from a point, say, two miles distant or more. The leader in taking his patrol out to the spot drops scouts at convenient distances, who will then act as runners from one post to the next and back. If relays are posted in pairs messages can be passed both ways.

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Flag Raiding
body:
(from "Aids to Scouting", 1s. Gale & Polden).

Two or more patrols on each side.

Each side will form an outpost within a given tract of country to protect three flags (or at night three lanterns two feet above ground), planted not less than 200 yards (100 yards at night) from it. The protecting outpost will be posted in concealment either altogether or spread out in pairs not more than 80 yards apart. It will then send out scouts to discover the enemy's position. When these have found out where the outpost is they try and creep round out of sight till they can get to the flags and bring them away to their own line. One scout may not take away more than one flag.

This is the general position of a patrol on such an outpost:

Outpost.

Any scout coming within 50 yards of a stronger party will be put out of action if seen by the enemy; if he can creep by without being seen it is all right.

Scouts posted to watch as outposts cannot move from their ground, but their strength counts as double, and they may send single messengers to their neighbours or to their own scouting party.

An umpire should be with each outpost and with each scouting patrol.

At a given hour operations will cease, and all will assemble at the given spot to hand in their reports. The following marks would be awarded:

    For each flag or lamp captured

    and brought in 5 marks

    For each report or sketch of the

    position of the enemy's outposts Up to 5 marks

    For each report of movement of

    enemy's scouting patrols 2 marks

The side which makes the biggest total wins.

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: Scouting Race
body:
Instructor stations three individuals or groups, each group differently clothed as far as possible, and carrying different articles (such as stick, bundle, paper, etc.) at distances from 300 to 1,200 yards from starting point. If there are other people about, these groups might be told to kneel on one knee, or take some such attitude to distinguish them from passers-by. He makes out a circular course of three points for the competitors to run, say about 1/4 mile, with a few jumps if possible.

The competitors start and run to No. 1 point. Here the umpire tells them the compass-direction of the group they have to report on. Each competitor on seeing this group writes a report showing—

1. How many in the group.

2. How clothed or how distinguishable.

3. Position as regards any landmark near them.

4. Distance from his own position.

He then runs to the next point and repeats the same on another group, and so on; and finally he runs with his report to the winning post.

Marks.—Full marks, 5 for each correct and complete description of a group—that is an aggregate of 15 marks for the course. One mark deducted for every ten seconds later than the first boy handing in his report at the winning post. Marks or half marks deducted for mistakes or omissions in reports.

author: Robert Baden-Powell
title: On Trek
body:
Make a trek through Central Africa—each scout carrying his kit and food packed in a bundle on his head; walk in single file with scout 200 yards out in front and find the way; he makes scout signs as to the road to follow; make bridge over stream or raft over lake: corduroy or faggots in boggy ground: leave signs and notes for any parties who may follow by day or night.

To teach your scouts, individually, ideas of time and distance, send each out in a different direction on some such order as this. "Go two miles to North-north-east. Write a report to show exactly where you are (with sketch map if possible, to explain it.) Bring in your report as quickly as possible."

Then test by ordnance maps or otherwise to see how far he was out of the distance and direction ordered.

Send out Scouts in pairs, to compete each pair against the other. Each pair to be started by a different route to gain the same spot, finding the way by map, and to reach the goal without being seen by the others on the way.

This develops map reading, eye for country, concealment, look-out, etc.

For judging time. Send out scouts in different directions, each with a slip of paper, to say how long he is to be away, say seven minutes for one, ten for another, and so on.

Note down his exact time of starting, and take it again on his return. Scouts must be put on their honour not to consult watches or clocks.

N.B.—Many of these games and practices can be carried out in town just as well as in the country.
